lawyer:
Mr. M. H. Khandker, Senior Advocate (Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali, Advocate with him) instructed by Mr. Sharifuddin Chaklader, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Appellants.
Mr. Sk. Afzalur Rahrnan, Advocate, instructed by Mr. Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ------ For respondent Nos. 1(a) to 1(h) & 2-5.
parties:
Abdul Matin & ors ------ Appellants
VS
Shuruj Mia, being dead his heirs: Taibunnessa & Ors ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J:- This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment in Civil Revision No.1163 of 1978.

2. Plaintiffs are the appellants. They filed Title Suit No.1974 in the 1st Court of Munsif, Maulvibazar, Sylhet against the respondents praying for declaration of their right of way over the suit lands, a pathway, and for permanent injunction restraining the defendants from causing any damage thereto and/or in the alternative interfering with plaintiffs access over the suit property.

3. The plaintiffs claimed that they and the other inhabitants of the locality, have been using the suit pathway from time immemorial and the pathway leads to the main road of the locality. They made improvement of the same at their own costs and it is the only and unavoidable way to reach the public road. The suit pathway had been recorded wrongly as cultivable land along with its contiguous lands and taking advantage of such recording the principal defendants are trying to change the nature of the pathway and also to interfere with the plaintiffs' right of way. The defendants contended that it is a ridge of its contiguous cultivable lands. There are convenient ways joining the two main roads of the locality and neither the plaintiffs nor other inhabitants of the locality used the suit land as a pathway. The plaintiffs have filed the suit out of grudge and enmity and hence it is liable to be dismissed.

4. The trial court on consideration of the evidence and the report of the Advocate Commissioner came to the conclusion that

"There might be a lot of pathways open for the people of the locality but I have no reason to reject the plaintiffs' claim which they proved to have been using from time immemorial." The learned Munsif considered the plaintiffs' claim "that they along with some other inhabitants of the locality have been using the suit pathway as of easement right from time immemorial." In this view of the matter, the suit was decreed. "The plaintiffs' right of easement over the suit pathway be declared."

5. On appeal the Appellate Court considered the evidence exhaustively and found that the plaintiffs had recently purchased the plot in the locality, but he did not exhibit his kabala before the Court. He purchased his homestead plots Nos. 2628 and 2629 in 1972. The suit was instituted on 24.9.74 "claiming easement right on the suit lands. In cross examination the plaintiffs admitted that a new pathway had been constructed through plot Nos. 2636, 2637, 2640, 2641, 2642 and 2643. In this view of the matter the Appellate Court below found that the plaintiffs must have constructed the pathway after put chase of the homestead. It was noticed that there was nothing before the Court to hold that the vendors of the plaintiffs enjoyed right of way by easement over the suit land. The Appellate Court below then concluded "plaintiffs failed to prove that they enjoyed any right of easement over the suit land for the period prescribed by law." In this view of the matter, the appeal was allowed and the decree passed by the trial Court was set aside.

6. The plaintiffs filed a second appeal along with Civil Revision No.1163 of 1978. Both were disposed of by the same judgment. The only contention that was made before the High Court Division was that the learned Additional District Judge acted illegally in reversing the decision of the learned Munsif without discussing evidence adduced by the respective parties. The High Court Division considered that the plaintiffs were only recent purchasers and in the absence of clear evidence that their predecessors in interest used the alleged pathway in terms of section 15 of the Easement Act, the plaintiffs could not get the decree as prayed for. The learned Single Judge concluded that mere existence of a pathway or the fact of its user even for a long time does not give rise to a right of easement unless there is clear evidence to show that the right of way was exercised peaceably and openly as of right and without interruption for a period of 20 years. In this view of the matter, the second appeal was dismissed along with the rule which was also discharged.

7. Leave was granted to consider the contention that the High Court Division wrongly assumed that the plaintiffs' suit was for declaration of their easement right over the suit lands and erred in law in applying of section 15 of the Easements Act. It was also submitted that the learned Single Judge erred in not holding that the suit path being a village path joining two other pathways on its two ends, no question of easement is involved herein.

8. Mr. M.H. Khandker, learned Counsel appearing for the plaintiffs argued that the Courts below have made a wrong approach throughout by taking the view that it was suit for easement under the Easements Act without noting the prayer in the plaint that it was a customary right that the plaintiffs were claiming. The point is attractive no doubt.

9. Easement Act, 1882 deals with customary easement. Easement Act does not deal with customary right. It refers to customary rights no doubt, but that is for the purpose of making it abundantly clear that while the Act governs the former it has no .concern with the later. The Rajasthan High Court cited Fredrick Peacock who in his well known treatise on the law relating to Easements in British India (page 203) pointed out the real distinction between the two rights. It says:

Customary easements, as they are called in 5.18 of the Indian Easements Act, should be distinguished from the customary rights referred to in 5.2 Cl. (b) of the same Act. The latter are rights arising by custom, but unappurtenant to a dominant tenement. No fixed period of enjoyment is necessary to establish these rights, but the custom must be reasonable and certain."

(AIR 1965 Raj. 219)

The Easements Act was not applicable throughout India, but even then the principles were taken for deciding the cases on the Act to embody the principia of equity and good conscience. See Shiv Dyal Vs. Ram Das AIR 1926Lah. 473 Karman Hai Vs. Ghulam Mustafa AIR 1927 Lah 492 and Mirza Ahmad Jan Vs. Ghulam Hassan AIR 1944 Lah 417. In Nunia Mal vs. Maha Dev AIR 1962 Punjab 299 it was observed:

There is an imposing array of authority for the view that in those parts of the country where Indian Easements Act is not in operation, there is no reason why the principles underlying the provisions of the Indian Act, should not be followed in so far as they embody the rules of equity, justice and good conscience.

What Mr. Khandkar canvassed was that the plaintiffs claimed customary right and not customary easement. Hence the Courts below while approaching the case made an erroneous decision by taking in view the principles of Easements Act. The submission is devoid of any substance because it makes a distinction without any difference.

10. Sections 2 and 4 read with section 18 of the Easement Act will clarify the position. In section 2 it has been made clear that a customary right is different from a customary easement and the Easements Act does not at all, deal with it. Again the definition of easement given in section 4 clarifies that an easement is always appurtenant to the dominant tenement and inseparably attached to it and cannot be severed from it. There can be no easement without dominant tenement and a servient tenement Section 18 deals with customary easement and it says that easement may be acquired by virtue of local custom. But it is completely different from customary right because customary right is not an easement.

11. On perusal of the three judgments, namely, trial Court, Appellate Court and the High Court Division it becomes clear what the plaintiffs claimed was customary right and not customary easement. Although we did not have the opportunity of going through the pleadings but this much appears to be the position that there was slight confusion in the Courts below as to what relief was claimed by the plaintiffs.

“ভুমি বাদীগণের পূর্ববর্তী ও পূর্বাধীকারী অনুক্রমে স্মরণাতীত কাল হইতে শতাধিত বৎসরের উধ্ব কালের বাড়ী হইতে বাহির হইয়া হাল, ভার, গো, মহিষ, শবজিবিকাদি সহ চলাচলের একমাত্র ও অলঙ্গনীয় রত্ন স্বত্বা রাস্তা রকম ভূমি থাকা বা প্রচার হওয়ার।”

The prayer as quoted above shows the claim was or customary right and not customary easement.

12. Mr. M.H. Khandker, learned Counsel for the appellants, has made much of his grievance out of this apparent distinction but on scrutiny the submission appears to be on a distinction without any difference.

<u>13. Although the learned Munsif decreed the suit he has not given his reasons for so doing in his judgment the burden of his decision appears to be the report of the Advocate Commissioner but how such pathway had become the public pathway and since when and how the custom was established is not found in the Trial Court judgment. The Appellate Court below kept the plot number in view and found on evidence that the plaintiffs could at best make out a case of two year's user. It observed:</u>

<u>"It appears that the plffs, enjoyed the alleged dominant heritage only for about 2 years before the institution of the suit".</u>

<u>Plaintiffs purchased the suit lands in 1972 and filed the-suit in 1974 and curiously enough the plaintiffs did not produce their documents of purchase before the Court. The Appellate Court below observed, "The presumption is that the plaintiffs having been aware that document would go against their claim did not produce it before the Court. There is nothing before the Court to hold that their Vendors enjoyed any right of way by way of easement over the suit land." The learned Single Judge noticed that the plaintiffs were recent purchaser and concluded that unless there was clear evidence to show that, the right of way was exercised peaceably and openly from time immemorial no relief can be claimed.</u>

<u>14. Analysis of the evidence aforesaid shows that notwithstanding confusion as to the nature of the relief that was claimed, the decision arrived at by the Appellate Court below was correct and that was affirmed by the High Court Division. Such, confusion are the results of the pleadings and instances can be found in the decision of Parbhawati Devi vs. ahendra Narain Singh AIR 1981 Patna 133 and Harisadhan De vs. Radhika Prosad AIR 1938 Cal, 202. The casement being a right which is super-added to the ordinary common law incidents of the ownership of a dominant tenement and which connotes a corresponding burden on a servient tenement can only be created by grant or by statute. An apparent exception to this rule is a customary casement, State of Bihar vs. Subodh Gopal AIR 1968 SC 281 it was noticed:</u>

<u>"An apparent exception to this rule is a customary easement. But a customary easement is not an easement in the true sense of that expression. A customary easement arises in favour of an indeterminate class of persons such as residents of a locality or members of a certain community, and though not necessarily annexed in the ownership of land, it is enforceable as a right to do and continue to do something upon land or as a right to prevent and continue to prevent something being done upon land. Sanction for its enforceability being in custom, the right must satisfy all the tests which a local custom for recognition by courts must satisfy." This being the nature of customary easement, the claim for customary right must be established on cogent grounds e.g. long-standing custom.</u>

15. The upshot of the discussion is that they failed to prove their customary right on evidence and the suit is liable to be dismissed for such reason. Precisely that was done by the High Court Division and the Appellate Court below.

In the result, therefore, this appeal is dismissed. There will be no order as to costs.

End.

Vs

full_judgment:
This Rule calls in question the legality and propriety of the judgment and order dated 22.10.89 passed by Sub-Judge, Chittagong, in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 125 of 1983 reversing the Judgment and order dated 20.3.83 passed by the Assistant Judge (Munsif) 1st Court, Chittagong in Pre-emption Case No. 608 of 1979.

2. Facts giving rise to this Rule may briefly be put thus:

Opposite party No. 1 pre-emptor petitioner filed the pre-emption case being Miscellaneous Case No. 608 of 1979 in the Court of Munsif, 1st Court, Chittagong contending, inter alia, that the land described in Schedule 1 of the application originally belonged to Tamizuddin as per CS record of right and after the death of said Tamizuddin his son Rahamatullah inherited the same and aforesaid Rahamatullah sold these schedule land to Abdul Bari Sowdagar. On 9.3.1929. Abdul Bari who subsequently sold the schedule land to his grandsons Abdul Gafur and Abdul Gaffar and put them in khas possession thereto. Both brothers purchased the same in 1/2 and 1/2 share and out of that share Abdul Gafur sold his purchased portion to Abdul Jabbar and Bashir Ahmed by registered sale deed dated 10.9.59 and since the purchase both the brothers namely Abdul Jabbar and Bashir Ahmed were in possession with another sharer. After the death of Abdul Jabbar petitioner and opposite parties No. 4 and 7 inherited the land and as such they became co-sharer of the land and they are in possession thereof.

3. Thus the pre-emptor is a co-sharer of the schedule land by inheritance along with other co-sharer including opposite party No. 2. All are co-sharer including opposite party No. 2. All the co-sharers of the entire land amicably are in possession as per their convenience.

4. Opposite Party No. 1 pre-emptor has been residing in Qatar, Middle East for considerable period of time in connection with his service and in August, 1977 he came back to this country and on 2.12.79 pre-emptor petitioner appeared in schedule land and found pre-emtpee purchaser petitioner cutting within half ripe paddy there from. On inquiry from pre-emptee purchaser petitioner, opposite party No. 1 came to learn that he had purchased the disputed land from opposite party No. 2 long before to construct a house thereon. At this the petitioner opposite party No. 1 asked him about the particulars of sale deed but opposite party No. 1 expressed his inability to supply him the particulars. This is the 1st time that pre-emptor opposite party No. 1 came to know of the transfer from opposite party No. 2 and before that pre-emptor opposite party No.1 was quite in dark about the fact of transfer.

5. Thereafter opposite party No.1 applied for urgent certified copy of the sale deed on the following day and having gone through the contents of the same came to learn in details about the fact of transfer. From the sale deed it transpires that opposite party No. 2 executed the sale deed in favour of pre-emptor petitioner on 13.3.77 at a consideration of Taka 10,100.00 and thereafter pre-emptor opposite party No. 1 tendered the consideration money with the compensation money but refused to accept the petitioner's offer. Thereafter the opposite party pre-emptor filed the pre-emption case.

6. Opposite Party No. 1 is a co-sharer by inheritance, whereas the transferee opposite party is a stranger purchaser. No notice of the transfer was ever served on pre-emptee petitioner. There is no impediment of law if any petitioner is allowed to pre-empt the land as the quantum of land under his possession will not exceed the ceiling fixed by law. Present petitioner who figured as pre-emptor opposite party in original pre-emption case filed written objection contending, inter alia, that there is no cause of action against this opposite party, that the allegations made in the pre-emption petition are false, frivolous and motivated one. That pre-emption case is hopelessly barred by limitation inasmuch as the impugned sale deed was registered on 6.10.78 and the pre-emption case was filed on 19.12.79 i.e., more than one year from the date of registration, that the opposite party No. 1 is in the know of transfer from very beginning inasmuch as he was at home on the date of kabala sought to be pre-empted. It is further stated in the written objection that purchaser pre-emptee-petitioner transferred his right, title, interest in the case land to his wife by registered deed of gift which was executed on 24.11.79 and registered on 23.7.81 and that the deed of gift having been executed on 23.7.81 i.e. prior to the filing of the pre-emption case there is nothing left to be pre-empted. In view of this fact the pre-emption case is not maintainable.

7. Both parties led evidence in support of their respective contention and on consideration of such evidence the learned Munsif held that the application is barred by time and being of that view he disallowed the pre-emption case.

8. Being aggrieved by that Judgment and order petitioner preferred an appeal before the District Judge, Chittagong and the appeal was heard by Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong and on reappraisal of the evidence on record he could not concur with the view taken by the trial Court on the point of limitation and having made proper analysis of evidence came to the finding that pre-emptor petitioner was not in the know of transfer from the beginning and that he acquired the knowledge of transfer on 2.12.79 and thereafter obtained the certified copy of the disputed sale deed and filed the pre-emption case on 19.12.79. The learned Subordinate Judge further held that pre-emptor petitioner was not in the know of transfer as he was serving in Qatar in Middle-East and his being of that view the learned Subordinate "Judge held that the pre-emption case is not hit by limitation as it was filed within 4 months from the date of knowledge, He being of that view held that pre-emption case was filed within time and allowed the appeal on setting aside the Judgment and order passed by the trial Court. The pre-emption case was allowed by the learned Subordinate Judge.

9. Being aggrieved by the Judgment and order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge opposite party pre-emptee moved the revisional jurisdiction of this court and obtained the present Rule.

10. The learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptee petitioner submits that the pre-emptee petitioner was in the know of transfer from the very beginning inasmuch as when the transfer took place he was in his native village and that at the time of transfer of the disputed land he was in Qatar is a false and fabricated story. It is further submitted that the application for pre-emption under section 96 of the SAT Act was filed on 19.12.79 and the disputed sale deed was registered on 6.10.78 and thus it is patent that Miscellaneous Case was filed more than one year after registration of the sale deed and that being the position the trial Court rightly held the petition to be out of time. The learned Advocate further urged that prior to the filing of the pre-emption case pre-emptee petitioner transferred this right, title in the disputed land by registered deed of gift dated 24.11.79 to his wife opposite party No. 8 and this transfer on the basis of deed of gift having been made prior to the filing of the pre-emption case there remains nothing to be pre-empted and in this view of the matter the pre-emption case should be held to be not maintainable.

11. In reply to this contention the learned Advocate appearing for pre-emptor opposite party submits that the trial court grossly misread the evidence on the point of limitation inasmuch as he failed to appreciate the evidence on the point that disputed transfer took place when pre-emptor opposite party was not in this country and that he was serving in Qatar in Middle East, consequently he did not have any knowledge about the disputed transfer. The learned Advocate continued to urge that pre-emptor opposite party is admittedly co-sharer of the case land and the opposite party transferor and transferee are in the know of this fact but despite this fact notice of transfer was not issued and served on pre-emptor opposite party who thus falls under the category of non-notified co-sharer and as such he is entitled to file the application within 4 months from the date of knowledge as contemplated by section 96 of SAT Act. The learned Advocate further urged that the subsequent transfer as per deed of gift is a conclusive transaction resorted to with a malafide motive to defeat the right of pre-emption. It is further submitted that no improvement was effected on the land and as such both the Courts below did not award any cost towards the alleged improvement.

12. I have been taken through the judgment pronounced by the court below as well as other materials on record. I propose to take up firstly the point relating to limitation, Pre-emptor opposite party while being examined by the trial Court as PW 1 asserted in his evidence that while he was in Qatar in Middle East opposite party No. 2 (transferor) made the transfer in favour of opposite party No. 1 who is stranger to the case holding and being away from this country pre-emptor opposite party did not have the occasion to know of this transfer. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence came to the finding that opposite party failed to prove that pre-emptor petitioner was in the know of the transfer from the very beginning and that he was in this country and he was residing at the relevant time in Qatar. Thus it is evident from the finding of the trial Court that evidence adduced by the opposite party pre-emptee was totally insufficient to fix the preemptor petitioner with the knowledge of transfer. The 1st appellate Court also on scrutiny of record found photo copy of the passport but it was not made Exhibit. The learned 1st Appellate Court also observed in judgment that pre-emptor petitioner asserted in his evidence that he went to Qatar in 1976 and he served there for 18 months and thereafter he returned to his native village. The evidence of PW 2 lends corroborative support to the evidence of PW 1 on the point that pro-emptor petitioner went to Qatar in the year 1976 and came back in the year 1979. Evidence of PW 1 Md. Ali also lent corroboration on this point and relying on this evidence of 3 PWs referred above, the 1st Appellate Court came to the finding that pre-emptor petitioner was in Qatar when the disputed transfer took place. Admittedly pre-emptor petitioner is a co-sharer of the case holding by inheritance. But no notice of the disputed transfer was served on him and as such he is entitled as per provision of section 96 of SAT Act to file pre-emption came within 4 months from the date of knowledge 1st appellate Court on proper analysis of evidence case to a finding that pre-emptor petitioner came to know of the transfer on 2.12.79 for 1st time and the pre-emption case was filed on 19.11.79. Thus it is evident that the pre-emption case was filed within 4 months from the date of knowledge.

13. It is settled law that the initial onus of proving a case is always on the petitioner and if the petitioner discharges that onus and makes out a case, the onus shifts on the opposite party to prove circumstances which would disentitle petitioner to that relief. In the instant case the opposite party failed to discharge the onus in the matter proving the circumstances that pre-emptor petitioner was in the know of the transfer from the beginning and that he was in his native village when transfer took place. Both the courts below came to a concurrent finding on the fact that pre-emptor petitioner was away from his native village when the transfer took place and that he falls within category of non-notified co-sharer. So 1st appellate Court rightly held that the application for pre-emption was filed within 4 months from the date of knowledge of transfer and as such it has rightly been held by the 1st appellate Court that pre-emption case is not hit by limitation.

<u>14. Now I pass over to consider that contention urged by the learned Advocate on the point of maintainability. It is submitted by the learned Advocate for the opposite party that the case prima facie is not maintainable inasmuch as prior to filing of the pre-emption case the land was transferred by pre-emptee to his wife opposite party No. 2 by registered deed of gift. In this connection it is to be mentioned that the deed of gift purported to have been executed and registered by pre-emptee opposite party has not been produced in court nor marked as exhibit. It is not known why the primary evidence has been suppressed. It is settled law that primary evidence of document means document itself and it is produced for inspection of the Court when a party seeks to prove the contents of document, the best "evidence rules" requires that party should produce the original", of that primary evidence thereof. A party cannot be allowed to defeat his opponent on the strength of document which he has in his possession and not produced. Therefore where a document is in possession of a party he will not be permitted to put any question as to the contents of it to his adversary. The alleged deed of gift has not been produced in court and since it did not see the light of the day it cannot be presumed as it is a deed of gift and that it was registered prior to the filing of the pre-emption case.</u>

<u>15. The learned Advocate for the opposite party pre-emptee sought to point out drawing very attention to para 4 of the application filed by pre-emptor opposite party for impleading the donee opposite party No. 8 as party. In other words the learned Advocate relied on secondary evidence. But secondary evidence is not admissible in evidence, when a primary evidence is available and lying in possession of the party concerned.</u>

16. It is further urged by the learned Advocate for the pre-emptee opposite party that despite the existence of evidence on record regarding improvement effected on disputed land, both the Courts below did not take cognizance of it. The trial Court framed an issue on the point of improvement. But on consideration of evidence on this point the trial Court held that pre-emptee petitioner failed to prove any improvement on the disputed land. He noticed that schedule of the Hibanama wherein the disputed land has been described as nal land i.e. agriculture land and further it appears an injunction was issued in this pre-emption proceeding and it was locally inspected by an Advocate Commissioner, All these materials were considered by the trial Court and the trial Court opined that opposite party pre-emptee ignoring the injunction order effected some improvement and as such he is not eligible to claim compensation. The 1st appellate Court also concurred with the view of the trial Court on this point and in view of this fact opposite party pre-emptee is not entitled to claim any compensation on account of alleged improvement.

17. Thus on consideration of the entire material on record I am of the opinion that the appellate Court did not commit any error of law in allowing Misc. Appeal referred above and as such his Judgment and order do not call for any interference.

In the result, the Rule is discharged with costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Fazle Munim, C.J:-This appeal arises from Civil Revision No. 195 of 1982 decided by a Single Judge of the High Court Division, Dhaka (Ranadhir Sen, J;) on 14th February 1983.

2. Plaintiff-respondent filed Title Suit No. 45 of 1977 in the 1st Court of Munsif at Madaripur for a declaration that the auction sale by the Circle Officer, (Revenue), Rajoir, Madaripur on 9th June 1967 in respect of 9.14 decimals of land as described in the Kha Schedule land of the plaint in Case No. 1145 RA. of 1959-60 and the lease granted of the same property on its basis to defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are illegal, void and without jurisdiction.

3. Facts of the case according to plaintiffs are: The disputed land appertaining to RS khatian No. 517 of mouza ShirajKathi originally belonged to the predecessors of some of the plaintiffs, and preform defendant Nos. 4-19. The rent roll was not correctly prepared. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 in collusion with Tahsilder managed to file a Certificate Case No. 1145 RA. of 1959-60 and by suppression of notices and sale proclamation managed to purchase the land in the name of the Government. Some of the certificate debtors were already dead. After the emergence of Bangladesh plaintiffs filed objection before Circle Officer (Revenue), Madaripur. Miscellaneous Case No. XII-37 of 1973-74 was started and on 27th July, 1974 Tk.325.80 was deposited. The disputed auction sale was then set aside by the Circle Officer (Revenue), Madaripur. Defendant No. 1 managed to take settlement of the disputed land on the strength of certificate sale in Miscellaneous Case No. XII-M-717 of 1969-70 and No. XII-M-718 of 1969-70. Further, defendant Nos. 1 and 2 never got possession of the land though, however, he managed to get the order of setting aside the sale cancelled in case No. XIII-37 of 1973-74. Defendant No. 1 also instituted several criminal cases against the plaintiffs.

4. Defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 filed two separate written statements contending, inter alia, that the suit as framed was not maintainable and barred by limitation and also pleaded the bar of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as no consequential relief was prayed for. According to defendants, Certificate Case No. 1145 R.A. of 1959-60 was started for arrear of rents and the disputed land was sold in auction on 9th June 1961 and sale was confirmed on 10th August 1961. The land was purchased by the Government and possession was delivered on 4th November, 1961. After the disputed land was settled with defendant Nos. 1 and 2 possession was delivered to them in Case No. XII-M-717 of 1969-70 and No. XII-M-718 of 1969-70. Two kabuliyats were executed by the defendants and registered on 21st June 1974. Defendants asserted possession of 6 acres of land. They denied title and possession of plaintiffs.

5. Suit was dismissed by the trial Court which decided the relevant issues against the plaintiffs. Its decision was affirmed by the first appellate Court which held that the suit was barred by limitation and not maintainable.

6. Being aggrieved plaintiff-respondents moved the High Court Division under Section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Rule issued in Civil Revision Case No. 195 of 1982 was made absolute in part. The learned Judge of the High Court Division held that the lease granted in favour of defendant nos. 1 and 2 was false, fraudulent, null and void. Though, however, the learned Judge did not set aside the auction sale.

7. Defendant-appellants moved this Court and obtained special leave to appeal on the following terms:

"Mr. Md. Nurul Huq, learned Advocate- on-Record has urged that the High Court Division erred in holding that the record was silent about delivery of possession while Ext. A-1 (2) clearly shows that the possession was delivered as early as on 21.11.61 and as such, the suit which is required to be filed under section 36 of the Public Demands Recovery Act within one year from the date of delivery of such possession but having been filed as late as on 3.2.77 after 16 years was barred by limitation. He also submitted that the suit was clearly barred under proviso (B) of section 36 of the Public Demands Recovery Act which prohibits such a suit while the plaintiffs already agitated the matter before the Certificate Officer under section 23 of the Act and lost the same on 5.12.75. The learned Advocate also contended that the learned Single Judge committed error of law in holding that the physical possession was not necessary to uphold the settlement made by the Government and that only remedy available for the plaintiffs, while the objection under section 23 of the Public Demands Recovery Act being unsuccessful was by way of appeal, revision or review under sections 51, 53 and 55 of the Act and not by filing the present suit."

8. Mr. Md. Nurul Huq, Advocate-on-Record, who appeared on behalf of the defendant-appellants submitted that in view of the provisions of section 36 of the Public Demands Recovery Act which required the plaintiffs suit to be filed within one year from the date of delivery of possession was barred by nearly 16 years. According to him, the delivery of possession was found to have been made on 21st November 1961, whereas plaintiffs' suit was filed on 3rd February 1977. Section 36 of the Public Demands Recovery Act reads as follows:

"36. Notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained, a sale of immovable property in execution of a certificate shall not be held to be void on the ground that the notice required by section 7 has not been served; but a suit may be brought in a Civil Court to recover possession of such property or to set aside such sale on the ground that such notice has not been served, and that the plaintiff has sustained substantial injury by reason of irregularity:

Provided that no such suit shall be entertained-- (a) if instituted more than one year from the date on which possession of the property was delivered to the purchaser, or

(b) if the certificate-debtor has made appearance in the certificate proceeding, or has applied to the Certificate-officer under section 22 or section 23 to set aside the sale."

9. It also appeared that the plaintiff-respondents had moved the Certificate-officer under section 23 of the Act but lost the case on 5th December 1975. Even counting from this date plaintiffs' suit was filed beyond one year, the suit was, therefore, barred under the provisions of the aforesaid Act. Plaintiff respondents could have resorted to the provisions of appeal, revision or review as contained in sections 51, 53 and 54 of the Act but did not do so. The learned Advocate-on-Record also pointed out that in spite of the concurrent findings of fact regarding the holding of auction sale, confirmation of sale and delivery of possession which appeared in official records, the learned Judge of the High Court Division reversed the decision of the 1st appellate Court. Finally, Mr. Huq submitted that in view of the provisions of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act also the suit was barred as no prayer was made for consequential reliefs. Since the Government took possession of the disputed land in execution of the certificate sale on 4th November 1961 and gave settlement of the same to defendant-appellants on accepting kabuliyats on 3rd November 1974 from them such prayer for consequential reliefs should have been made.

10. Mr. S.S. Halder, Counsel for the plaintiff respondents, submitted that in view of the restoration of Certificate Case No.1145 R.A. of 1959-60 by an order of the Certificate Officer on 20th February 1972 the settlement of the disputed land with the appellants by the acceptance of the kabuliyats dated 3rd June 1974 became illegal. Moreover, the plaintiff-respondents deposited Tk. 325.80 on 27th July 1974. Mr. Halder also assailed the settlement being illegal on the ground that the order of the Circle Officer (Revenue) on 5th December, 1975 cancelling the order of setting aside the auction sale was an ex-parte order. He further submitted that the suit was neither barred by limitation nor barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

11. To determine the respective contentions of the learned Counsels reference to a few dates will be useful in clarifying the true position. Plaintiffs' suit for declaration of their title and for declaration that the auction sale of "Kha" schedule land of the plaint in case No. 1145 R.A. of 1959-60 on 9th June 1961 was false, fraudulent and void was filed on 3.2.77. The progress of this case which culminated in the auction sale, confirmation of sale and delivery of possession appears from the following order sheet, Ext. Al(2):

"15.4.59 : Certificate under section 4 signed. Register and issue notice under section 7 returnable by 21.9.59.

11.2.60 : S.R. received. No payment made and no objection filed. Issue notice under section 46 fixing 5.4.60:

17.4.61 :Notice N/46 duly served. No objection filed. Issue S.P. to be served on the Notice Board Thana Notice Board and Kismat fixing sale on 9.6.61.

9.6.61 : Sale held to-day. No outside bidder. Sold to Government at 2 paisa paid. Put up on 10.8.61 for confirmation of sale.

10.8.61 : 60 days expired from the date of sale. No objection, the sale is confirmed.

21.11.61 : Possession elivered no objection. The case is disposed of. Note in Register."

<u>12. No steps were taken by the plaintiff respondents until after the emergence of Bangladesh, nearly 11 years after the delivery of possession was made in the aforesaid certificate case. The plaintiff respondents filed objection in Miscellaneous Case No. XII-37 of 1973-74 and deposited the aforesaid amount upon which the Circle Officer (Revenue) set aside the auction sale. In the meantime, however, the disputed land which the Government had taken possession of in pursuance of the certificate sate in Miscellaneous Case No. XII-M-717 of 1969-70 and NoXII-M-718 of 1969-70 was settled with the defendant-appellants who executed two registered kabuliyats on 21st June 1974 and since the settlement they have been in possession of the disputed land.</u>

<u>13. Ignoring the clear provisions of law as contained in section 36 of the Public Demands Recovery Act for setting aside an auction sale plaintiff-respondents had, it appears, moved the Circle Officer (Revenue) for setting aside the impugned sale in 1973 and succeeded in obtaining the order for setting aside the sale. This being clearly contrary to law was set aside or cancelled. On 5th December, 1975 the following orders were passed by the Circle Officer (Revenue) vide Ext. AI-3:</u>

<u>"Meno No. 1145 RN69-60</u>

<u>XIII-37/73-74</u>

<u>Back page: 5.12.75: The case is taken up For suo motu decision. It has come to my knowledge that the lands of RS. 517/SA, S.A. khatian No.535 of 79. No Serajkati Mouza were not free from encumbrances as a total area of 6 acres of land under plot Nos. 1193, 1194, 1195, 1196 and 1197 were entitled with one Amjad Ali Sk. and one Zoinuddin Sarder of P.S. Rajoir vide S.C. No. 219/6917 under XIIM/717/69-70.</u>

<u>220/69-70</u>

<u>XIIM-718/69-70 and the cases were approved on 26.3.70 so the petitioners cannot get any benefit of restoration of holding. Hence ordered that the order dated 20.2.74 be cancelled. The petitioners may take shelter in the competent court if they desire. The money deposited by them may be refunded on proper prayer. Inform the party concern and the TDR, Amgaon accordingly."</u>

14. Strangely enough, plaintiff-respondents kept quiet until as late as 3rd February 1977 when they filed the present suit. Even after moving the Circle Officer for setting aside the auction sale which was granted but ultimately cancelled by the Circle Officer on 5th December 1975, plaintiff-respondents did not seek any relief against the order of cancellation within time.

<u>15. So far as the plaintiff-respondents alleged collusion and fraud in holding auction sale they could not substantiate the allegations. The trial Court referred to the evidence regarding issuing of notices and sale proclamation and did not find any irregularity therein. His findings were affirmed by the first appellate Court. Defendant-appellants were not in the picture when the auction sale was held or confirmation and delivery of possession was made. They appeared in the scene in 1974 when settlement of the disputed land was made by the Government by accepting the kabuliyats executed by them on 21st June 1974. As already mentioned above, no fraud as alleged by the plaintiff-respondents has even been proved against either the Government or the defendant-appellants.</u>

<u>16. It appears that by realising the difficulties as discussed above the learned Judge of the High Court Division did not set aside the auction sale but declared the lease granted in favour of defendant appellant Nos.1 and 2 as false, fraudulent, null and void as was prayed for by the plaintiff-respondents. In our opinion, if the auction sale stands, plaintiff respondents can no longer claim any right, title and interest in the disputed land. Since possession was delivered to the Government which made the disputed land khas and were giving eksana leases to different persons during the years beginning from the date of delivery of possession till the Government settled the land with the defendant-appellants. Their right was lost. Whatever legal remedies were available to the plaintiff-respondents for setting aside the auction sale in time were not resorted to by them. They twice got the opportunity to do so, once immediately after the auction sale was held and delivery of possession was made and again in 1972-73 when they came to know of the auction sale. Even after being unsuccessful in setting aside the auction sale which appeared from the order of the Circle Officer (Revenue) on 5th December 1975, plaintiff-respondents did not file the present suit but waited till the period of limitation for filing such a suit expired. In view of the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case and also because no consequential reliefs were sought for by them as required under section 42 of the specific Relief Act the present suit appears to be not maintainable.</u>

17. In the result, the appeal is allowed with costs and the judgment of the High Court Division is set aside and that of the trial Court is restored.

End.

parties:
Commissioner of Taxes, E Zone, Dhaka ----- Appellants.
Vs.
Mallick Brothers ----- Respondent.
case_source: From the Judgment and Order dated 8-1-84 & 10-1-84 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in Application Nos. 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 of 1981.
full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury J: These five appeals by special leave are directed against the judgment and order passed by the Division Bench of the High Court Division in Application No.6 of 1981. 

2. The Commissioner of Taxes, East Zone, Dhaka, filed an application under section 66(1) of the Income Tax Act and the question of law was framed thus: 

"Whether on the facts and circumstances of the case the Tribunal was justified in allowing the appeal setting aside the order of the Appellate Joint Commissioner as well as of the Deputy Commissioner under section 18A imposing additional amount of tax and whether notice under section 23 (2) of the Income Tax Act is sufficient for the purpose of determining additional tax under section 18A of the Income Tax Act." 

3. In this case, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes found that the assessee did not comply with the provision of section 18A of the Income Tax Act. Upon the total income of the assessee, the Deputy Commissioner charged an additional amount of tax of Taka 4,689 The assessee filed an appeal before the Appellate Joint Commissioner of Taxes and it was dismissed. 

The assessee then preferred an appeal before the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. The majority decision of the Tribunal was that a fresh notice ought to have been served upon the assessee before imposing additional taxes under section 18A of the Income Tax Act. In this background, the Revenue filed this application under section 66(1) of the Act and framed the question as mentioned above. 

3A. The learned Judges of the High Court Division took the view that a fresh notice was necessary and grolmded such opinion on the principle of natural justice. The learned Judge observed. 
"We hold that in order to levy additional tax u/s 18A of the Income Tax Act fresh notice is necessary because of the fact that the mode of levying of tax u/s 23 (3) and u/s 18A are completely different. The principle of natural justice also demands that while levying additional tax u/s 18A (6) and (8) of the Income Tax act notices are to be served upon the assessee to show cause why the additional tax shall not be levied against the assessee." 

Leave was granted to consider to correctness of the proposition of law laid down by the High Court Division. 

4. Mr AM Mahmudur Rahman, learned Counsel, appearing for the appellant contended that the High Court Division erred in law in taking the view "the modes of levying of tax under sections 23(3) and 18A are completely different." The learned Counsel contended that section 18A is not an independent proceeding apart from regular assessment under sub-section 23(3) and, as such, no fresh notice is required for levying additional taxes. It was contended that additional tax is to be determined on the basis of regular assessment for which notice under sub-section (2) of section 23 had already been served. 

5. Mr Chowdhury Rahman Ali, learned Counsel, appearing for the respondent attempted to justify the view of the High Court Division by citing a decision Commissioner of IT vs Fazlur Rahman (1964) 16 DLR(SC) 506; PLD 1964. SC 410 which was given under section 33- A of the Act and further pointed out the provision of section 29 which postulates the issuance of notice. 

6. The aforesaid decision has no manner of application as it was given under section 33- A and it was held that the opportunity of hearing should be given to the assessee otherwise the proceeding would be void and of no legal effect. Section 23 (2) provides that the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes may issue notice upon the assessee "requiring him on a date to be therein specified either to attend as the office or to produce any evidence." Then sub-section (3) reads as follows: 

"On the day specified in the notice issued under sub-section (2), or as soon after- wards as may be, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, after hearing such evidence as such person may produce and such other evidence as the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes may require on specified points shall, by an order in writing assess the total income of the assessee and determine the sum payable by him on the basis of such assessment." 

Sub-section (4) provides if the assessee fails to make the return required by law or fails to com- ply with the terms of notice etc, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes shall make the assessment to the best of his judgment and determined the sum payable by the assessee on the basis of such assessment. Section 18A (8) reads as under: 

"Where, on making the regular assessment, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes finds that payment of tax was not been made in accordance with the foregoing provisions of this section, additional tax calculated in the manner laid down is sub-section (6) shall be added to the tax as determined on the basis of the regular assessment: 

7. Section 18A has a little history. It provides for advance payment of tax. It was inserted in 1944. The principle of section is the principle of "pay as you earn" that is pay tax by installment in respect of the income of the very year in which the tax paid But this section can- not directly levy tax on the income of the assessment year. The advance payment of tax is only provisional and if after the regular assessment is made the tax paid in advance is found to be in excess of the tax payable, the assessee would be entitled to refund of such tax. Vide section 23B (6) (7). Income is assessed and tax payable is determined under section 23. Assessment may be made (1) on the basis of the return, (ii) on the basis of the evidence adduced and (iii) to the best of the Income Tax Officer's judgment, which is called best judgment assessment. The Privy Council pointed out in Badridas Daga V CIT. 1949 ITR 209 that assessment refers primarily to the computation of the amount of income. Section 18A (8) opens up by saying "where on making the regular assessment the Income Tax Officer finds that no payment of tax has been made in accordance with the provision of section 18A additional tax calculated in the manner laid down in sub-section (6) "shall be added to the tax as determined on the basis of regular assessment. (Emphasis added). The learned Judges of the High Court Division unfortunately overlooked the crucial expression in sub-section (8), namely, "shall be added to the tax as determined on the basis on the regular assessment." Once regular assessment is completed under section 23 then the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes is under statutory obligation to work out the additional tax that is payable if the same has not been paid already. He will calculate it in the manner laid down in sub-section (6) and the total amount shall then be added to the tax on the basis of the regular assessment. Notices are to be given under section 232 (2) and also under other sections of the Income tax Act. The question is whether another notice is to be issued after concluding the regular assessment for determining the additional tax payable. Reading the two sections together we have no hesitation in saying that the law has not provided for another notice for the purpose of section 18A, inasmuch as, it is the continuation of the same proceeding and not a "different proceeding" as viewed by the learned Judges. In this view of the matter, the opinion is that the High Court Division erred in law in taking the view that a separate notice is required for imposing additional tax under section 18A. The other contention that section 29 contemplates a notice is also misconceived. That section deals with notice of demand when the tax is due in consequence of any order and such notice shall specify the sum due. But has nothing to do with the calculation of tax under section 18A. 
	
In the result, therefore, these appeals are allowed and the judgment and order of the High Court Division are set-aside. There will be no order as to costs.

End.

parties:

Vs.
Asstt. Custodian of Enemy Property & Addl. Deputy Commissioner (Rev) patuakhali & others ------ Opp-Parties.
case_source: In the matter of an application under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1906 for sitting aside the Jt. dt. 10.11.83 and decree dt. 16.11.83 passed by the learned Addl. District Judge 1st Patuakhali in Title Appeal No. 34 of 1982, affirming the Judgment dt. 28.1.82 and the decree dt. 27. 2. 82 passed by Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Patuakhali in Title Suit No. 4 of 1982.
full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of defendant No. 1 is directed against a judgment and decree of the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court Patuakhali in Title Appeal No. 34 of 1982 affirming those passed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, 2nd Court, in Title Suit No. 4 of 1982.

2. The facts of the case lie in a narrow compass and may be stated thus :—One Taramoni, the mother of defendant No. 1 Sabitri Barai instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 397 of 1961 in the 1st Court of Munsif, Patuakhali against opposite party No. 2 Surendra Nath Sen for declaration of her title to 5175. acre of land recorded to plot Nos. 7048, 7049, 7050, 7051 and 7047 appertaining to SA Khatian No. 2071 of Mouza Patuakhali. She obtained an exparte decree on the 14th December, 1961. On the 22nd January 1974 opposite party No. 1 the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings), Patuakhali brought a suit being Title Suit No. 12 of 1974 in the 1st Court of Munsif, Patuakhali praying for declaration that the aforesaid decree in Title Suit No. 397 of 1961 was void and not binding upon the plaintiff by reason of fraud. The suit was originally instituted in the First Court of Munsif, Patuakhali but was subsequently transferred to the Second Court of Subordinate Judge of that place and was renumbered as Title Suit No. 4 of 1982. According to the plaintiffs case opposite party No. 2 was the owner of the disputed property. He left the territory now comprised in Bangladesh in 1950 leaving the property in the custody and care of Taramoni. Her son-in-law Bisheswar Barai, taking advantage of the absence of the owner managed to obtain the ex-parte decree upon fraudulent suppression of summons showing a false settlement of the land in suit by opposite party No. 2 in favour of Taramoni, the mother of defendant No. 1. The property was legally and properly declared as Enemy Property in EP Case No. 667 of 1967-68 and leased out to different persons. It was his further case that 0375 acre of land of plot No. 7049 was under requisition and allotted to postal peon Aroj Ali and linesman Arsed Ali but no notice was served upon the Additional Deputy Commissioner (General), Patuakhali.

3. Defendant No. 1 contested the suit denying the allegations made in the plaint. It was contended, inter alia, that the suit was not maintainable, that the plaintiff had no locus standi to file the suit and that the suit was barred by limitation. Her positive case was that Surendra Nath Sen settled the land in suit as Chandina Bhiti with her mother Taramoniin Magh, 1357 BS. Since then she had been in possession of the land erecting dwelling huts. As the land was recorded in the name of opposite party No. 2. Taramoni was constrained to file Title Suit No. 397 of 1961. The Suit was decreed on 14th December, 1961 after due service of summons upon opposite party No. 2. Taramoni having died leaving defendant No. 1 as her only heiress she became the owner thereof and got her name duly mutated in SA Khatian No. 2071/1. Surendra Nath Sen was all along a citizen of erstwhile Pakistan and was never a citizen of India. It was asserted that the property was not an Enemy Property.

4. After the trial the learned Munsif found that the suit was maintainable, that the suit was not barred by limitation and that the plaintiff had proved the claim. Accordingly he decreed the suit on contest against defendant No 1 with cost and exparte against the rest without cost.

5. There was an appeal being Title Appeal No 34 of 1982 to the learned District Judge, Patuakhali. The appeal was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, First Court Patuakhali who affirmed the decision of the trial Court. Being aggrieved defendant No. 1 has obtained the present Rule challenging the propriety of the said judgment and decree.

6. The principal question in this Rule is whether an Assistant Custodian Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) can maintain a suit in 1974 in respect of the properties vested in the Government of Bangladesh under President's Order No 29 of 1972 as amended by PO No. 134 of 1972 and under Act XLV of 1974.

<u>7. Before adverting to the submissions of the learned Advocates of the respective parties it will be useful to trace the legal history which led to the passing of President's Order No. 29 of 1972. On the outbreak of the war between Pakistan and India on the 6th September 1965 the President of erstwhile Pakistan issued a Proclamation of Emergency under clause (1) of Article 30 of the Constitution of Pakistan 1962 and on that very day he promulgated the Defence of Pakistan Ordinance (Ordinance No, XXIII of 1965) in exercise of the power under clause (4) of Article 30 read with clause (2) of Article 131 of the said Constitution to meet the emergency and to provide for special measures to ensure the security, the public safety and interest and the defence of Pakistan and for the trial of certain offences. Section 3(1) of the Ordinance authorised the Central Government to frame Rules there under. Accordingly, the Defence of Pakistan Rules was framed. Rule 182 of the Rules provided, inter alia, for appointment of the Custodian, Deputy Custodians and Assistant Custodians of Enemy Property and the vesting of Enemy Properties in the Custodian.</u>

<u>8. Following an appointment of the Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property, the Governor of East Pakistan under authority delegated to him by the Central Government issued in exercise of the powers conferred by clause (b) of sub-rule (1) of Rule 182 of the said Rules a notification being No. 1199 Genl. dated 3rd December, 1965 which was published in the Dhaka Gazette Extraordinary on the 4th December. 1965. In pursuance of the notification all lands and buildings which were enemy property within the meaning of sub-rule (4) of rule 169 of the Rules and which were not connected with enemy firm at defined in sub-rule (2) of that Rule were vested in the Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) with effect from the date of that order.</u>

9. The Proclamation of Emergency was, however, revoked on the 16th February, 1969 resulting in the repeal of the Defence of Pakistan Ordinance and the Rules framed there under but the provisions of the Defence of Pakistan Rules relating to the control of trading with enemy and the control of enemy firm and the administration of the property belonging to the enemies were made to continue by the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) Ordinance, 1969 (Ordinance No. 1 of 1969).

<u>10. Bangladesh emerged as a Sovereign Independent State on the 26th March, 1971 and under the Laws Continuance Enforcement Order all laws which were in force in the territory now comprised in Bangladesh were continued subject to Proclamation of Independence and to such consequential changes as may be necessary as a result of the creation of the new state of Bangladesh, On the 26th March, 1972 the President of Bangladesh promulgated President's Order No. 29 of 1972 vesting all properties and assets which were vested in the Government of Pakistan or were vested in or managed by any Board constituted by or under any law or in the former Government of East Pakistan in the Government of Bangladesh on and from 26th day of March 1971. The clause (1) of Article 2 of this Order has been amended by the Bangladesh (Vesting of Property and Assets) (Amendment) Order, 1972 being President's Order No. 134 of 1972. By virtue of this amendment properties and assets which were vested in any officer appointed by the Government of Pakistan including the Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) were also vested in the Government of Bangladesh with effect from that date.</u>

<u>11. The aforesaid Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provision), 1969 (Ordinance I of 1969) was repealed by the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) (Repeal) Act, 1974 and under clause (a) of sub-section I of section 3 thereof all enemy properties which were vested in the Custodian of Enemy Property appointed under the provisions of the Defence of Pakistan Rules were again vested in the Government. On that day another Act titled the vested and Non-Resident Property (Administration) Act, 1974 was made providing, inter alia, for administration of such properties through committees to be constituted by the Government. On 27th November, 1976 this Act was replaced by the Vested and Non-Resident Property (Administration) Repeal Ordinance, 1976 (Ordinance XCII of 1976). Under another Ordinance called the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) (Repeal) (Amendment) Ordinance 1976, Ordinance No. XCIII made on that day the Government was authorised to administer, control, manage and dispose of the property by itself or by such authority as the Government may direct.</u>

12. With this background I now proceed to consider the submissions of the learned Advocates of the respective parties. It is first urged on behalf of the petitioners that in view of Article 2(1) of the President's Order No 29 of 1972 as amended by President's Order No. 134 of 1972 and in view of Sec 3(1)(a) Act XLV of 1974 mutatis mutandis all enemy properties which were vested in the Deputy Custodian, Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) under the provisions of the Defence of Pakistan Rules have been vested in the Government with effect from the 26th March, 1971 and it is, therefore, the Government which alone was competent to maintain the suit in respect of the disputed property, and as the present suit has not been brought by the Government the same is not maintainable in law.

13. I find considerable force in the submission of the learned Advocate. In the case of Bangladesh Enemy Property Management Board and ors vs Md Abdul Majid 27 DLR (AD) 52 the Appellate Division had the occasion to examine similar question whether the Government of Bangladesh is a necessary party in a proceeding with respect to vested property. Their Lord-ships held as under:—

"The first question involved in this appeal is whether having regard to the provisions of the President's Order No. 29 of 1972 and the fact that the ownership, dominion and control of the properties and assets of the firm came to be vested in the Government of Bangladesh thereunder, the said Government was a necessary party in the application before the High Court Division and whether on account of the failure of the respondent to make it a party in the application, the declaration prayed for could be made at all.

<u>14. Article 2(1) of the President's Order No. 29 of 1972 makes it abundantly clear that all properties and assets which were vested in the Government of Pakistan or were vested in or managed by any Board constituted by or under any law or in the former Government of East Pakistan shall be deemed to have vested in the Government of Bangladesh on and from the 26th day of March, 1971. Under the impugned notification issued in pursuance of the powers conferred under the laws then in force, the East Pakistan Enemy Property Management Board had directed that the properties and assets of the firm, which were treated as enemy properties, shall vest in the Additional Custodian of Enemy Property in East Pakistan which, in pursuance of the said notification, took over the management of the firm. This being the state of affairs, the properties and assets of the firm were deemed to have vested in the Government of Bangladesh on and the 26th day of March, 1971 under Article 2 (1) of the President's Order No. 29 of 1972 and the Government of Bangladesh stepped in the place of the erstwhile authorities in whom the properties and assets had vested or by whom they were managed.</u>

<u>15. "It is a question of vital importance to the Government of Bangladesh which, having regard to the provisions of Article 2(1) of the President's Order referred to above, was alone the party interested in controverting, if it so desired, the contentions raised by the respondent in the application. We have, therefore, no hesitation in coming to the finding that the Government of Bangladesh was a necessary party in the application and the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, in the absence of such a party, have become infructuous and are of no legal consequence."</u>

<u>16. In a subsequent decision in the case M/s Dulichand Omraolal vs Bangladesh, through the Secretary, Ministry of Industries and ors. 33 DLR (AD) 30 the Appellate Division after reviewing the relevant laws on the subject pointed out the above legal position in the following terms:—</u>

<u>"The effect of provisions of Act XLV of 1974 as amended by Ordinance XCII and XCIII of 1976, is that the vesting of the property as enemy property by virtue of Defence of Pakistan Rules in the Custodian or Additional Custodian or the Board continued as vested property in the Government of Bangladesh. The vesting occurred by operation of aforesaid Defence of Pakistan Rules in those authorities and those vested properties as enemy properties as past and closed transaction continued to be so in the Government of Bangladesh, and the Government acquired by the aforesaid laws all the right of management, control and disposal of the property by transfer or otherwise. Upon a true construction of the laws aforesaid, we get, that all rights in such property vest in the Government of Bangladesh."</u>

<u>17. I am, therefore, of opinion that all rights of the Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) in the enemy properties which were vested in him under the provisions of the Defence of Pakistan Rules having already been vested in the Government under President's Order No. 29 of 1972 as amended by President's Order No. 134 of 1972 and under Act XLV of 1974 the Government of Bangladesh is the proper person to institute suits in respect of such properties in accordance with the provisions of section 79 and Order XXV I of the Code of Civil Procedure. With the vesting of the property in the Government and the repeal of the Ordinance I of 1969 the office of the Deputy Custodian or Assistant Custodians of Enemy Property which was a creature of the Defence of Pakistan Rules stood abolished and there cannot be any legal existence of the office of the Deputy Custodian or Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property (lands and buildings) any longer.</u>

<u>18. On the face of the clear legal position the learned Deputy Attorney-General finds it difficult to contend that the Government is not a necessary party for prosecution of the suit. He has, however, attempted to submit that the Government was added as a co-plaintiff in the suit. I have carefully perused the record of the case. It appears that the plaintiff in the instant case, has sought for a declaration that an ex-parte decree passed on the 24th December, 1961 was fraudulent. He has claimed that the subject matter of that decree was vested in the Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property as enemy property under the Defence of Pakistan Rules. He has figured himself as Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property, Patuakhali. Admittedly the Government did not bring the suit nor the Government was made a party while instituting the suit. Specific objection was taken, in the written objection that the suit was not maintainable at the instance of the present plaintiff. The defendant has also raised an issue over it. Being conscious of the defect in the constitution of the suit, the Government appears to have filed an application on the 28th January 1980 praying for addition of the Government of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Patuakhali. It is alleged in the said application that the property is under requisition and that Enemy Property Ordinance has been replaced by Vested Property Ordinance and so the Government should be impleaded as a co-plaintiff. On this application the learned Munsif passed the following order :—</u>

<u>"Deft, files hazira. plff. files a petition (i.e. on behalf of Govt. of Bangladesh represented by DC Patuakhali) praying for permission to conduct the suit on the ground stated therein. Copy served, Objection raised Let be kept with the record, to 16-2-80."</u>

<u>19. The subsequent orders do not show that the application was disposed of at any time. On 7-4-80 an unstamped copy of the plaint appears to have been filed showing the Government of Bangladesh as plaintiff No. 2. The same was simply ordered to be kept with the record. It is thus manifest that the Government was not brought on the record of the suit by any order of the Court. The fact that the prayer for addition was not allowed gets further confirmation from the fact that in the decree framed in the suit the name of the Government does not find place. Consequently in the appeal before the learned District Judge the Government was not impleaded as a party. The learned Additional District Judge took the view that the Deputy Commissioner, Patuakhali was legally added as a plaintiff in the suit upon an assumption that the copy of the plaint which was filed on 74-80 was a separate plaint completely overlooking that the same was unstamped and that the learned Munsif did not pass any order accepting the same as a fresh plaint. Even in this Rule the Government is not a party. In view of the above discussion I am unable to hold that the Government was brought on record as co-plaintiff.</u>

20. Now I pass on to the merit of the case. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has contended that the learned Additional District Judge has wrongly placed the onus of proof. A perusal of the judgment of the learned Additional District Judge shows that the onus of proof of the case was entirely placed upon the defendant merely became the decree was an exparte one. In course of his judgment he observed as follows :—

"As regards the service report of the summons the learned lawyer for the deft-appellant submitted that the record of TS No. 396 of 1961 shows shat the summons of that suit was duly served upon the deft No. 2 Surendra Nath Sen. I find no substance in this contention of the learned lawyer because the decree in question passed in TS No. 397/61 was an ex-parte to one and the onus was entirely upon the deft-appellant to prove her mother's lease to the entire satisfaction on the Court and beyond all reasonable doubt. The deft-appellant has totally failed to discharge her onus in this respect."

<u>21. There being a presumption of regularity of a judicial act under section 114 (c) of the Evidence Act whenever a judgment debtor or anybody stepping into his shoes seeks to have a decree passed by a court of competent jurisdiction adjudged void by reason of fraud, a heavy onus lies on him to prove the alleged fraud by cogent and reliable evidence. In the case of Ahsan Ali vs District Judge PLD 1969 (SC) 167 (173) the Supreme Court of Pakistan pointed out that the burden of proving fraud, it must be remembered, is on the party alleging it and that too by clear and convincing evidence, particularly, where a long period has expired and valuable rights have accrued to the other suit." There is hardly any difference between an ex-parte decree and a contested decree in this respect. The mere fact that a decree is an ex-parte one does not absolve the party seeking the declaration from discharging the initial onus which squarely lies on him to show that the decree is fraudulent. It is only after the initial onus is discharged that the onus shifts on the other side. The learned Additional District Judge, therefore, seems to have misdirects himself in law in having approached the case from a wrong standpoint.</u>

22. From the above discussion I am inclined to hold that the Court of appeal below has fallen into error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. It has already been noticed that an application was filed by the plaintiff for addition of the Government as a co-plaintiff. Unfortunately the learned Subordinate Judge before whom the application was made, did not dispose of the same. It is, therefore, necessary in the interest of justice to send back the case to the learned Sub-ordinate Judge for disposal of the said application.

23. For these reasons I make the Rule absolute, set-aside the judgments and, decrees of the courts below and remit the case to the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Patuakhali for disposal of the suit afresh in accordance with law. He will first consider the application of the plaintiff for addition of the Government and then proceed to dispose of the suit.

24. Before I part with the case I like to mention that I must not be understood to have expressed any opinion on the merit of the suit. The learned Subordinate Judge shall be at liberty to dispose of the case on the basis of the evidence that may be adduced before him. I, however, make no order as to cost.

End.
