full_judgment:
This Rule is against the order passed by the learned District Judge, Chittagong, vacating the order of temporary injunction granted by Assistant Judge, Chandnaish, restraining the opposite-party No. 1 from participating in the election of the local Union Parishad as a candidate for the post of Chairman.

2. The petitioner instituted Other Suit No.4 of 1988 for declaration that the opposite-party No. 1 was not a voter in the electoral roll of No. 17 (ka) Kanchanabad Union Parishad and was not qualified as a candidate for the post of a Chairman and for further declaration that the Returning Officer-opposite party No. 2 illegally accepted the nomination paper of the opposite party No. 1 in violation of the provisions of Section 7 of the Local Government (Union Parishad) Ordinance, 1983, hereinafter shall be called as the Ordinance. The petitioner alleged, inter alia, that he was a permanent resident of village Kanchan Nagar within the Kanchanabad Union Parishad, and his name was duly published on 5.8.83 in the voter list against Voter No. 315 of Ward No. 2 of the said Union. But the oposite party No. 1 was not a Voter of the said Union Parishad and his name did not appear in the electoral roll of any ward of the said Parishad. The opposite party No. 1 was a permanent resident of Chittagong City and his name appeared in the electoral roll of the Jamalkhan Ward of the Chittagong Municipality against Voter No. 797 published on 5.8.83. The plaintiff further alleged that the name of the opposite party No. 1 is Mofizur Rahman Chowdhury son of late Mahmudur Rahman Chowdhury but he submitted nomination paper wherein the name of his father was shown as Ahmedur Rahman and thus by false personation he filed the nomination paper. But Returning Officer accepted his nomination as valid on scrutiny. The petitioner raised objection to the acceptance of the nomination paper filed by the opposite Party No. 1 before the Returning Officer-opposite party No. 2. But opposite-party No. 2 rejected the objection and the petitioner took an appeal to the Upazila Nirbahi Officer-opposite party No. 3 against the order of the opposite party No. 2. The opposite party No. 3 rejected the appeal. The plaintiff further alleged that in all educational certificates of the opposite party No. 2 his father's name was shown as Mahmudur Rahman Chowdhury and not as Ahmedur Rahman.

3. The plaintiff after institution of the suit filed an application (or temporary injunction under Order 39 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure for an order restraining the opposite party No. 1 not to contest in the election of the said Union Parishad scheduled to be held on 10.2.88 (the date however has been shifted to 9.4.88).

4. The opposite. party No. 1 contested the said application by filing written objection contending inter alia, that the suit was not maintainable as it related to an election dispute, that the name of the opposite-party No. 1 duly appeared in the electoral roll as a voter and the Returning Officer legally accepted his nomination paper on scrutiny. And both the Returning Officer and the Upazila Nirbahi Officer legally rejected the objection of the petitioner against acceptance of the nomination paper. The opposite party No. 1.further contented that his father was knownto the local people as both Ahmedur Rahman and Mahmudur Rahman Chowdhury and as such thename of his father in the electoral appeared as Ahmedur Rahman. He contended that his name was dulypublished in the electoral roll of Kanchanabad Union Parishad. He denied the allegations brought againsthim by the petitioner that he submitted nominationpaper by false personation.Both the parties filed number of documents and papers in support of their respective cases.

5. The learned Assistant Judge by an order of temporary injunction dated 4.2.1988 restrained the opposite party No.1 from contesting in the said election scheduled to be held on 10.2.88 (which date has since been shifted on 9.4.88) till the disposal of the suit.

6. The opposite-party No. 1 preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 44 of 1988 to the Court of District Judge, Chittagong, against the said order. The learned District Judge on contest allowed the appeal by his impugned judgment and order dated 8.2.88 and vacated the order of temporary injunction and rejected the prayer for temporary injunction.

7. Mr. A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, first, submitted that the judgment and order of the lower appellate court was without jurisdiction as the appeal was not admitted under Order 41 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure; secondly, the judgment of the lower appellate court was not a proper judgment of reversal; thirdly, that the balance of convenience was in favour of the petitioner. Lastly, that the suit was maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act although there was a negative prayer for declaration.

8. Mr. Mozammel Hossain, the learned Advocate for the opposite-party No. 1, on the other hand, submitted that the suit was not maintainable as it relates to an election dispute. He further submitted that as the appeal was heard on contest it shall be deemed that the appeal was admitted by the lower appellate Court although it was not formally admitted and Order 41 rule 11 of the Code of Civil procedure is not for admission but for dismissal of the appeal and as such the judgment of the lower appellate court does not suffer from want of jurisdiction. He further argued that the finding of lower appellate Court that the petitioner failed to prove the balance of convenience in his favour was based on consideration of documents the impugned order vacating the order of temporary injunction granted by the trial Court should not be interfered with by the High Court Division in its revisional jurisdiction in that the impugned judgment and order caused no occasion of failure of justice.

9. Now let us consider the submissions of the learned Advocates. The learned Advocate for the petitioner referred met Order No.1 dated 7.2.88 of the lower appellate court and urged that the order shows that the appeal was filed and registered on 7.2.1988 and the lower appellate court called for the record of the lower Court and directed issuance of notices upon the respondents fixing 9.2.88 for return and order.Therefore, according to the learned Advocate the appeal was not admitted before 9.2.88 and as such hearing of the appeal on merit on 7.2.88 and the judgment passed on 8.2.88 was without jurisdiction. In support of his contention the learned Advocate referred me to the case of Shudhir Biswas Vs. Obenash Chandra Biswas, 5 D.L.R. 451. That case arose out of an application under section 174(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act filed on 7.5.51 for setting aside sale of certain land on the ground of fraudulent suppression of process and material irregularity in conducting the sale. The case was dismissed on the ground of limitation. On appeal the lower appellate court reversed the decision of the trial Court and set aside the sale on the ground of fraud and suppression of the notice by the decree-holder. Against that decision of the lower appellate Court the auction-purchaser moved the High Court in its revisional jurisdiction. In the High Court it was con- tended that the lower appellate Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal for noncompliance withTherefore, according to the learned Advocate the appeal was not admitted before 9.2.88 and as such hearing of the appeal on merit on 7.2.88 and the judgment passed on 8.2.88 was without jurisdiction. In support of his contention the learned Advocate referred me to the case of Shudhir Biswas Vs. Obeahs Chandra Biswas, 5 D.L.R. 451. That case arose out of an application under section 174(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act filed on 7.5.51 for setting aside sale of certain land on the ground of fraudulent suppression of process and material irregularity in conducting the sale. The case was dismissed on the ground of limitation. On appeal the lower appellate court reversed the decision of the trial Court and set aside the sale on the ground of fraud and suppression of the notice by the decree-holder. Against that decision of the lower appellate Court the auction-purchaser moved the High Court in its revisional jurisdiction. In the High Court it was contended that the lower appellate Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal for noncompliance with the provision of sub-section (5) of section 174 of the Bengal Tenancy Act which provided that the amount for which the property was sold was to be deposited before admission of the appeal and that being not done the appeal was incompetent and subsequent deposit after submission of appeal did not cure the defect. In Sudhir Biswas it was held: 

"On the day the memo of appeal was presented, the Court directed it to be registered and to issue notice on the respondent fixing the date for hearing which shows that in fact the appeal admitted on the day it was presented". 

The learned Advocate also referred me to case of Jugesh Chandra Basu and others Vs. Khoka Mondal and others reported in 6 D.L.R. 434. That also arose out of an application under section 174(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act. In that case it was urged that the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge without admitting the appeal under Order 41 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure was without jurisdiction. In that case the appellate Court passed the following order:-

"Register the appeal. Issue notices to the respondents, fixing 3.4.52 for hearing. Call for original records of the case." 

The facts of the aforesaid case are almost similar to the facts of the instant case before me. From the order dated 7.2.88 made by the lower appellate court it appears that he recorded the order as under: 

"Appeal is filed to-day. Register. It is within time. Court fees paid on the memo of appeal are correct. Call for the L.C. Records. Requisites filed. Issue notice upon the report through nezarath as well as by regd. post with A.D. fixing 9.2.88 for return & order". 

Where the appellate Court registers an appeal, issues notices to the respondents and calls for the record of the lower Court and fixes a date [or return and order although the appeal is not admitted formally it shall be deemed that the appeal was admitted by the appellate court on application of his judicial mind because Court will not issue any notice upon the respondents unless it admits the appeal. This view of mine finds support from the decision in the case of Jogesh Chandra Basu and others vs. Khoka Mondal and others, 6 D.L.R. 434, wherein it has been held that: 

"If the Code of Civil Procedure does not contemplate the issue of any notices to a respondent in an appeal until after the admission thereof, then in my opinion, an order fixing a date of hearing, calling for the original records and directing the issue of notice to the respondents must be deemed to be an order admitting the appeal after the application of the judicial mind of the court." 

In the light of the aforesaid principle of law I am of the opinion that in this case although there was no formal admission of the appeal and the appeal was heard on 7.2.1988 prior to 9.2.1988 which was fixed for return and order, the judgment and order of the lower appellate Court is not without jurisdiction. In this case as the respondent appeared and the appeal was not dismissed under Order 41, rule 11 there is no scope for saying that the appeal is not admitted. Therefore, the decision in the case of Jogesh Chandra Basu does not help the learned Advocate for the petitioner rather it is against him. He further relied upon the decision in the case of Prafulla Kumar :Bose Vs. The Mymensingh Cooperative Town Bank Limited and another, 9 D.L.R. 394.;. But the decision is not also of any assistance to the learned Advocate as the principle enunciated therein is' in the line of the decisions referred to above. Being in respectful agreement with the view of their Lordships expressed in the aforesaid decisions I am of the opinion that the contention of the petitioner that the judgment of the lower appellate Court suffers from want of jurisdiction has got no. substance. Mr. Mozammel Hossain, the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1 in this respect submitted that the petitioner already having had appeared before the lower appellate Court and having had contested the appeal which was heard on merit and disposed of finally the petitioner is not entitled to raise this question of jurisdiction at this stage before this Court. The contention is misconceived as the question of jurisdiction can be raised even in the Court of last resort. As I have already held that the appeal shall be deemed to have been admitted. Ineed not discuss this point any further.

10. Mr. Shafiqur Rahman further contended that the judgment of the lower appellate Court was not a proper judgment of reversal in as much as it did not advert to the reasoning which weighed with the trial Court and the evidence on which the trial court's judgment was based. He relied upon the decision in the case of Afazuddin Mollah and others V Moyezuddin Shaikh and others (1985) B.L.D. (AD) 54, wherein it has been held:

"Reversal of the trial court's judgment without adverting to the evidence on which trial court's judgment is based is not a proper judgment of reversal.............." 	

In that case an application for pre-emption was filed under section 96( 1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 on the ground that the preemptor was a co-sharer to the holding transferred.But the purchaser contested on the ground that the case was not maintainable as the jote was split up. In support of his contention he put in C.S, Khatians Ext. C and C(I) and Dhakhilas, Ext. B series. Thetrial Court on the basis of those documents held that the pre-emptor was not a co-sharer as the jote was split up. But while reversing the finding of the trial court the appellate Court had not relied upon those Exts. and held that there was no reliable evidence that the holding was split up. The facts of that caseis quite distinguishable from the facts of the present case as there are other material evidence before the lower appellate Court to arrive its finding contrary to the finding of the trial court. The materials the learned lower appellate Court relied upon have al-ready been mentioned. And there is nothing to showfrom the judgment of the lower appellate Court that it held that there was no reliable evidence. So, in the facts and circumstances of the instant case, the decision cited has little application to the facts of this case. Mr. Shafiqur Rahman, further cited the decision in the case of Syed jan Bibi and other Vs. Musammat Jahura Khatun and others, 39D.L.R. 322 to which I was a party. In that case the trial court relied upon the material evidence which did not receive due consideration by the lower appellate Court. As the evidence was a material one the lower appellate Court having not considered that I observed that the judgment of the lower appellate Court was not a proper judgment of reversal and the finding of the trial Court was based on surmises, conjecture and assumption and without adverting to the reasons of the trial court given for its finding. But in the present case the finding of the lower appellate Court is not based on surmises and conjecture but on evidence. Therefore, the decision also does not help the petitioner.

11. Mr. Hossain, on the Other hand, repelled the contention of the petitioner that balance of convenience is in favour of the petitioner submitting that the opposite party No. 1 was known to the locality and as such it was perfectly right for the, member and the chairman to give certificates. The argument seems to be convincing. Admittedly, there is nothing on the record that the Member and the Chairman had any enmity with the petitioner. If that is so, why they will issue such certificate more so when issuance of false certificates may implicate them in a criminal case? It is also pertinent to note in this respect that whether the opposite party No. 1 by filing nomination paper has misled any of the voters or whether if injunction is refused the voters will suffer irreparable loss? The answer so far the first part of the question is concerned it is in the negative and so far the second part is concerned it is in the affirmative. Because if there is a contest the voters who are entitled to exercise their valuable right of franchise will be debarred from exercising the same. On the other hand, thy petitioner will be at liberty to contest in the election if no injunction is granted and thereby he will suffer no irreparable loss and if the order of injunction is maintained he will have to steal a march on and the opposite party No. 1 will suffer ire reparable loss and in that event the opposite party No. 1 will be left with no remedy but challenging the election by way of election petition which will give rise to multiplicity of proceedings raising complicated questions of law and facts to be decided after taking into consideration the evidence and examining the questions of law that may be raised. In view of the scope of Order 39, rule 1 where the plaintiff fails to satisfy the requirements in .getting the order of injunction, the defendant should not be forced to institute another suit. In this view of the matter I am of the opinion that the balance of convenience is against the petitioner." 

12. Mr. Hossain, in support of his contention that in order to succeed in obtaining an order for tern porary injunction the plaintiff is to prove, amongst other conditions, that in the event of success in the suit if injunction is not granted he will suffer irreparable loss referred me to the decision in the case of Main Mohammad Latif Vs. Province of West Pakistan, 22 D.L.R (S.C) 98, wherein it has been held: 

"In a case where temporary injunction is claimed, the plaintiff has only to make out that he has a good prima facie case meaning thereby that an important question of law is to be tried in the suit and that in the event of success if the injunction is not issued he will suffer irreparable injury." 

In this respect it is also profitable to refer to the decision in the case of Shahzada Muhd. Umar Beg Vs. Sultan Mohammod Khan, 22 D.L.R. (S.C) 41, wherein the principles for grant or refusal of temporary injunction have been laid down. Their Lordships of the Supreme Court of Pakistan have laid down that: 

"......the well settled principles for grant or refusal of temporary injunctions in accordance with law, which are, firstly, whether the plaintiff has a prima facie good case, secondly, whether the balance of convenience lies in favour of grant of the injunction and, thirdly, whether the plaintiff would suffer an irreparable loss if injunction is refused." 

In view of may finding that the petitioner failed to prove that he will suffer irreperable loss and injury if no injunction is granted I hold on the strength of the aforesaid judicial pronouncement of the Supreme Court of Pakistan that the learned appellate Court rightly refused temporary injunction and set aside the order of the trial Court.

13. Mr. Shafiqur Rahman, further cited the decision in the case of Rameshwar Singh and another Vs. Bajit Lal Pathak and others, A.I.R. 1929 (P.C) 95 in support of his contention that as the opposite party witheld the best evidence an adverse presumption should have been drawn against him by the lower appellate Court. In that case it was held: 	

"In the change of attitude on the part of the defence and in its failure to produce documents-presumably available and probably decisive one way or another if examined, the learned Judges saw a design on the part of the defendant to take advantage of the abstract doctrine of the burden of proof upon a plaintiff in ejectment". 

The aforesaid observation was made as the defendants in that case were called upon by the court to file the measurement Khasras which were with the defendants and which, in the opinion of the Court, was probably the "decisive" evidence. The defendant took time to produce the same but did not produce. But in this case before me the defendant was not called upon by the lower appellate Court to produce any document which was in its opinion decisive for deciding the issue. The facts of the case cited by the petitioner are quite distinguishable and the principle laid down therein has no manner of application to the instant case. As I have already indicated that his father was known sometime as Mahmudur Rahman Chowdhury and sometimes as Ahmedur Rahman and as there was also material on record viz, the certificates given by the member and the chairman before the lower appellate Court to hold to that effect. I do not consider that the best evidence were withheld. Facts of each particular case will determine what the best evidence for that case. It seems to me that the lower appellate Court relied upon the certificates to be the best evidence rightly.

14. Mr. Shafiqur Rahman in support of his contention that in a suit under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act a negative declaration can be sought for and the present suit in which a relief is sought for declaration that the opposite party No. 1 was not competent to seek election to the post of Chairman is maintainable. He relied upon the decision in the case of Bipin Chandra Roy Vs. Bunchuki Barmani, 37 D.L.R, 49. He further submitted that in view of the relief sought for in term of prayer (খ) in the plaint the suit is within the mischief of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Prayer (খ) is in the following term:

(খ) বিগত ১০-১-৮৮ ইং তাং ২নং বিবাদী কর্তৃক ১৭(৬) নং কাঞ্চনাবাদ ইউনিয়ন পরিষদের ১০-২-৮৮ ইং তারিখের অনুষ্ঠিতব্য নির্বাচনে প্রতিদ্বন্দিতা করিবার জন্য ২নং বিবাদী কর্তৃক ১নং বিবাদীর মনোনয়নপত্র গ্রহণ স্থানীয় সরকার (ইউনিয়ন পরিষদ) অধ্যাদেশ ১৯৮৩ ইং সনের ৭ ধারায় পরিপন্থি বলিয়া ঘোষণামুলক ডিক্রি প্রদান করা হউক।

In Bipin Chandra the plaintiff brought a suit for declaration that the defendant No. 1 was not the adopted son of her father Sree Kanta. Although the declaration sought for was a negative declaration, the Court held that: 

".......merely because a negative declaration has been sought that cannot be any ground to hold that the suit does not come within the ambit of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The said section does not really bar a negative declaration as such if otherwise its decisions and terms are fulfilled, as the section does not debar to get a negative declaration provided the conditions for obtaining such declaration are satisfied with" 

The learned Judge in observing as quoted above finds support from the decisions in the case of Waryam Singh Vs. Mahtab, 26 P.R. 1903, Secretary of State Vs. Dhobu Ram, LL.R (1944) Lahore 168. In view of the prayer" " and in view of the provisions of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the judicial pronouncements in those cases I hold that a suit where a negative declaration is sought for is maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. In this case from the facts as narrated-above, it seems to me that the suit is well within the mischief of section 42 more so in view of the prayer" Therefore, the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner is of no substance.

15. For the reasons stated above, I do not find any reason to interfere with the impugned order. However, as the matter involves question of public importance, I direct the trial court to hear the suit with utmost expedition specially in view of the date fixed for holding the election. 

In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J. - This appeal against acquittal raises the point as to whether the nationalised Sonali Bank comes under the purview of the Shops and Establishments Act, 1965 (Act No. VII of 1965) hereinafter referred to as the said Act.

2. The prosecution case, in brief, in that the accused respondent Abdul Awal, Manager, Sonali Bank, Stadium Branch, Dhaka contravened the provisions of the Shops and Establishments Rules, 1970 in that on 24.3.78 at about 2-15 P.M. the informant P.W.l Md. A. Khaleque, Inspector of Shops and Establishments visited the Stadium 'Branch of the Sonali Bank and the accused respondent as Manager thereof failed to satisfy that he furnished particulars of his establishment in Form 'A' (Rule 10) that he maintained Visit Book in form 'B' (Rule 12), that he maintained Attendance Register in Form 'C' (Rule 13), that he maintained Pay Register in Form 'D' (Rule 14) and that he maintained Leave Register in Form 'E' (Rule 15) and therefore he committed an offence under section 24 of the said Act. The defence case was that the former National Bank of Pakistan with all its branches in Bangladesh was nationalised by the Government under P.O. No. 26 of 1972 on 26.3.72 and after nationalisation the Sonali Bank and its branch offices have fallen under the category of "offices under the Government" and therefore, in terms of section 1(6) (i) of the said Act the Sonali Bank is exempted from the purview of the said Act.

2A. Mr. A.R. Pathan, Magistrate. 1st Class, Dhaka trying the case against the accused-respondent accepted the contention of the defence any acquitted the accused respondent of the charge against him. He did not discuss the merit of the case. Thereafter, the State preferred this appeal under section 417 (2) Cr.P.C. Mr. Matiur Rahman, learned Assistant Attorney General appears for the State and Mr. Asrarul Hossain with Mr. Abdul Azim learned Advocates appear for the accused respondent Abdul Awal.

3. The Shops and Establishments Act, 1965 repealed and with certain amendments re-enacted the East Bengal Shops and Establishments Act, 1951 for regulating the holidays, payment of wages leave, hours of work and certain other allied matters concerning the workers employed in shops, commercial establishments, not being factories. This is what is contained in the preamble of the said Act.

4. The words "commercial establishment" have been defined in section 2(d) of the said Act. Among other concerns "banking company" and "a bank" was also "included" within the definition of the said words. It is undisputed that before the nationalisation of banks in Bangladesh the National Bank of Pakistan and its branches were included within the definition of the words "commercial establishment." The definition of "commercial establishment" in the said Act has undergone no change after the nationalisation of banks. The nationalised banks and their offices maintain their character as "a bank" and therefore, even after nationalisation the said Act, it appears, has full force and application to all the nationalised banks and their offices, including the Sonali Bank. The learned Magistrate does not appear to have noticed the definition of "commercial establishment" at all.

Further, the application of the said Act to the former banks before nationalization being undisputed Articles 31 of P.O. No. 26 of 19'72 ensures a continuity of the application of the said Act to the new nationalised banks Article 31 of P.O. No 26 of 1972 is as follows:

"All laws relating to banks and banking companies shall, subject to such adaptation and modification as may be made from time to time shall be applicable to the new banks”

The learned Magistrate has also failed to notice Article 31 of P.O No. 26 of 1912.

5. Section 1 (6) of the said Act contains 7 sub-clauses which describe the offices and other establishments to which the said Act has no application. Clauses (i) and (iii) are important for the purpose of this appeal and Section 1 (6) (i) & 1(6) (iii) of the said Act are as follows:

"(6) Notwithstanding anything contained in the foregoing sub-section, this Act shall not apply to--- (i) offices of or under the Government; (iii) offices of or under any local authority, a trust, a corporation or any other public statutory body, which is not run for profit or gain or in the course of its business does not make any profit or gain:"

6. Mr. Asrarul Hossain submits that the offices and branches of the nationalised Sonali Bank are "offices under the Government" 'within meaning of section 1(6) (i) of the said Act and therefore these are excluded from the operation of the said Act. He has taken us through various provisions of P. O. No. 26 of 1972 as amended upto, date and has argued that as the Board of Directors of the Sonali Bank is appointed by the Government, as the Board is guided by such general or special order as the Government may give it from time to time. as the officers and employees of the bank may enjoy such terms and conditions of service as the Government may determine in the interest 'of uniformity and as the nationalised banks function within the framework of governmental control, supervision and direction, the Sonali Bank is nothing but an office under the Government. Mr. Asrarul Hossain has also placed before us the dictionary meaning of the word "under" as contained in the Oxford English Dictionary (1933) Volume XI, 121, as follows:

"7. Denoting position at the bottom or foot of something or besides it but at a lower level......sometimes with implication of shelter or protection.

*** ** ***

9. With reference to persons acting in a certain capacity, considered in relation to one holding a superior position or office.

10. Denoting subordinate to, or controlled by, a person or persons having or exercising recognised authority or command".

7. Applying the dictionary meanings of the word "under" Mr. Hossain submits, the Sonali Bank falls within the category of an office under the Government.

From a reading of P.O. No. 26 of 1972, as amended upto date it appears that the mechanism of running the nationalised banks in Bangladesh is not different from that of running several other public statutory bodies before the liberation of Bangladesh. The nationalised banks, in their structure and organisation, were conceived to be public statutory bodies. The legal character of these public statutory bodies, their structures, the methodology of their functioning, their finance and the governmental superintendence and control over them followed the time honored structural pattern of public statutory bodies as they existed before the liberation of Bangladesh with some variation to suit the changing needs. This public statutory bodies including the natinalised banks came to have a corporate personality and a juristic entity of their own and they can sue and be sued in the ordinary courts in their own names. They do not have any special privilege in legal proceedings brought by them or against them. The special period of limitation enjoyed by the Government in many cases are not applicable to them, unless the statue establishing them specifically so applies. They are also subject to income tax and other revenue legislations to the same extent and hi accordance with the same regulations as are applicable to the other citizens of Bangladesh. These public statutory bodies have not been required by the statute establishing them to act for and on behalf of the Government. As far as Government control and direction are concerned, all public statutory bodies, in large or small measure are controlled and directed by the Government. P.O. No. 26 of 1972, establishing the Sonali Bank appears to us to be no different from any such public statutory body. The then Supreme Court of Bangladesh had occasion to consider the true nature and character or what it called "public corporation" and it observed as follows in the case of B.S.I Corporation Vs. Mahbub Hossain Chowdhury 29 D.L.R. (S.C) 41:-

"11. Study of techniques adopted by the Government indicates that one of the methods applied is to set up Corporations. Broadly speaking they are called public corporations in contradistinction with private corporations set up under Companies Act by the citizens. The State policy is to utilize the principle of corporation. A corporation has its own independent existence distinct from the shareholders or directors or administrators and has all the attributes of a Juristic personality. A statutory corporation therefore is neither a dependent on Government nor its agent unless there is something expressly contrary in the statute vide Tamlin Vs. Hannaford 1950 (1) KB. 18

12. Public Corporation set up by the State again may assume various forms. It may choose to set up a corporation under the Companies Act either contributing entire share capital by the Government or dividing the contribution of share capital between the Government and the public. It may set up a Corporation by a statute. This statutory corporation again is sometimes made amenable to different provisions of the Companies Act subject to the statute and sometimes it is kepttotally outside the ambit of operation of the Companies Act, governable wholly by the incorporating statute itself. A public corporation may function as a Government department or its agent or both or may be totally independent of either having its own independent corporate personality.

13. We, therefore, find that a public corporation is a hybrid organism showing some of the features of a Government Department and some of a business company and standing outside the ordinary framework of Central and Local Government."

We find nothing in the P.O. No. 26 or 1972 which can lead us to hold that the Sonali Bank being a public statutory body has been statutorily designed to function as a Government Department or its Agent.

8. The dictionary meaning of the word "under" as referred to by Mr. Asrarul Hussain refers to offices belonging to the same class, following a chain of command. The Sonali Bank is not an office belonging to the same class as Government department, nor does it function under the Government following a chain of command.

We have earlier quoted section 1(6) (iii) of the said Act. It will be seen from the said sub-clause (iii) that any public statutory body can claim exemption from the operation, of the said Act provided it is not run for profit or gain or provided in the course of its business it does not make any profit or gain. It is to, be noted that the legislature has specineally noticed public statutory bodies in section 1(6)(iii) of the said Act. Such form of Government enterprise as is embodied in public statutory bodies was known to the legislature and these bodies came up for special treatment in the said Act. A public statutory body remains a public statutory body, whatever be the measure of control the Government exercise over it.

9. Besides, it was the clear intention of the legislature that only those public statutory bodies which are not run for profit or gain or which do not make any profit or gain in the course of their business should be exempted from the operation of the said Act. It is not the case of the accused-respondent that the Sonali Bank is not run for profit or gain. If public statutory bodies like the Sonali Bank also come within the category of "offices under the Government." then sub-clause (iii) will be rendered nugatory, because all public statutory bodies whether they run for profit or gain or not, will claim exemption under sub-clause (i) on the footing that they are offices under the Government" and on the simple ground that the Government holds the rein over them.

10. We, therefore, hold that the said Act has full force and application to the Sonali Bank and that the learned Magistrate acted illegally in acquitting the accused respondent solely on the ground that the said Act does not apply to the Sonali Bank.

11. Coming now to the merits of the case, we find that the case against the accused-respondent rests solely on the evidence of P. W.1 Md. Abdul Khaleque, Inspector, Shop's and Establishments. He stated that he visited the Stadium branch of the Sonali Bank on 24.3.78 at about 2.15. P.M. and found that the register, etc. mentioned earlier were not maintained by the accused-respondent who was the Manager of the said branch of the Sonali Bank. In his cross-examination it was suggested that he did not visit the said branch of the Sonali Bank at all and prepared his report from his house and submitted a false and concocted complaint against the respondent just to harass him. He denied the suggestion in cross-examination be also stated that he went to visit the Stadium Branch of the Sonali Bank alone and he kept no witness. There were also no customers at that time.

12. We have perused the Shops and Establishment Rules, 1970 and particularly Rules 10,12,13,14 and 15 thereof- the violation of which is the cause of action against the accused respondent. If an Inspector visits a shop or establishment and asks for the particulars or registers mentioned in the aforesaid Rules and if the employer fails to produce those particulars and registers instantly to the Inspector then that failure per se does not attract any penal provision. There must be evidence that the employer does not maintain those particulars and registers at all and that evidence is best furnished by calling for those documents by a notice and by a failure of the accused to respond to that notice. There is no evidence that after his visit on 24.3.78 P.W.1 served any notice on the accused-respondent to produce the required particulars and registers to him for his inspection. Mere failure to show him the particulars and registers during the course of one surprise visit is no criminal offence. It is the failure to furnish the particulars and maintain the registers which is an offence. P.W.1 the Inspector should have served a notice on the accused-respondent to prove that the accused-respondent not only failed to produce the particulars and registers on demand but also failed to maintain the same which is evident from his failure to produce the same upon receipt of notice.

13. In the absence of ally evidence in this regard the accused-respondent cannot be convicted of the offence charged with.

The learned Magistrate, therefore rightly acquitted the accused respondent though the reasoning’s given by him are not approved by us.

The learned Magistrate ought to have discussed the merits of the case and as a trial Court he should not have acquitted the respondent on a mere technical ground.

14. In the result, the appeal is dismissed. The order of acquittal passed by the learned Magistrate dated 28.6.79 is affirmed.

Let the records be sent back. Let a copy of this judgment be forwarded to the learned Magistrate wherever he is posted now.

Mohammed Habibur Rahman, J -I. agree.

End.

lawyer:
K. S. Nabi ----- For the appellant
Ruhul Amin ----- For the respondent
parties:
Kiron Chandra Das ----- Appellant
Vs.
Sirajul Hoque Patwari ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
This appeal at the instance of the plaintiffs is against the decision of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, Noakhali affirming those of the Munsif, Third Court, Noakhali passed in a suit for mere declaration that a sale deed No. 5058 registered on 30.6.70 at the Senbagh Sub-Registrar Office purported to have been executed by the plaintiff on 17.4.70 with respect to 1.25 acres of land was fraudulent and a collusive document.

2 Defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement controverting all the material allegations made in the plaint asserting, inter alia, that the sale deed in his favour was duly executed on proper consideration. The trial court dismissed the plaintiff's suit. On appeal the lower appellate court concurring with the Trial Court dismissed his appeal. Hence this appeal.

3. Both the courts below found concurrently that the certified copy of the impugned deed was not enough to prove the execution of the sale deed in the absence of any opinion of an handwriting expert as to the forged character of the signatures appearing in the sale deed and in the absence of the original sale deed, the court was not in a position to pass any opinion in favour of the plaintiff with reference to the averments made in the plaint and in spite of repeated instruction by the trial court the said original was not produced but rather it was wrongly argued by the plaintiff that the certified copy of the same as submitted was enough and the original was not necessary for the purpose of the suit, to prove that it was a fraudulent document, executed and registered by impersonation. In that view of the matter both the courts below held that in the absence of the said original document and in the absence of any opinion of any handwriting expert in this regard as to forgery the plaintiff had failed to prove prima facie the plaintiff's case and hence the plaintiff's suit must fail.

4. The short points that arise for the disposal of this appeal are whether the plaintiff had an onus upon him to prove a prima facie case by producing the best evidence that is the document itself and whether the plaintiff was entitled to a decree ex parte as of right on the failure of the contesting defendant to appear on the date of hearing without proving a prima facie case as contended by the learned Counsel for the appellant. Under the law the contents of a document is to be proved by producing the document itself for inspection of the court. Secondary evidence of the same by way of producing a certified copy of the same is admissible only when the original is lost or it is beyond the reach of the person asked to produce or beyond the jurisdiction of the court. After a notice was duly served upon the party on whose possession and however the document is as required under section 66 of the Evidence Act. But such secondary evidence would be admissible only to prove the contents but never the execution or non-execution of the same. It was primarily alleged in the suit that the document was obtained by fraud and registered by impersonation committing a fraud upon the registering authority and hence the onus was on the plaintiff to prove the same

<u>5. There is a presumption of good faith in human transaction as there is a presumption of innocence in criminal matters. That being so the burden of proving every species of bad faith such as fraud, collusion, misrepresentation, impersonation, undue influence, absence of consideration rests on the person who asserts the same and only after that burden was discharged prima facie the burden would shift on the other party to prove that it was not so. Apart from this general principle of Law, section 60 of the Registration Act provided that a registered document duly certified by the Registrar, is an evidence of its due registration and due execution (Reference 102 IC. 283) and who alleges that it was not so the burden would rest on him to prove the same. The initial onus that was upon the Plaintiff to prove had not been discharged by adducing the primary evidence, namely, the original document itself for enabling the court to examine the document in order to be satisfied prima facie as to its genuineness by comparing the signatures of the plaintiff, appearing in record of the case before the 1st court with those appearing in the Kabala and the said having not been produced by the plaintiff or caused it to be produced by the person who had the original in his custody the plaintiff would not be entitled to any relief prima facie by illegally shifting the onus of proving due execution upon the defendant. Further, a plaintiff without proving his case prima facie would not, as of right, get a decree in his favour merely because the contesting defendants were absent on the date of hearing as argued vehemently by the learned Counsel for the appellant before me Mere absence of the contesting defendants on the date of hearing will not ipso facto prove that the plaintiff's case was true so as to entitle the plaintiff to any decree as of right, ex-parte, he would still have the burden of proving the case prima facie. I find no illegality committed by the courts below arriving at the concurrent finding to the effect that the initial burden of proving the case prima facie was upon the plaintiff and having not teen done by the plaintiff in spite of opportunities given, the plaintiff cannot get a decree ex-parte.</u>

All the points having been found against the appellant. I find no substance in this appeal. In the result, this appeal is dismissed. The judgment and decree of the courts below are affirmed but in the facts and circumstances of the case I direct the parties to bear their own costs,

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Abdul Quayum, Advocate ------ For the Petitioner.
Mr. Tapan Kumar Chakroborty, Advocate ------ For the opposite Parties.
parties:
Al-haj Abdul Aziz ------ Petitioner
VS
Kalipada Das & ors ------.Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule issued at the instance of the plaintiff-petitioner Alhaj Abdul Ariz on an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and order passed on 4.12.79 by Mr. M.A. Rahman Mia, Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Bakerganj in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 214 of 1978 reversing the judgment and order dated 26.9.76 passed by Mr. Md. Habibullah, Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Bakerganj in Miscellaneous Case No. 23 of 1972 under Order 9, rule 13 of the said Code arising out of Title Suit No. 212 of 1971.

2. The plaintiff-petitioner instituted the suit on 27.10.71 in the Court of the learned Subordinate Judge against Hara Mohan Das, predecessor-interest of the opposite parties for specific performance of a contract in respect of some landed properties situated in Barisal town. The defendant did not appear and the suit was decreed ex-parte on 4.3.72. On 24.3.72 defendant Hara Mohan Das filed the Miscellaneous case No. 23 of 1972 under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex-parte decree on the allegation that summons in the suit was not duly served on him and that he learnt about the decree on 7.3.72 from his Karmachari Haripada Das. The case was contested by the plaintiff by filing a written objection denying the allegation of non-service of the process. In course of the proceeding Hara Mohan Das died and his legal heirs were brought on record.

3. Including the parties 2 P.Ws. and 2 O.P.Ws have been examined at the time of hearing. P.W.1 Kalipada Das is a son of Hara Mohan Das. P.W.2 Haripada Das is the alleged informant. On the other hand, O.P.W.1 Alhaz Abdul Aziz Howlader is the opposite-party himself and O.P.W.2 Abdul Hashem is an alleged Mokabila witnessing the service of summons upon the defendant in the suit. The learned Subordinate Judge has held that the summons upon Ham Mohan Das was duly served. He has however observed that in view of the satisfactory evidence on behalf of the plaintiff-Opposite party there is no necessity to examine the serving peon and that the petitioners were very much aware of the suit. He has accordingly dismissed the re-hearing case. The heirs of Hara Mohan Das preferred an appeal against the judgment and order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 214 of 1978 which has been heard by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Bakerganj who has on consideration of the evidence on record and the circumstances of the case arrived at a finding that the summons was not duly served upon defendant Hara Mohan Das. He has held that the evidence adduced by the plaintiff-Opposite party in discharge of his onus has not been satisfactory and "in such a predicament of the case of the O.P., it was incumbent upon him to examine the serving officer. In the instant case the best evidence could be obtained from the serving officer upon his examination before Court with reference to the return of service of summons in question. "In order to give emphasis upon the point the learned Additional District Judge has referred to the decision reported in 25 D.L.R. 91 wherein it has been held that the compliance with the provision of Order 5, Rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure is mandatory. He has accordingly allowed the appeal and set aside the ex-parte decree restoring the original suit, by his judgment and order dated 4.12.79. The plaintiff has obtained the instant Rule against this order.

4. Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner has urged that the learned appellate Court has in allowing the appeal committed an error of law which is apparent on the face of the record. According to him the learned Additional District Judge has fallen into the error by relying on the decision reported in 25 D.L.R. 91 which is not applicable to the instant case for the reason that in the instant case the service return contains a declaration of the process server as to the manner of the service of the process. On the other hand Mr. Tapan Kumer Chakraborty the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties besides referring to Rule 70 of the Civil Rules and Orders Vol. 1 as to the service of the process in presence of two independent local witnesses submit that the learned Court below having already come to a legal finding that the plaintiff opposite party has failed to prove the service of the summons upon the defendant has cited the ruling although it was not necessary. According to him the absence of signature of the alleged Mokabila witnesses in the service return without any explanation of the serving peon therein in that respect goes a long way to show that the process was suppressed. He submits that the process server would have been the best person to explain such deficiency in the service return and the learned Judge has very rightly commented upon his non- examination at the hearing.

5. The service return has not however been marked Exhibit in the case. It shows that it was served by a special peon who received the process from the Nazarat on 5.11.71 and served it on the morning of 10.11.71 within this town at a place named Daptarkhana on the identification and in the presence of two witnesses named Abdul Majid and Abul Hashem, residents of the same place Daftarkhana. No. signature of these two alleged witnesses appear in the service return and their names arc written by the serving peon himself. The peon has not explained in his report why it was not possible for him to obtain signatures of the Mokabila witnesses. The process appears to have been served on Harmohon's refusal by affixing a copy on his outer door. The service return contains a declaration made by the process server as to the facts of the service.

6. P.W. 1 Kalipada Das, son of the original defendant Hara Mohan Das, has denied service of the process upon his father and P.W. 2 Haripada Das gave information to Hara Mohan regarding the exported decree. On the other hand, O.P.W who is the plaintiff himself has disclaimed any knowledge of service of the summons. O.P.W. 2 Abul Hashem whose name appears in the service return as one of the two identifier-Mokabila witnesses has come to prove service of the process. He has testified to the service of the process upon Hara Mohan in the manner as stated in the service return. But he does not say that he identified Hara Mohan to the serving peon. On the point of absence of his signature in the service return he in his cross-examination says that the process server asked him 10 put his signature in the service return but later on after two or three sentences he prevaricates and states that he was not asked to put his signature in the service return by the process server.

<u>7. Under Order 5, rule 19-A of the Code of Civil Procedure the declaration of the process server is an evidence of the fact as 10 the service of the summons upon the defendant. The report that the service was made on the identification of the Mokabila witnesses implies that the process server did not know the defendant and or his house. So in absence of any statement by O.P.W. 2 on the point of his identification, the recital as to the identification which is like any other evidence remains uncorroborated, and in the face of denial by the defendant there remains a genuine suspicion that the service was made, if at all, upon a wrong person. There is yet another factor confirming the suspicion. The process server has given the address of O.P.W.2 (with his father's name) as Daftarkhana which is also the address of the defendant. But O.P.W. 2 clearly states that he resides at Kailaghat for the last 15/16 years. This indicates some sort of foul play on the part of the witness. Rule 70 of the Civil Rules and Orders Vol. 1 provides for service of the summons in presence of at least "two independent local residents." service in presence of a resident of a different locality without any explanation about his competence is not certainly in accordance with the Rule. Again, under this Rule 70 the process server is required "whenever possible" to obtain the signatures of the Mokabila witnesses. This implies that in the case of absence of signatures of the Mokabila witnesses the process server is required to explain in the report why it could not be possible to obtain the signatures. The absence of such an explanation also raises a reasonable suspicion that no Mokabila witness was at all present. In such a case it is the process server alone who may on oath in the witness box dispel the suspicion by giving satisfactory evidence. It is for this reason that the observation of the learned Additional District Judge that the process server ought to have been examined seems to be quite opposite. It was in this connection that he has referred to the decision reported in 25 D.L.R. 91 merely by way of putting emphasis upon his view of the necessity for further clarification, although it was neither necessary nor relevant for the purpose of the instant case, as the said decision relates to examination or the process server for preliminary satisfaction of the court receiving back the process in absence of any declaration.</u>

8. For the above reasons it is clear that the Court below has quite rightly disbelieved the story of due service or the summons upon Hara Mohan. The learned Additional District Judge has not committed any error of law in arriving at such a decision and in this view of the matter the judgment and order passed by him on the basis of such a decision calls for no interference in revision.

9. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
B.N. Chowdhury with G.G. Shaha ----- For the Petitioner.
Anwarul Huq Chowdhury, D.A.G. ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Sultanuddin Chowdhury ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
S.M. Husain, J.—This Rule arising out of an application under Article 102 of the Constitution directed against a taking over of the petitioner's property as a non-resident vested property by the Government.

2. The petitioner admittedly purchased the property from one Sushil Kumar Gangali by a kabala executed and registered at Badarganj Sub-Registry office in the district of Rangpur in 1975. The said Sushil Kumar Gangali had purchased the said property by a kabala executed and. registered at Calcutta in undivided British India in 1945. It is alleged that the said Sushil Kumar. Gangali was although a national and citizen of Pakistan and subsequently of Bangladesh and having always resided in East Pakistan and Bangladesh never migrated to India nor acquired the nationality and citizenship of India, only during the war of independence for nine months the said Sushil Kumar Gangali was away from in this country. In the affidavit-in-opposition by the Custodian of the vested property nothing has been alleged that the said Sushil Kumar Gangali ever acquired Indian nationality or that he, permanently resided in India and thereby became enemy national between September, 1965 and December, 1971. In this connection it may be mentioned that a kabala executed and registered in Bangladesh in 1975 creates a presumption that the registration authority satisfied that the executants was a valid citizen and national of Bangladesh since an Indian national as such could not transfer any property in Bangladesh by way of any registered deed. Mr. Anwarul Huq Chowdhury, the learned Deputy Attorney General appearing for the Government and Custodian of vested property has pointed out that notwithstanding the aforesaid kabalas the names of the petitioner and his immediate predecessor in interest Sushil Kumar Gangali do not appear in the records of rights. The records of rights of the Government which at best are evidence of possession at the time when such records are prepared and not an evidence of title as such. This is a well established principle of law. A registered kabala is an evidence of title which will prevail over the other records of rights as such until and unless such kabala is cancelled on a specific allegation of fraud by any civil court in an appropriate civil suit.

<u>3. In the foregoing facts and circumstances of the case the petitioner's valid purchase of the property from the said Sushil Kumar Gangali remains undisputed uptil now. This is quite evident from the order passed on 15.3.77 by Mr. M.A. Samad, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms of the Government of Bangladesh, wherein it was held that the petitioner's property was never listed as a vested property nor was it made khas property of the Government. In such circumstances it was further ordered that it was not necessary to treat the property in question to be under any unauthorized possession of the petitioner and on that account the petitioner's eviction was avoided. It is surprising to note that only after four months on 22.7.77 another order was passed by Mr. So. Hossain Khan, Joint Secretary in the Ministry of Land Administration and Reforms of the Government of Bangladesh wherein it was held that the property in question appeared to have been held as vested property and on 15.3.77 was reviewed and revised. In passing the subsequent order of 22.7.77 it was observed that the petitioner's title in the property in question was doubtful. Apart from the act that the petitioner's title is based upon valid purchase of the property by a duly registered deed. The authority in the Government could not question and annul the validity of such title by an executive order. If the Government wanted to claim in such property it could only do so by way of an appropriate suit for declaration of title and cancellation of the petitioner's registered kabala as such. Be that as it may it is surprising to note that a Joint Secretary in the Ministry of Land Reforms could revise an order passed only four months before by his predecessor, another Joint Secretary in the said Ministry of land Administration and Land Reforms. The subsequent order passed by Joint Secretary Mr. S. Hossain Khan on 22.7.77 is obviously based on illegal assumption of fact and as such suffers from clear illegality. The said impugned order being marked as Annexure B to the petition is accordingly set aside.</u>

<u>The Rule is therefore made absolute. There will be no. order as to costs.</u>

Sultan Hossain Khan, J.-I agree.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 59 of 1981
lawyer:
Habibul Islam Bhuiya, Advocate ------ For Appellant.
Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed ------ For Respondent.
parties:
Niropoma Ritchel ------ Appellant. 
Vs. 
Mohammad Abdul Jalil Mea & ors ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman, J.:—This appeal is directed against the Judgment and decree passed by the Additional Court of Subordinate Judge, Mymensingh in O.C. Suit No. 270/79 decreeing the plaintiffs suit for simple declaration of title.

 2. The plaintiff filed a Suit for declaration of his title in the suit land stating, inter alia, that defendant No. 1 Hemanta Kumar Areng while owned and possessed the Suit land entered into a contract to sell the suit land to the plaintiff at a consideration of Taka 45,000/-on 15.1.63. The plaintiff paid Taka 4,000/-as earnest money and a bainapatra was executed in favour of the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 put the plaintiff in possession of the suit land. Since then the plaintiff has been possessing the schedule land in assertion of his ownership by purchase openly, peacefully, continuously and adversely against defendants and others. The plaintiff installed flour and rice-mill, constructed a godown and sanitary latrine in the suit land. After purchase the plaintiff raised the level of the land which was lower at a cost of Taka 10,000/-. The defendant No. 1 with his family members migrated to India in March, 1964 with executing the registered sale-deed in pursuance of the agreement for sale. The defendant No. 2 who is the daughter of defendant No. 1 filed petition before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Welfare Mymensingh), defendant No.4 asserting her title to the suit property and seeking aid for getting possession by evicting the plaintiff therefrom. The defendant No. 4 sent the petition to the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar (North) for enquiry and after enquiry the relevant Magistrate directed the plaintiff to vacate the suit land and to hand over possession of the same to the defendant. The threat of the Magistrate and the claim of defendant No. 2 having cast a cloud on the plain-tiffs title, the suit was filed for a simple declaration.

 3. The defendant No. 2 alone contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit property did never belong to her father but it belonged to her mother MijiRichel. The contesting defendant inherited the suit property from her mother and in order to remove all doubts in respect of her title she filed O.C. Suit No. 95/66 in the 2nd Court of Munsif, Sadar, Mymensingh and obtained a decree on 2.5.67. After the death of defendant No.2's mother, the defendant No. 1 had no connection with this defendant and used to live with his second wife somewhere else. The contesting defendant constructed a shop but and a gadighar in the suit property and one NarendraAring was a bharatia and he used to run his business in the said gadighar godown. In 1964 Narendra left the country and in June, 1967 the suit premises was leased out to the plaintiff at a rental of Taka 50/-. The plaintiff paid rent to this defendant up to middle of 1975 and there-after did not pay any further rent and consequently this defendant was bound to submit an application to defendant No. 4 for eviction of the plaintiff from the suit land. The proceeding for eviction having been started by defendant No. 4 this suit was filed by the plaintiff. The defendant No. 2 also denied the con-tract of sale as set up by the plaintiff with defendant No. 1. According to this defendant, the bainapatra is a forged document and the suit is liable to be dis-missed. 

4. The trial Judge decreed the suit. Being aggrieved by that, present appellant has preferred thisappeal before this court. 
5. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiya, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant firstly submits that acquisition of title by adverse possession having not been claimed either in the plaint or at the trial and there being no evidence of claim by adverse possession from a specific point of time and admittedly the plaintiff having gone into possession by virtue of contract for sale and there being no specific pleading of Adverse Possession as such, the trial court acted illegally in declaring title on the basis of ad- verse possession alone. The learned Advocate next contends that in the suit no specific issue was framed by the parties regarding the acquisition of title by ad- verse possession and as such the trial court acted wrongly in law and fact in framing an issue of adverse possession suo motu and decreeing the suit on that basis alone. The learned Advocate lastly contends that the plaintiff having lawfully gone into possession by virtue of a contract for sale is entitled under law to retain his possession but he cannot file a suit for declaration simplicity on the basis of possessoryinterest. 

6. Mr. Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent submits that the trial Judge has acted correctly in declaring title in favour of the plaintiff on the basis of ad- verse possession alone. The learned Advocate further submits that there is an averment in paragraph I of the plaint that the plaintiff is possessing from 15.1.63 by virtue of a contract for. sale and the defendant No. 1 put him into possession-and this assertion of his ownership by purchase openly,  continuously and peacefully leads to the presumption of adverse possession in the facts of the present case. 

7. At the outset it is to be stated that the question of adverse possession is a mixed question of law and fact. Before going into this question of adverse possession, we will consider the plaint case as set up by the plaintiff in praying for a simple declaration of title. Admittedly the plaintiffs case is that there is a contract for sale on 15.1.63 and by virtue of the agreement for sale he got peaceful possession in the suit land as inducted by defendant NO.1. The plain- tiff asserted that since the date of agreement he is in peaceful possession of the suit land. The contesting defendant on the other hand also admits the possession of the plaintiff. Thus we find from the averment in the plaint that the defendant No. 1 has parted with his possession by an agreement for sale in favour of the plaintiff with a desire to register a sale-deed of title at some future point of time. The trial Judge found that defendant No. 1 executed a bainapatra in favour of the plaintiff and put the plaintiff in possession on the basis of that bainapatra. It is to be re- membered here that lawful possession and claiming adverse possession arc two distinct and separate things. The most essential element of adverse possession is that the possession of a property by a person having no right to possess the property and such possession must be adverse to the true owner. The question of adverse possession in a case is to be determined on the basis of the specific averment made in the plaint. On a reference to the plaint, it appears to us that the plaintiffs case is in substance one for declaration of title on the basis of an agreement for sale and possession and in so doing the plaintiff has just stated he is in continuous possession since that time. The learned Advocate for the respondent submits that the plaintiff is claiming possession by set- ting up a hostile title from the very inception of his possession. In other words, possession as set up by the plaintiff and as argued by the learned Advocate is referable to the date of agreement. We will refer here the oral and documentary evidences led by the parties in the instant case for proper understanding of the claim of plaintiffs adverse possession. P.W.! Abdul Jalil, the plaintiff deposed that he entered into a bainapatra with' the defendant No.1 on 15.1.63 and the defendant delivered possession to him from the date of execution of the bainapatra and since contract he is in possession of the suit land as purchaser. The plaintiff proved the bainapatra, Ext. 1. The plaintiff also admitted in cross-examination that he is willing to pay the balance consideration money to defendant No.1 for the agreement for sale. He also denied the suggestion of the contesting defendant that defendant No.1 had no interest in the suit land and he did not execute the bainapatra. P.W. 2 Md. Hosain, P.W. 3 Abdul Jabbar are all witnesses of bainapatra and they testified that the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land from 1963 on the basis of his purchase. P.W. 4 Golam Hossain testified that the plaintiff is in possession since 1963. P.W.5 Ruhul Amin is another witness of bainapatra and testified that the plaintiff is in possession since 1963. This is all the oral evidence that was adduced by the plaintiff in the case in pursuance of his pleading. There is assertion in the plaint that the plaintiff is in possession since agreement for purchase from the rightful owner and all the witnesses on the plaintiffs side have testified about the bainapatra and possession since that time. The plea of adverse possession as argued before us has of course not been specifically stated neither in the plaint nor in the deposition before the court. The material consideration in a case where title is declared on the basis of adverse possession is the starting point of limitation. We have already referred herein above that in the present case starting point is the date of agreement. Apart from this there is no assertion either in the plaint or in the deposition before the court that by plaintiff’s adverse possession for more than 12 years, the plaintiff has acquired title by adverse possession. 

8. It is needless to say that plea of adverse possession must be specifically set up in the plaint. We must say that apart from what has been mentioned above, it is difficult for us to say that there was any such specific plea either in the plaint or at the trial stage regarding adverse possession. We will refer here below to some statements of the law on adverse possession from Rustomji's well-known book on Limitation, page 610 (3rd edition). "It is not indispensable that the should be adverse in its inception. 

"Unless adverse in its inception, possession will be presumed to continue as it began, yet this does not preclude the occupant for setting up an adverse claim at any time he chooses by any act which changes the character of his occupancy from amicable to adverse" Again the learned Author says :-"Where a party is in possession of lands in probity with the original owner nothing short of an open and explicit disavowal and disclaimer of a holding under that title, and assertion of title in himself brought home to the owner, will satisfy the Law." 

9. These propositions are very well settled now. This being the Law, let us now examine whether in the fact of the present case, the decree that was passed by the trial court on the basis of adverse possession alone is sustainable in law and fac.. M. In the present case admittedly the plaintiff entered into possession on the basis of a contract and as such we are to see when he repudiated the contract and intended to claim possession in assertion of a hostile title. We could not lay our hands as to the point of time from where the plaintiff claimed ad-verse possession against the owner and, on the other hand, we only find that the plaintiff lawfully entered into possession and continued to remain so. Herein we will refer some of the reported decisions to appreciate the present case as to whether a decree for title could be given on the basis of adverse possession. In a case reported in ILR Born. series Vol. 7 page 34 it has been observed that, When a person entered into possession and re-mains in possession in the first instant in accordance with the contract he could not change the character of the possession by his mere will. To change such character he must repudiate the contract and intended to go into possession in opposition to any right which the owners might assert while there subsisted any contract, express or implied, between the patties in and out of possession to which the possession might be referred as legal and proper, it could not be pronounced as adverse. A reference may be made to the case reported in AIR 1958 Punjab 335. Wherein paragraph 6 reads as follows:-

"If possession is permissive and not antagonistic to the owner, it cannot ripen into title by mere possession. Thus the possession of a ten-ant is that of his landlord and will be so presumed until the contrary is proved by clear and convincing evidence, for every presumption is in favour of possession in subordination to the true owner. Although possession of a tenant, however full and complete, does not of itself operate as an ouster of the owner, the mere fact that a per-son enters as a tenant does not preclude him from asserting title against his landlord by adverse possession. It can operate as an ouster if he abandons the idea of holding as a tenant and sets up and adverts an exclusive right in him- self. He must either give notice of his claim or his possession should be accompanied by some overt act asserting an ownership of such an open, notorious and hostile character as not to be easily misunderstood." 

Same view has also been expressed in ILR Pat, Vol. 25 412. In that decision it has been held that a person who bases his title on adverse possession must show by clear and unequivocal evidence that his possession was hostile to the real owner and amounts to denial of his title, and that possession that is at its inception permissive must be shown to have been adverse by some subsequent changes in its character, notice actual or constructive, of which is given to the true owner. In that reported decision it has also been said that there is no difference in prin- ciple in considering the question of adverse possession as between the two co-owners and between a co- owner and a transferee from another co-owner. 

11. A case reported in PLD 1960 Azad Jammu & Kashamir page 26 may be mentioned. In that reported decision one Md. Afser Khan filed a suit for declaration against the appellant on the basis that he was in adverse possession of the suit land for more than 12 years on the basis of an agreement for sale and as such he prayed for declaratory decree that he is the owner of the land. The suit was' contested stating tinteralia, that the possession of Md. Afsar Khan could not be treated as adverse to others on the basis of an agreement for sale as Afsar Khan's possession under the contract for sale was of a permissive nature and could not be treated as adverse. The subordinate judge held that Afsar Khan's possession was not adverse and the District Judge held that the possession of Afsar Khan had ripened into owner- ship. In that reported decision the findings of the District Judge was set aside and the finding of the trial Judge was restored. The observation of their Lordships in that reported decision may be quoted as follows:- 

"When a contract for sale is executed it does not bestow any right of ownership on the person in whose favour it is executed until regular sale deed is executed. A Promise who is al- lowed to take possession of the land before a regular sale deed is executed merely holds it on behalf of the promisor and if the promisor is not willing to part with the possession the Promise cannot compel him in law to part with possession." 

Their Lordships further held in that decision that possession under a defective sale deed is different from possession under a contract for sale. In the former case the person in whose favour the sale deed is executed considers himself owner to all intents and purposes and there is a disclaimer of the vendor's title by open assertion of hostitle. Whereas in the latter case he docs not consider himself the owner and has yet to get a proper sale deed to become owner in the true sense of the term and his possession cannot be considered as hostile to the Promisor. Thus it becomes very much material for the plaintiff to assert as to from which point of time he disclaims the title of the owner and set up claim by adverse possession. The trial Judge declared the plaintiffs title on the basis of adverse possession without determining the starting point of limitation in the present case. If the starting point is the possession on the basis of an agreement then the plaintiff lawfully went into possession by virtue of a contract for sale. But can he get a declaration on the basis of adverse possession as found by the trial judge? On our query to Mr. Khondker Mahbub Uddin Ahmed as to how the trial court has declared title on the basis of adverse possession, he only referred to paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 of the plaint which in turn show that the plaintiff is in possession on the basis of contract and nothing else. In the plaint alternative title on the basis of adverse possession has not been pleaded and in the prayer portion as well there is no prayer that the possession of more than 12 years has matured into a title by adverse possession. This alternative claim must he clearly made and proved before a decree on the basis of adverse possession can be granted. The law requires a plea of adverse possession to be raised and decided to show when possession becomes ad- verse so that the starting point of limitation against the party affected could be found. It may further be mentioned here that in the relevant paragraphs also there is not a word that the plaintiff is in uninterrupted possession for 12 years and that plaintiff had acquired absolute title by adverse possession for continuous and peaceful possession for more than 12 years. Thus we find that the first point raised by the learned Advocate for the appellant that the trial Judge without reference to the plaint and evidence on record wrongly decreed the suit on the question of adverse possession is correct. It is needless to say that from a review of the cases as mentioned herein above, the requirements to make possession adverse vary according to the peculiar facts of each case and relation- ships of the parties and other like circumstances in which the adverse possession commences. To take up the second point of the learned Advocate for the appellant we find that issues were framed by Order No. 26 dated 5.5.79 and the following issues were framed:- 
1. Has the plaintiff any cause of action of the suit? 
2.	Is the suit maintainable in its present form? 
3.	Is the story of contract between plff.and defendant genuine? 
4.	Is the plaintiff in possession of suit land? 
5.	Is the plff. entitled to get a decree as prayed for: 
6. What relief if any is the plff.entitled to? 

At the trial the learned Subordinate Judge took up an additional issue to the effect. "Has the plaintiff acquired any title to the suit land by adverse possession " There is nothing on record to show that the trial court gave notice to the parties and amended the issues but formulated this issue suomotu and de- creed the suit on this issue alone. In the case of Miser Ali Vs. Abdul Rashid and others reported in 5 DLR 490 Ibrahim, J. observed as follows:- 

"I must say at the very outset that the learned Munsif should not have allowed the plaintiff to set up a case of adverse possession at the last moment during the argument. The plaintiff never set up any such case in his plaint. The question of acquisition of title by adverse possession involves questions of both law and fact. The plaintiff having never set up such a case in the plaint, cannot succeed in this suit on the theory that he acquired title by adverse possession. The facts made it absolutely clear that the case is governed by Article 142 of the Limitation Act. The plaintiff had to establish two things affirmatively, firstly, that he had title, and, secondly, that his suit was not too remote from the date of his dispossession, or, in other words, that he was in possession within twelve years before the institution of the suit. Even if his possession is made out, he cannot succeed, if the title lies with the defendant." 

12. It is really surprising to note that a decree has been passed on the basis of adverse possession alone without framing any issue on such vital question of law and fact. On our query Mr. KhondkerMahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate could not lay his hand on any material piece of evidence and .the averment in the plaint on which such a decree .could be passed in the present case.
