Thus we find that the trial court was not justified in raising the plea of adverse possession suomotu by not framing any issue on this point and this is not a defect in the proceeding itself but material defect in substance and as such the second point of the learned Advocate for the appellant must succeed. 

13. With regard to the last point raised by the learned Advocate for the appellant it is to be stated that the plaintiff filed a simple suit for declaration on the basis of agreement for sale. It is true that to protect plaintiffs possessory right in the property he can file a suit to protect his possession alone. The plaintiff has not acquired any title by the bainapatra Ext. I, but he has certainly acquired a right to protect his possession as a shield and not as a sword and the possessory right is available to the plaintiff who is not a trespasser. But in the facts of the present case we hold that on the basis of the agreement alone such a suit for declaration simplicity could not be filed. The agreement for sale being not per se a document of title, the suit for simple declaration as framed is not maintainable. 
	
In the result, the judgment and decree of the trial court are set aside and the appeal is allowed without any order as to cost and the suit is dismissed. 

Let the records of the case be sent down at once. 

End.

lawyer:
Abu Taher Chowdhury ----- For the Petitioner.
M. Fazul Karim ----- For the Opposite Party No.1.
parties:
Abul Basher Chowdhury ----- Petitioner
vs.
Mehar Khatun ----- Opp.-Party
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J: The question involved in this Rule is whether the appellate Court below has the power to review its own judgment under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the appeal having arisen from a proceeding u/s. 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for pre-emption.

2. The miscellaneous case was allowed by the trial Court. The appellate Court below set aside the judgment and order of the trial Court and dismissed the miscellaneous case on the ground that since it was filed before the registration of the kabala under pre-emption, it was premature. The pre-emptor opposite party thereafter filed an application under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure for a review of the lower appellate Court's judgment and filed a certified copy of the kabala under pre-emption. The learned successor Subordinate Judge found that the kabala under pre-emption was registered u/s. 60 of the Registration Act on 30.10.73. The miscellaneous case for pre-emption was filed on 12.6.73 and the trial Court allowed the Miscellaneous case on 24.4.76. It held that the premature character of the miscellaneous case was cured during the pendency of the pre-emption proceeding. The appellate Court below therefore allowed the pre-emptor's application for review, dismissed the miscellaneous appeal and upheld the judgment and order of the trial Court allowing the miscellaneous case.

Thereafter the pre-emptee-petitioner obtained the present Rule.

3. Mr. Abu Taber Chowdhury, learned Advocate for the petitioner, does not challenge the merit of the order passed on review. He challenge the very jurisdiction of the lower appellate Court to review its own order. He submits that the appellate Court below exercised the power of the appellate Court because the provisions of a special statue, namely, section 96(12) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act conferred on it the powers of an appellate Court. No power to review the appellate decree or order has been granted to the appellate Court by the said special statue. Mr. Chowdhury submits that both the right of appeal and the right of review are substantive rights, and not merely procedural rights, and unless a special Act or statute confers the right of review specifically, no appellate Court, assuming jurisdiction under a special Act or statute can exercise the right of review under Order 47 rule I of the Code of Civil Procedure

4. Mr. Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate for the pre-emptor opposite party No. 1, on the other hand relies upon section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure which provides that the procedure provided in the Code in regard to suits shall be followed, as far as it can be made applicable, in all proceedings in any Court of Civil jurisdiction. He submits that the remedy of a review under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code is a procedural remedy and not a substantive right. As such the lower appellate Court has every jurisdiction to review its own order.

5. When a regular suit is filed, it is not difficult to see that all the remedies provided for in the Code of Civil Procedure, including appeal and review, are available to the pal ties. But when a suit is filed under a special statute and the special statute confers only the right of appeal, maintaining silence over the right of review, can it be said that section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure may be pressed into service and the remedy of review may be made available to the parties?

6. This question has been answered in the negative in at least two case cited from the Bar. In the case of Mst Maqsoodan Bibi vs. Mst. Blzano, PLD 1965 (Lahore) 181, the facts are that a Guardian Judge ordered the return of a petition for appointment of a guardian of the person and property of a minor on the ground that he had no jurisdiction in the case. Upon review of the said order the Guardian Judge assumed jurisdiction in the case. It fell for determination before a learned Single Judge of the High Court of West Pakistan (Lahore Bench) as to whether the order passed under the Guardians and Wards Act can be reviewed. It was held as follows:

"Relying on section 141, C.P.C., it was next argued that the orders passed by a Guardian Judge can be reviewed under "section 114, read with Order XLVII, Rule 1, C.P.C. a is specifically provided in section 141, C.P.C. that, the procedure provided in this Code in regard to suits shall be followed, so far as.it can be made applicable, in all proceedings in any Court of Civil jurisdiction. There can be no denying the fact that the Guardian Court is a Court of Civil jurisdiction and a proceeding under the Guardians and Wards Act is a proceeding in the Court of Civil jurisdiction. The Code undoubtedly applies to the procedure of all Courts of Civil I jurisdiction. The provisions of the Code, therefore, will be applicable to regulate the procedure of a Guardian Court. This provision, however, cannot be pressed into service to say that where the Code has created certain substantive Fights like the right of an appeal or review, the same also become applicable in similar proceedings in all Courts of Civil Jurisdiction. The right of an appeal or review is a substantive right and not a mere right of procedure. Taus section 141, C.P.C. is not applicable in this Case, and the provisions of the Code providing for an appeal or review are not attracted to proceedings under the Guardians and Wards Act."

The decision .cited above was followed by another learned Single Judge of the Karachi Bench of the High Court of West Pakistan in the case of M.Y. Siddiqi Vs. Bavaqar Co, Ltd., PLD 1968 (Karachi) 231. It was held therein that the provisions of section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure do not make Order 47 applicable to proceedings held under the Companies Law, the reason of inapplicability being the distinction between procedural and substantive provision.

With respect, the views expressed in the said two decisions do not commend to me. They do not take into account the provision of section 114 and Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

7. Section 114 of the Code of Civil Procedure contains the provisions for review in the following terms:-

"Review- Subject as aforesaid, any person considering himself aggrieved-

(a) by a decree or order from which an appeal is allowed by this Code, but from which no appeal has been preferred.

(b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is allowed by this Code, or

(c) by a decision on a reference from a Court of Small Causes, may apply for a review of judgment to the Court which passed the decree or made the order, and the Court may make such order thereon as it thinks fit."

8. It was held in a few decisions that the words "appeal is allowed by this Code" in section 114(a) and (b) restrict the scope of review only to those judgments passed in the exercise of jurisdiction derived from the Code of Civil Procedure. Thus the Allahabad High Court held by a majority judgment in a Full Bench decision in the case of Mt. Abilakhi Vs. Sada Nand ILR 53 All 535: AIR 1931 All 244 as follows :-

"The criterion in sec. 114(a) and (b) whether an appeal is allowed by the Code would not be introduced if the section were intended to apply to judgments passed in the exercise of jurisdiction not derived from the Code." ,

9. This decision was overruled by a unanimous Full Bench decision of the Allahabad High Court in the case of Jwata Prashad V. Jwala Bank Ltd. (in liquidation), AIR 1961. All 381. Srivastava, J. observed as follows:

"With the utmost respect I find it difficult to see the justification for referring to the jurisdiction in the exercise of which the judgment sought to be reviewed was made. That jurisdiction mayor may not have been derived from the Code. The fact appears to be immaterial. What is really to be seen for the application of sec. 114 is whether the decree or order which followed the judgment was or was not appealable under the Code. Irrespective of the source of jurisdiction under which the matter came to the Court, if procedure to be followed was that laid down in the Code the test for deciding whether the order or judgment passed was reviewable or not was whether under the Code the decree or order was appealable There appears to be nothing in section 114 to require that the proceeding in which the judgment to be reviewed was passed should have been one which, was either permitted or not permitted by the Code."

<u>10. I am in respectful agreement with the ratio dividend of the aforesaid decision. The appellate Court below assumed jurisdiction to hear and dispose of the miscellaneous appeal not because the jurisdiction was conferred by the Code of Civil Procedure, but because section 96(12) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act conferred jurisdiction upon the Civil Court. In deciding whether a review of the appellate order of decree will lie or not, it is immaterial how the appellate Court below came to exercise the jurisdiction, Section 114 (a) and (b) set down only one yardstick—whether the order 'or decree of which a review is sought for is appealable under the Code or not. If it is appealable and no appeal has been preferred, the case will fall under clause (a) of section 114; if it is not, the case will fall under clause (b). In the present case no second appeal is provided for in the Code itself against the appellate decree or order. It falls squarely under clause (b) section 114.</u>

<u>11. With respect I am also unable to hold that the right or review, as farmed under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, is a substantive right like the right of appeal. Whether the right of review is a substantive right or a procedural right depends, in my opinion, upon the extent of power granted to the reviewing authority. If the powers of the reviewing authority are co-extensive with the powers of the appellate Court, then it Can be reasonably held that the right of review is a substantive right, but if the power of review is so circumscribed that it can be described as no more than a more correcting agency, then I do not see why, this power should be equated with the appellate power and why the right of review should be regarded as a substantive right. A bare reading of Order 47 rule 1 will show that the review may be granted only under specific circumstances to meet certain specific situations and not for re-opening the order of decree on any pretext. A party to a decree or order may have discovered a new and important matter of evidence which was not within his know-ledge or could not be produced by him after the exercise of due diligence when the decree was passed or order made. Or there may be some clerical or arithmetical mistake or error apparent on the face of the record or there may be any other sufficient reason within the meaning of order 47 rule 1 which, if present, would give jurisdiction to the reviewing authority to review the decree or order passed earlier. To say that this remedy amounts to granting the parties a substantive right is to ignore the, character of benefits conferred by Order 41 rule 1. The benefits arisa out of special situations and they confer special procedural benefits. They confer no substantive right of reopening and re-agitating the decree or order afresh. They confer a special procedural remedy to the parties if only their case is covered within the narrow limits of Order 47 rule 1. The provision of section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure seems to be fully applicable under the circumstances. For all the above reasons I do not think that the impugned 'order of the appellate Court below calls for any interference in revision.</u>

In the result the rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 405 of 1978, With C.R. No. 1169 (s) of 1979
lawyer:
B. N. Chowdhury ----- For the appellant
A. Khaleque ----- For the respondent.
parties:
Amulla Kumar Ghose  ----- Appellant
Vs.
Khama Prava Haldar ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
This appeal at the instance of the defendant Amulla Kumar Ghose is against the judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, First Court, Barisal, affirming those passed by learned Munsif, First Court, Barisal, in a suit for eviction of the defendant from the suit premises and recovery of arrear rents, with compensation also and for permanent injunction.

2. Plaintiff's case, in short, is that the defendant took monthly lease of the suit premises from the plaintiff at rental of Tk. 16/- per month on the basis of an oral agreement. He paid upto the month of Kartick, 1371 B S. but defaulted thereafter, when through the intervention of Babu Prosanna Kumar Datta, the defendant paid Taka 75/- when rents for the months of Agrahayan to Chaitra again became due and deducting Taka 75/- taka 5/-was still due when the plaintiff enhanced the tent to Taka 20/- from the month of Baisakh, 1372 B,S. with knowledge of the defendant. As the defendant became a habitual defaulter and the plaintiff having require) the premises for her own use she served a notice upon the defendant under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act but the said notice was returned to the plaintiff on 13.3.1975 as refused. The plaintiff again served a notice upon the defendant but the said could not be traced out after it was posted so the plaintiff again served a notice terminating the tenancy by expiry of the month Bhadra, 1382 B.S. claiming arrear, rents. The defendant refused to accept the notice this time also and the postmen returned the notice to the plaintiff's Advocate on 1.9.1975. The defendant would neither pay nor vacate hence the suit

3. Defendant No. 1 contested the suit denying all the material allegations made in the plaint contending that he had paid rent upto the month of Falgoon, 1377 B.S. regularly; that during the war of liberation be left for India leaving his shop but returned in the month of Magh, 1378 B.S. when he found that the plaintiff had looted away all the properties of the defendant that were in his grocers shop. The defendant demanded looted properties and possession of the suit premises when it was settled in a local salish that the plaintiff would pay Take 2,500/- to the defendant as value of the looted properties giving back possession of the premises. It was also settled that the said money could be adjusted against the monthly rent of the premises. So the defendant was not a defaulter.

<u>4. The Court of first instance on a consideration of the pleadings of the parties and the Evidence on record came to a finding that the defendant was a defaulter as there in fact existed no such looting, no such salish and no such agreement as to adjustment of the arrear rents. In that View of the matter the suit was decreed on contest with costs. On appeal the said was affirmed by the learned Additional District Judge. An against that this appeal has been preferred by the defendant.</u>

<u>I have heard Mr. B. N: Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the appeal and Mr. Md. Abdul Khaleque, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent. Perused the judgment and examined the evidence on record Mr. B. N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the appeal, has urged that the Court of appeal below erred in not considering that in view of the defendant denial of having received any quit notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, the burden would be however upon the plaintiff to prove the existence of any such notice and said burden could never be discharged without examining the postal peon as to service and this having not been done in the instant case the Court of appeal below erred in holding that notice was duly issued and tendered. He has next urged that the Court of appeal below came to a Ending of fact erroneously without considering the witnesses for the defendant and the surrounding circumstances of the case as to the question of the defendant being a defaulter Mr. A. Khaleque, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent, on the other hand, has urged that in view of provisions of section 114 (1) of the Evidence Act there would exist a legal presumption in the facts of the instant case to the effect that the notice had reached the addressee in due course after it had been proved to have been posted and the legal presumption being in favour of the plaintiff the burden would be upon the defendants to prove otherwise. He has further urged that Court of appeal below on a consideration of the evidence on record and particularly the fact that in the absence of any complaint made by the defendant as to looting of his articles of the grocer shop on his return from India with any police station and on a consideration of the evidence of the defendant himself to the effect that he never did know as to who had looted his articles but only heard about it from others who never came to depose, came to a finding that there existed no looting and hence no salish and also no award as to which salish there is also no documentary evidence and hence it could not be said that the Court of appeal below came to a finding of fact as to the defendant being a defaulter upon a non-consideration of the material witnesses for the defendants. There is enough substance in the contentions of the learned Advocate and it needs to be sustained. The only point that arises for the disposal of the appeal is whether the defendant was legally found to be defaulter and whether a notice under section 106 of the T.P. Act was validly issued and tendered. On a reference to the evidence on record it is seen that the notice under section 106 of the T.P. Act was posted at the office address of the defendant as to which address no exception was taken by the defendant at the time of hearing of this appeal or at the trial. It is further seen that the postal cover under which the notice was sent bears the endorsement of the postal peon to the effect that it was refused. Now, the defendant argues that the same would not by itself be an evidence of due service unless it would be corroborated by the postal peon and prove the endorsement and its refusal. There is no substance in this contention also because if a letter is found to have been properly addressed and posted but returned with the endorsement. "refused", the presumption under section 114(f) of the Evidence Act would be that it was presented to the addressee and he had refused to receive it and in such a case it would not be necessary to call the postal peon to prove the endorsement and refusal. This is well settled and supported by a number of decisions and of good authorities. In the case reported in 27 C.W.N. at page 1073, a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court in deciding a similar matter as to notice terminating a tenancy observed in the relevant portion thus:-</u>

<u>"It is suggested that the tender and the refusal by the defendant of the cover containing the notice was not sufficiently proved by the endorsement on the cover or envelop. That contention, however, is met by the decision of the Court of Exchequer in England in the case of Papillon vs. Brunton, and the decision of this Court in the case of Jogendra Chunder Ghose vs. Dwarka Nath Karmokar. In the latter case it was held that "proof of the posting of a notice in registered cover and the production of the cover in Court, that cover containing the notice with an endorsement upon it purporting to be by an officer of the Post Office stating the refusal by the defendant to receive the document" was sufficient proof of service. The circumstances here are very similar and the Judge was therefore at liberty to find as he found."</u>

5. In the case of Sultan Ahmed Vs. Syed Ahmed, reported in (1967) 19 D.L.R. at page 42, Murshed, C.J. in the matter of eviction of a tenant and the corresponding notice issued under section 106 of the T.P. Act, observes in the relevant portion of his judgment, thus:

''The question then is, has the notice been served validly? It has been proved that it was sent by post to the address of the defendant and that it has come back to plaintiff on refusal by defendant to accept service of the said notice. The postal cover under which the notice was sent bears the endorsement of the postal peon to the effect that it was refused. It is therefore, clear that the appellate Court below has rightly held that the said tenancy was terminated by a good notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act and that it has been properly served, as required by law.

6. I am in respectful agreement with the observations above which are in complete accord with the view I have taken hereinbefore to the effect that when a letter is properly addressed and posted but was returned with the endorsement "refused" the presumption would be that it was presented to the addressee and that he refused to receive it and the proof of the endorsement would be enough to prove a valid service and it would not be necessary to call the postal peon to prove the endorsement and the refusal. In that view of the matter I find no substance in the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant to the effect that the postal peon ought to have been examined to prove the endorsement and refusal in order to constitute a valid service.

7. The defendant's specific case was that during the liberation war he went to India leaving his grocer's shop at the mercy of the Pak Army but when he returned from India he found that the plaintiff's party men had looted away his articles from the grocer's shop and the plaintiff's party was running the said shop. The plaintiff herself deposed before the Court categorically denying this allegation. According to her, the defendant did go to India and returned after liberation but no damage was caused to his grocer's shop either by the plaintiff or by anybody else as the defendant continued his business and possess-session even after liberation. On a reference to the evidence on record it is seen that the neighboring shop-keepers deposed to say that during the liberation period this particular shop was kept under lock and key by the defendant shop-owner and after he returned from India be again started his grocer shop without any damage being caused to his property. The report of the Revenue Deputy Collector in this regard stows that this particular shop was not damaged during the liberation period. All these were considered by the Court of first instance and it came to the view that the allegations that the plaintiff looted away his articles from the grocer's shop during his absence and as compensation he was obliged to pay though a salish an amount of Tk. 2,500/-to the defendant which sum was agreed to be readjustment against arrears of rent to be without any basis and thereby found the defendant to be a defaulter. The Court of appeal below having found on a further consideration that the defendant himself stated that he never had lodged any complaint with any police station regarding the looting of his properties by the plaintiff after he came to know of it and his testimony to the effect that he never saw the plaintiff looting his property but only heard from others and also on a further consideration of the fact that there existed no documentary evidence as to any salish or any inventory of the property allegedly looted and the value thereof, came to a finding that there existed no looting. The defendant was found to be a defaulter by the Court of appeal below concurring with the finding of the Court of first instance with cogent reasons.

Appreciation of evidence is a question of fact but a non-consideration of a material evidence may be a question of law if the testimony of the said witnesses would cut at the root of the findings arrived at by the Court, which is not the case here.

<u>8. At the time of hearing of this appeal, the point that proper issues were not framed at the trial was not agitated, rather it was admitted that such a point could be agitated only if it had caused prejudice. It is well settled that defective framing of issues or absence of proper issues being framed is merely an irregularity not effecting the merits of the case, if evidence were led and the parties fought out the case knowing the points to be answered causing no prejudice; absence of proper issues would not affect the judgment and decree. In the case of Mussumat Mitna Vs. Syed Fuzl Rub 13 Moors Indian Appeal at page 573, their Lordships of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council observed thus:</u>

<u>"Their Lordships, in coming to this conclusion, have had regard to the circumstance that no objection seems to have been taken in the Court below to dealing with the case without the settlement of the issues. If the objection had been taken, their Lordships think that the appellant would have stood on higher grounds, and it would then have been very difficult to say that a trial, proceeding in the face of the objection, could be held to be regular for any purpose. They do not however, mean to affirm that mere waiver or rather the omission to take the objection is in all cases sufficient to purge the irregularity. They are of opinion that if it had appeared that substantial justice had not been done, the objection might well have been taken when it was taken before the appellate Court and when taken ought to have prevailed. But being of opinion that there has not in the case been a failure of justice in consequence of the omission to settle the issues, their Lordships are not prepared to send it back for further litigation, and they must; therefore, advise Her Majesty to dismiss the appeal with costs."</u>

<u>I am in respectful agreement with the observation as above.</u>

<u>No other points urged and all the points having been found against the appellant, I find no substance in this appeal which needs to be dismissed.</u>

9. In the result, this appeal is dismissed. The judgment and decrees of both the Courts below with the modification as made by the Court of appeal below is hereby affirmed but in the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs before this Court.

Connected Rule being Civil Rule No. 1169(s) of 1978 and ordering an interim stay of Title Execution Case No. 11/77 till disposal by this Court vide order dated 2.8.78 is hereby vacated and the Rule is discharged accordingly.

End.

lawyer:
Md. Fazlul Karim ----- For the Appellant
Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Fida M. Kamal ----- For the Respondent
parties:
Gopal Chandra Mondol ----- Appellant
Vs.
Lashmat Dasi ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff Sree Gopal Chandra Mondal and others is against the judgment and decree of the learned Special and Additional District Judge, Dacca, reversing those passed by the learned Munsif Second Court Narayangonj in a suit for partition

The plaintiff's case may briefly be stated as follows: That the suit property originally belonged to Gour Majhi who had 2 sons namely Defendant No. 1 and Nagar Mondal. Nagar Mondal pre-deceased his father leaving the plaintiff Debendra Mondal as his only son. After the death of Gour Majhi the plaintiff as grand-son of Gour Majhi and defendant No. 2 Jagadish as his son became the heirs of Gour Majhi in equal shares. The plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 have been possessing the suit land jointly as co-sharers but due to some difficulties the plaintiff requested the defendant No. 1 for an amicable partition of the land in suit but the defendant did not agree and hence this suit for partition. Jagadish defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement Defendant Nos. 2, 3, and 5, the transferees from Lakhan Dasi, daughter of defendant No. 1 also appeared and contested the suit by filing another joint written statement. Defendant No. 1 in his written statement denied all the material allegations made in the plaint contending, inter alia that the plaintiff is a stranger to the property, having no right, title, interest and possession of the land in suit. It was further alleged that the suit land originally belonged to Gour Majhi who died leaving only one son defendant No. 1 and he had no other son by the name of Nagar Mondal. The said Nagar Mondal was the son of Gour Majhi's brother Keroly Majhi, Nagar Mondal, son of Keroly Majhi married the daughter of one Hari Charan Mondal and lived in Hari Charan Mondal's house as a domesticated son-in-law. Nagar Mondal always lived in his father-in-law's house leaving behind the plaintiff as his son and the plaintiff also had always been living in that house of his maternal uncle and not in the suit homestead. The plaintiff has no interest in the suit and being not a co-sharer the suit needs to be dismissed. Defendant Nos. 2, 3, and 5 contended that Gour  Majhi died leaving only one son namely Jagadish (Defendant No. 1) who died leaving one daughter in Lakhan Desi and that Jagadish during his Iife time made a gift of the suit land in favour of Lakhan Dasi by a registered deed of gift and Lakhan Dasi sold the suit land to defendant Nos. 2, 3, and 5 by a registered sale deed and they have been possessing the land in suit since the said purchase. Their further case was that Nagar Mondal was the son of Gour Majhi's brother Keroly Majhi and never the son of Gour Majhi, that the plaintiff was the grand-son of Keroly. Majhi, brother of Gour Majhi and not of Gour Majhi and hence the plaintiff has no right, title and interest as a co-sharer in the property of Gour Majhi.

2. On these pleadings the parties fought out the suit. The court of first instance on a consideration of the evidence on record both oral and documentary came to the view that the defendant No. 1 had the onus to prove that the plaintiff was not the grand-son of Gour Majhi and he having failed to prove so the plaintiff would be considered to have proved that he was the son of Gour Majhi and that being the position the plaintiff would be a co-sharer of the suit land and therefore would be entitled to partition, holding further that the absence of the name of the plaintiff in the rent receipts, S A. Khatian and land acquisition case records, would not prove that the plaintiff was not a co-sharer and would not deprive the plaintiff from his share in the suit land. In that view of the matter the suit was decreed on contest without costs, in preliminary form. On appeal the said judgment was reversed by the learned Additional District Judge, on a finding that the court of first instance erred in law in shifting the onus upon the defendant to prove that the plaintiff was not the grand-son of Gour Majhi and allowed the appeal on a finding that the plaintiff was never the grand-son of Gour Majhi, but was the grand-son of ptoly Majhi, brother of Gour Majhi and thus had no interest and was not a co-sharer in the partible land and as such he could claim 8 annas share thereof on partition. In that view of the matter, the impugned judgment and decree of the learned Munsif were set aside and the original title suit bearing No. 171 of 1969 was dismissed. As against that the plaintiff has preferred this appeal to this court.

3. Mr. Md. Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the appeal, having taken me through the judgment of both the courts below and the evidence on record, has urged that the court of appeal below erred in finding that the onus was upon the plaintiff to prove that he was the grand-son of Gour Majhi in view of the fact that it was the defendant who was pleadings in the negative and the onus was therefore upon the defendant to prove so. It was next contended that the court of appeal below erred in taking into consideration the entry in the record of right, the rent receipts and the L.A. case records in deciding pedigree when in fact those papers were not papers relating to genealogy and hence not relevant to form an opinion, as provided under section 50 of the Evidence Act. These papers could not be regarded as part of the family conduct to prove relationship. It was lastly argued by the learned lawyer that the court of appeal below erred in law in coming to a finding of fact as to relationship of the plaintiff with Gour Majhi on a total non-consideration of the oral evidence on record which were quite sufficient for such a finding on either way.

4. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the respondent, on the other hand, has urged that the court of appeal below in arriving at the finding of fact committed no error of law or procedure as the documentary evidence relied upon by the court of appeal below were relevant and admissible document to lent support to the witnesses deposed in favour of the defendants and would be a very strong circumstantial piece of evidence in deciding family conduct and hence it could not be said that the court erred in law in arriving at finding of fact on a consideration of irrelevant evidence.

5. In the instant suit there was no dispute that Gour Majhi was the original owner of property in question. There was also no dispute that there existed a person called Nagar Mondal the father of the plaintiff. The issue was whether the said Nagar Mondal was the other son of Gour Majhi and thus a brother of defendant No. 1 or a son of Keroly Majhi, brother of Gour Majhi and thus a cousin of defendant No. 1. The court of first instance in view of the pleadings of the parties framed Issue No. 3 thus:

Is the plaintiff a co-sharer of the schedule properties If so what is the extent of his share."

<u>6. It was framed so by the court as it was the duty of the plaintiff to prove that he  was a co sharer of the property in question in order to be entitled to ask for partition. To prove that co-sharer-ship of the property the plaintiff has also to prove that he was the co-owner and that he was a co-owner because he was an heir of the original owner. The law is that the person who pleads in the affirmative of the issues is to prove the same. In the instant case the affirmative of the issue was whether the plaintiff was the grand-son of Gour Majhi and thus a co-sharer of, the partible land. There is, therefore, no error caused by the court of appeal below in coming to the view that the onus was upon the plaintiff to prove by admissible evidence that he was the grand-son of Gour Majhi and thus a co-sharer of think property left by Gour Mjahi, which was illegally shifted upon the defendant by the court of first instance. A finding of fact arrived at by wrongly shifting the onus is erroneous and cannot stand the scrutiny of law. Only on this ground the finding of fact of the court of first instance is liable to be set aside.</u>

<u>7. It was next contended by Mr. Fazlul Karim that the court of appeal below erred in taking into consideration the exhibits in considering the question of pedigree as they were not relevant to prove any family conduct within the meaning of Section 50 of the Evidence Act. The information gathered from the entry in S.A. Khatian, the L.A. case records and the rent receipts were not opinions of persons who had special means of knowledge in proving relationship. I do not find much substance in that contention. Under section 50 of the Evidence Act, opinion, belief or judgment of a person, having special means of knowledge as members of the family or otherwise of the relationship between two persons are relevant. Under section 144 of the Evidence Act, a court may presume the existence of any fact which it thinks likely to happen regard been had to the common course of natural events and human conduct. Section 50, read with section 114 of the Evidence Act would make the conduct of the members of a family, evidenced by the acceptance of the members of the family, the devolution and distribution of the family property amongst its, members, a very valuable evidence of family conduct, as contemplated under section 50 of the Evidence Act. In the instant case it is seen that the partible land in suit stood in the S.A. khatian solely in .the name of defendant No. 1 without its being objected to by the plaintiff at any point of time. If the plaintiff was the co-owner or a' co-sharer of the property left by Gour Majhi he would have made some attempt to rectify the mistakes in recording the co-sharer property in the khatian in the sole name of defendant No. 1. It. is further seen that in the Tahsil office the jama in respect of the partible land also stood in the name of defendant No. 1. It stood there unchallenged and uncertified by the plaintiff although. It is seen from the rent receipts that the defendant No. 1 always paid the rent for the whole property and there is nothing on record to show that the plaintiff ever paid rent for his own share and if defendant No. 1 and the plaintiffs were equal owners it is not understood as to why defendant No. 1 would be obliged to pay for the whole. It further appears that a portion of the partible land was acquired in L.A. case No. 2 of 1966 and it is seen that in that L.A case the compensation was assessed in the name of defendant No. 1 alone who withdrew the compensation money without any protest from the plaintiff. If the plaintiff was 8 annas shareholder of the property he would also be 8 annas owner of the compensation money and the entire amount could not be paid to one co-sharer without the authority of another. This clearly shows that the plaintiff was never a co-sharer to the extent of 8 annas share of the property as claimed. Those exhibits were documentary evidence and they would have been enough for a finding as to the alleged co-ownership of the property to the extent of 8 annas by the plaintiff which was the subject matter of the partition suit and the learned court of appeal below on a consideration of the testimony of both the P.Ws. and D.Ws. found those to be equal on both sides and hence it considered the documentary evidence as a corroborating evidence to lend support to the oral testimony of persons, who were considered by the Court to have special means of knowledge as members of the family or otherwise, to testify to the relationship of the plaintiff with Gour Majhi. Those statements found on various Government records as to distribution and devolution of the family property and as to ownership, was rightly considered by the Court of appeal below as a piece of evidence of family conduct under section 50 of the Evidence Act is pedigree as a relevant circumstantial evidence, corroborating the testimony of the witnesses.</u>

<u>8. In the case of Seshammat Vs. Kuppanatyyangar, reported in A.I.R 1926 Madras, at page 475 their Lordships of the Division Bench of the Madras High Court in similar matters of pedigree, held thus:</u>

<u>"It is true that distribution and devolution of family property is often very valuable evidence of conduct under section 50 But in this case the material is wanting from which any inference in favour of the plaintiff can be drawn. It is possible that Cuppanniyya purchased as a stranger might have done, the property which was once in the possession of Krishna Mandchari. It is for the plaintiffs to make that there was devolution of property which would support their case. The statement of the learned Judge that the natural inference is that there was a family partition is not borne out by any evidence."</u>

<u>I am in respectful agreement with the observation as above, which is in complete accord with the view I have taken herein before to the effect that evidence as to devolution and distribution of family property would be a very valuable circumstantial evidence of conduct of the family members under section 50 of the Evidence Act and would be a very relevant evidence to prove pedigree and relationship between the members of the family.</u>

9. It was next argued by Mr. Fazlul Karim that the Court of appeal below erred in coming to a finding of fact as to relationship on a non-consideration of the oral evidence on record and hence the said finding was bad in law. This also appears to be of no substance as on a reference to the impugned judgment it is seen that the Court of appeal below after considering the testimony of the P.Ws. and D.Ws. found them to be equal and balanced and therefore found it unsafe to rely on the testimony of either side without considering those evidence in the light of the circumstantial evidence as evidenced by the documentary evidence on record. This finding of fact arrived at by the Court of appeal below, which is the ultimate Court of fact. on a consideration of both oral and documentary evidence on record need not be interfered with in appeal as those were not arrived at causing any error of law or procedure affecting the merits of the case. It could not be said to be a finding arrived at without consideration of the material facts and circumstances on which the trial Court based its decision. The finding as to the ancestry of a party is a finding of fact and need not be very lightly interfered with on an appeal.

No other points urged, all the points having failed, I find no substance in this appeal.

In the result, the appeal is dismissed. The Judgment and decree of the Court of the Additional District Judge, Dacca are hereby affirmed. But in the facts and circumstances of the case the parties are directed to bear their own costs.

End.

lawyer:
Mostafa Kamal with Lutful Karim ----- For the Petitioners. 
R. Hoque with T. Islam ----- For the respondents.
parties:
Mahmudur Rahman and others ----- Petitioners.
vs.
Monipur Tea Company Ltd. and another ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
This application for winding up under section 162 clauses (v) and (vi) read with section 163(1) clause (iii) of the Companies Act, 1913 (hereinafter called the Act) has been presented by four petitioners holding approximately 16% Of the shareholding interest in the Company, namely, Manipur Tea Company Ltd. a private limited company, which was incorporated in 1954, the objects inter alia being to carry on the business of planters, growers, cultivators, producers, manufacturer, buyers and sellers of tea. The subscribed and paid up capital of the Company. is Tk. 10,00,000/-(ten  lacs) divided into ten thousand shares of Tk. 100/- each of which petitioners hold 1565 shares. The Company has as its fixed assets a tea garden. at Maijgaon, adjacent to Fenchuganj Fertiliser Factory, in the district of Sylhet and some movables in the garden. The running of this tea garden constitution the business of the Company. This tea garden was acquired out of the joint capital of the sons and daughters of late Khan Bahadur Waliur Rahman of Jalpaiguri. Its share-holding interests are limited to family members and under Articles 6 and 7 of the Articles of Association, its shares cannot be sold outside the family circles. According to the petitioners, the Company is a joint family business and is like a family partnership. The petitioner No. 2 , Sayeedur Rahman is the full brother of respondent No. 2, Ahmedur Rahman, the Managing Director of the Company, and petitioner No. 3, Mahmuda Banu is the wife of petitioner No. 2, while petitioner No. 1 Mahmudur Rahman and petitioner No. 4 Imtiaz Banu are the son and daughter respectively of petitioner No. 2. It may be noted that, petitioner No. 1 is one of the Directors of the Co. Out of six Directors.

2. In their application for winding up the petitioners have alleged that the mismanagement and maladministration of Respondent No 2 have led the Company to a position where, as on the date of the presentation of his petition the Company is unable or is deemed to be unable to pay its debts. That owing to the effective control being exercised over the Company is unable for a number of years last past, as Managing Director, respondent No. 2 has gained control over other share-holders other than these petitioners and has been running the. Company arbitrarily, capriciously and whimsically rendering these petitioners into a minority group ignoring their demands to place the accounts before meetings of the Board of Directors and to give the actual picture as to the happenings in the garden. Relations between the majority group led by the respondent No. 2 and these petitioners have come to such a pass that this family business can no longer be run with amity and harmony and it is just and equitable that the Company should be wound up.

3. As evidence of their case that the Company is unable to pay its debts and that it is just and equitable to wind up the Company the petitioners lave stated, infer alia, that the Company has no working capital to run its tea garden and which was being run against loan taken from a Bank, namely Pubali Bank for the last several years. The assets of the tea garden are completely mortgaged to the Bank and the yearly crop is hypothecated against the loan which was being adjusted by deposits of sale of tea, but from 1971 onwards the Bank overdraft (i.e. loan) has not been adjusted. The present liabilities of the Co. from 1972 upto 15-7-74 as shown by the original statements of the Bank, Annexure A. stand at Tk, 24,92,375.30. The audited balance sheets of the year 1971 and 1972, marked Annexure B and C, show a heavy recurring annual loss of Tk. 6,74,474.26 and Tk. 7,30,434.71 respectively, and that there are arrear Income Tax dues of Tk. 9,14,824.54, sundry liabilities of Tk. 1,21,421.91 and unpaid dividend declared and partly paid for the year 1970 of Tk. 90, 000/-. Thus the total liabilities of the company on the date of presentation of this petitioner stands at Tk. 36,18,621.75.

4. Production of the tea was 8,657 maunds in 1966 which has been falling since 1967 and reached the rock bottom figure of 5,172 maunds in 1972.Total expenditure as per Profit and Loss Account for the year 1972, Annexure 'C' is Tk. 15,03,300.00, accordingly cost of production per pound of tea stands at Tk. 3.54 while the selling price is Tk. 3.50. The present production of 5172 maunds per year cannot be increased substantially within the next 5 years regard being had to the fact that unlike manufacturing industries, production cannot be increased overnight by additional investment as tea plants are to be pruned, manured, tended with great care with adequate rest periods and definite programme has to be followed over a number of years by which production can be gradually increased. Even assuming that production will go upto 5,500 maunds per year in near future, the Company canont per year in near future, the Company cannot earn more than Tk. 15 lacs per year, taking the selling price of tea at Tk. 3.50 per pound. So taking the annual expenditure at Tk. 15, 03,314.44 as per balance sheet for the year 1972 (Annexure 'C') the Company far from making any profit, will go on borrowing from the Bank each year for its working capital and will earn just enough, if at all, to pay for its expenses, and will perennially be unable to meet its present liabilities of Tk. 36,18,621.75 which amount will go on increasing because the said Bank charges 15% compound interest, further each year for the amount of working capital of Tk. 10-15 lacs that the Company will be obliged to borrow from the Bank will continue to add up to the Company's liabilities with 15% compound interest thereon. It may be mentioned that in the profit and oss account of 1972 Annexure (`C' shows payment of Tk. 1,24,527.71 towards Bank interest and charges and that of year, 1973 filed by Respondent No.2 shows payment of interest of Tk. 2, 04,378.59 as such, the accumulation of 15% compound interest each year for the borrowed working capital from the Bank does not appear to be convincing. The fixed assets of the company as per latest Balance sheet for the year 1972 stands at Tk. 10,30,192.92 and taking the depreciation each year into account these fixed assets cannot fetch a value more than Tk. 9,50,000.00 and that the current assets stand at Tk. 5,00,000-00. The Company has also puchased Income Tax Bonds of Tk. 22,400.00 and the cash balance stand at Tk. 1,02,820.98. The Company has shares of Tk. 21,44,500.00 in M/S W. Rahman Jute Mills Ltd. but as this Mill has been nationalised by the President's Order No. 27-of 1972, Bangladesh Industrial Enterprises Nationalisation Order, and although Article 9 thereof provides that the Government shall pay compensation in respect of shares of the Company as may be determined by it not exceeding the paid up value of such shares, this amount is not immediately available to the Company to pay its debts and as there is no knowing when the Government will pay compensation and what amount actually they would pay. It is a speculative, highly uncertain and indeterminate amount and is not immediately available to the Company to pay its debts and as such, no reliance can be placed on its for payment of liabilities.

5. On the facts stated above the petitioners submit that the Company is now wholly unable to pay its current debts of Tk. 36,18,621.75 as the existing and probable assets are insufficient to meet the existing liabilities and as such, it is commercially insolvent, and it is just and equitable that it should be wound up because it is impossible to carry on the business of the Company except at a loss as there is no reasonable hope that the object of trading at a profit for which it was incorporated can be attained.

6. The petitioners have further cited specific instances of gross mismanagement by respondent No. 2 as follows :—

a) Advancing Tk. 3,00,000.00 as share capital out Reserve Fund of the Company to Rahman Storage Ltd, in 1941 without the approval of the Board and without any security or interest which could be recovered with difficulty in 1967 as the said project ended in a fiasco, thereby causing a loss to the Company of huge sum of money by way of interest.

b) Advancing Tk. 12,24,670.00 for purchase of shares in M/S W. Rahman Jute Mills Ltd. for which, as per Promototer's Agreement, the Company was entitled to 6% interest. From 1964 to 1969 the interest due to the Company from the said Mill on the said sum stood at Tk. 3,75,000'00 which was never claimed by respondent No. 2 causing a huge loss to the Company deliberately.

c) Advancing Tk. 30,000/- to Marina Tea Estate and Tk. 5,000/- Manager, Dhamai Tea Estate, without any sanction of the Board, in the year 1971 at a time when the Company sustained a loss of Tk. 6,74,474-26.

d) Unauthorised advance of Tk. 2,56991 to Rahman Cold Storage, Tk. 5,025.73 to Rahman & C. (private) Ltd. and Tk. 26,800'00 to W. Rahman Jute Bailing Press, for which though the Audi-tors have recommended immediate adjustments (vide) Annexure 'B' and 'C' Yet the respondent No. 2 has taken no step to adjust the same.

e) Surreptitious and illegal manufacture by respondent No. 2 of 26,694 lbs of tea belonging to Rajnagar and Sakera Tea Estates at the Company's own factory without knowledge of the Board and without taking any step to recover the cost for the manufacture with ulterior motive for making illegal gain.

f) Respondent No. 2 has visited the tea garden in March, 1974 after the laps of 4 years and, as such, is not discharging his duties faithfully ;

g) Respondent No. 2 is reported to have sold tea and scrap iron while visiting the garden in March 1974 but has not placed the account thereof by convening's single meeting of the Board inspite of Notice by the petitioners. He never reports the financial position of the Company to the Board.

h) He has shifted the registered office the Company at his will twice in the last few years without any reference to the Board according to his personal convenience involving considerable expenses and creating confusion for the Company's business associates, commercial organisations connected with the Company, statutory bodies, Income Tax Department, Tea Board etc.

i) The fall in production of the gar-den and the bad quality of tea are due to his mismanagement as he does not give any guidance because of his lack of interest in the management and sitting over at Dacca.

7. The petitioners have further stated that because of their protest against the mismanagement of respondent No. 2 they have become eyesore to the respondent No. 2 and the majority share holders under his control, and all the legitimate suggestions of the petitioners are voted down in the Board meeting (where only petition No. 1 is a Director) and in Annual General Meetings.

8. No accounts for the year 1971 were even presented before the Board in 1972, although there was a loss of over Tk. 6 lacs as per Balance sheet of the year 1971. For willful and deliberate non-submission of the audited balance sheet before the Board and total absence of discussion on the Company's financial position these petitioners had to file T.S. 350 of 1972 in the Third Court of Munsif at Dacca against the respondents praying for declaration that the notice of annual general meeting dated 11-12-72 calling the annual general meeting on 30-12-72 was void, illegal, unauthorised and ultra vires. The said suit is still pending. There has been no meeting of the Board of Director in 1973 to discuss accounts of the year 1972.

9. The petitioner No. 1 also had to file T.S. No. 378 of 1973 in the Third Court of Munsif at Dacca against the Company including respondent No. 2 challenging the convening of the annual general meeting on 31-12-73 without putting the Auditor's report to the Board and without preparing any Directors report as illegal and has obtained an ad-interim injunction. This suit is still pending. The respondent No. 2 thereafter has filed an application before this Court, being Matter No. 7 of 1974, for condonation of delay in holding the Annual general Meeting in 1973 in which the petitioner No. 1 has appeared and filed his affidavit-in-opposition and the said matter is still pending.

10. The petitioners have also made grievance of their not being paid in full the declared dividend of 12%on the profits for the year 1970. They have been so far paid only 3 % dividend. Because of their insistence to pay it fully the petitioners have antagonised and been an eyesore to the respondent No. 2, and his group.

11. The above facts according to the petitioners go to show that the respondent No.2 with his group are locked in law suit and litigation with the petitioners. There is no love lost between them and this family business cannot be run with amity and harmony any more. Further the position that the minority share-holders (obviously the petitioner's group) are getting no return on their investment nor is any likelihood of getting in future.

12. On perusal of this application for winding up, when it was moved on 25-7-74, before Ruhul Islam, J, taking Original Side matters, his Lordship thought it fit to issue notice on Respondent No. 2, Ahmedur Rahman, the Managing Director of the Company, and to the Pubali Bank the main and major, so to say, the sole creditor to be reckoned with, of the Company, and to hear them before taking any action in the matter. Accordingly notices were issued and they have appeared and filed their statements on affidavit on 29-8-74 though separately against the prayer for winding up, but prepared and filed by the same learned Advocate, Mr. T. Islam and the learned Advocate Mr. Rafiqul Huq has argued the cases for respondent No. 2 as well as for the creditor, Pubali Bank.

13. The Creditor Pubali Bank, has opposed the application for winding up and has stated in its affidavit that the Company has been enjoying cash credit facility of this Bank since 1969 and the entire fixed assets of the Company were mortgaged with this Bank in 1969 as security for the loan, over and above hypothecation of yearly crops. The outstanding liabilities of the Company to the Bank under different accounts as on 30.6.74 and 22. 8. 74 are Tk. 24,17,365.30 and Tk. 25,31,768.89 respectively. The repayment during the period from 1971 upto date (i.e. 29. 8. 74 the date on which it has filed its affidavit) is Tk. 26,39,598.02. The Bank considers this repayment performance as very satisfactory as according to its view during the year 1971-72 there had been very bad period for all tea gardens in Bangladesh but even then the Company had repaid the aforesaid substantial amount towards liquidation of the loan including repayment of Tk. 7,48,714.35 in the year 1971 as per C. C. Account No. 28 and of Tk, 3,56,531.15 and 12, 570.31 in the year 1972 as per C.C account No. 28 and 57 respectively.

45. There is another important fact to be borne in mind. This is a share-holder's petition. It is true that as the law stands today, he is under no disability as compares with a contributory nor is he under any obligation, as he at one time was, to satisfy the Court that on a winding up there would!' be surplus assets. But there is a special rule that the courts have laid down in exercising their discretion in winding up a company on the petition of a share-holder. The Court constantly bears in mind that the internal management of the Company is its own concern, and it is a much better judge of business prospect of a trading venture than the court can ever hope to be. If, therefore, the majority of the share-holders show confidence in the management of the company and have faith in its future prospects, the court has rarely interfered. In 39 Boom 16, Macleod, J. Stated that a share-holder's petition must be scrutinized much more carefully than, a contributory's. In (1867) 2 Ch. The principle of these decisions is well stated in (1880) 14 Ch. D. 104, where James, L.J. stated (Page 109):

"Here a great majority of the share-holders are opposed to winding up, and desire to be left to manage their affairs for themselves.
