The second ground is C. (vi) of S. 1.62 of the Act limey, if the Court is of opinion that it just and equitable that the Company should be wound up.

<u>66. Under the 1st ground, namely, inability to pay its debts, petitioners case is based not on any current demands actually made by a creditor and the Company has not paid that or is unable to pay that, but is based on the existing state of liabilities of the Company which, according to the petitioners, the Company existing and probable assets are insufficient to meet, that is, the Company is Commercially insolvent (in re European Life Assurance Society, (1869) X.. R. 9 Eq. 122 (128). In considering the question of commercial insolvency the Court will have to take into. account the second ground as well, whether it would be just and equitable to wind up the Company and for that purpose amongst others the question whether at the date of the presentation of the winding up petition there was any reasonable hope that the object of trading at a profit, with a view to which the Company was formed could be attained (A.LR. 1936) P.C. 114 D. Davis Co. Ltd. V. Brunswick Ltd.).</u>

67. In order to substantiate their case on the ground of commercial insolvency the petitioners have made various allegations First, the company has no working capital to run its tea garden and runs its business by taking over draft from the Pubali Bank on the yearly hypothecation of the crop against the loan which is to be adjusted by deposits of sale of tea, but from 1971 onwards the Bank's overdraft has not been adjusted and the present liabilities from 1972 up to 157-74 to the Sank stand at Tk. 24,92,375.30.

<u>68. The Pubali Bank has stated in its affidavit in opposition that the company is enjoining cash credit facility of that Bank since 1969 and the entire assets of the Company were mortgaged with this Bank in 1969 as security for the loan, over and above, hypothecation of yearly crops. I do not find anything uncommon in the practice of hypothecating with a bank the yearly crops against cash credit facility and loans being gradually liquidated from the sale proceeds of the year. It is usual for a company to borrow money for running its business and is recognised under the Companies Act. Bank has stated that during the period from 1971 upto date (i.e. 29-8-74, the date on which it has filed its affidavit-in-opposition there has been a repayment of Tk. 26,39,598.02 which, according to the Bank is very satisfactory. This has been challenged by the petitioners in their affidavit-in-reply, according to them, cash credit facility is granted on an annual basis from year to year and i each year's account is to be adjusted within the year, if not, repayment cannot be said to be satisfactory. Loan for 1971 has been paid, as admitted by respondent No. 2 after 3 years and that of 1972 and 1973 still remain unpaid, repayment therefore cannot be said to be satisfactory. Granting of cash credit advances year after year without the advance of previous year being adjusted arc grossly against all commercial practices and is detrimental to the interest of the share-holders, the Bunk having fixed assets mortgaged to it not interested in Co's capacity to repay. The petitioners have further alleged in their affidavit in reply that the statement made by the Bank that the company is a solvent garden and financially better than i many other tea gardens in Bangladesh without substantiating it, is without jurisdiction and authority and shows an apparent collusion with Respondent No. 2 and actuated with a motive to rescue respondent No. 2 and to cover up Bank's irregularities in sanctioning cash credit advances to the Company without adjusting advances of previous year and the fact that the statement on affidavit of the Bank as well as respondent No. 2 were prepared in the office of the same advocate and sworn by the same advocates on the same day clearly suggest such collusion and consultation between the Bank and Respondent No. 2.</u>

69. In its affidavit-in-opposition the Bank has clearly stated. that it does not want that the Company to be wound up, as, in that case the interest of the Bank, which is a nationalised Bank, will be seriously affected as its security will be deteriorated and desires that the Company should be allowed to continue its business as the Bank expects that in due course Company's dues to the Bank will be liquidated. Bank is the better judge of its own interest and if it thinks its interest would be better served in supporting the respondent, I see no reason, why its taking a defence, even in consultation with respondent No. 2 and by engaging the same learned Advocate, could be interpreted as collusion. Of course, it has a separate entity as a creditor and usually maintains that position by independent advice. Obviously, its interest is to get the money, which it has advanced by way of loan, in the normal course of the banking business although the entire assets of the Company stand mortgaged to it. Its apprehension that its interest will be seriously affected as its security will be deteriorated if the Company be wound up cannot be ignored. In winding up under just and equitable ground the Court will have greater regard to the interest of the creditor than that of the share-holder and greater weight is to be attached to their views. See A.I.R. 1971 S.C. 2600. Messrs Madhusudan Gobardhan Das & Co. Vs. Madhu Woolen Industries Private Ltd., Supra quoting Palmer's Company Law, 21st Edition, page 742. In this case Pubali Bank is not only a creditor, but admittedly the only major Creditor. It is also a fact that the petitioners hold approximately 16% of the share-holding and that the rest of the share-holders, according to the petitioners own admission belong to the group of Respondent No. 2 and support him, and, as such, it is evident that majority of 84% of the share-holding interest show confidence in the management of the Company and do not support the petitioners. This fact, as well, has to be taken into consideration in ordering winding up. See A.I.R. 1942 Bom., 231, In re Cine Industries and Recording Co. Ltd ; A.I.R. 1968 S.C. 722, Seth Madan Ltd Vs. Grain Chambers Ltd., Muzaffarnagar ; A.I.R. 1956 Pepsu 89, Fatech Chand Kad Vs. Hindsons Patialal Ltd. (interest of the general body of share-holders is a matter of primary consideration in such cases) A.I.R. 1962 Guj 269, Mohanlal Dhanji Bhai Mehta Vs. Chunilal B. Mehra (as between share-holders wishes of majority shall prevail) ; Supra. 70. As regards the income Tax dues of Taka 9,14,824/- the Respondent No. 2 has contended and which has not been denied, that the amount involved are subject a matters of different appeals before the appellate authority and Tribunal. Unless and until they appeals are disposed of the payment cannot be made. In the circumstances, in my opinions this liability cannot be treated as presently due and cannot be a consideration for winding up on a charge of insolvency. The Income Tax Act has provided a machinery for realisation of taxes and if the Company made defaults certificate proceedings would have been started for non-payment of taxes. No such proceedings have been alleged to have been started against the company. A.I.R. 1965) Cal. 98, In re Sulekha Works Ltd ; see also A.I.R. 1952 Cal. 323 (DB), Mohammad Amin Brs. Ltd. Vs. Dominion of India, Supra, where application for winding up was adjourned awaiting results of I.T. Appeals which were pending although the application for winding up was filed at the instance of Revenue Authorities.

71. As regards, sundry liabilities of Tk. 1,21,421.91 an examination of items in Schedule ‘L’ of Annexure 'C' Audit Report for the year ended 31st December, 1972, will show that it is very common to have these liabilites. The petitioners have not taken any exception to them.

<u>72. Regarding unpaid dividend of Taka 90,000/- for the year 1970, Respondent No. 2 has stated in his affidavit in opposition that because of sudden set back in 1971 the declared dividend could not be paid and asserted that the payment will be made in due course. That the year 1971 was an abnormal year, there is no doubt about that. Further the fact that dividends had not been paid regularly is no ground for winding up the Company. See A.I.R. 1932 P.C. 1, The Ripon Press and Sugar Mills and Co. Ltd. Bellary Vs. V. Gopal Chetti, Supra.</u>

73. Another important fact which has a great hearing in considering the assets of the Company, is the amount of Tk. 21,44,500.00 invested as shares purchased by the Company in Messrs W. Rahman Jute Mills Ltd. This Mill has been nationalised under the President Order No. 27 of 1972, Bangladesh Industrial ill Enterprises Nationalisation Order f. Petitioners case is that although Article 9 of the said Order provides that Government shall pay compensation in respect of shares of the Company as may be determined by it not exceeding the paid up value of such shares, this amount is not immediately available to the Company to pay its debts as there is no knowing when the government wile Day compensation and what amount actually they would pay. No reliance can be placed on it for payment of liabilities.

74. Respondent. No. 2 has stated in his affidavit, on the other hand, that this amount cannot be treated as speculative nor uncertain and indeterminate rather it is a must and should be taken into consideration and has averred that the compensation money may be received very soon and the compensation rule is expected to be announced very soon. it is true that the amount of compensation money and the time when it will be received is not certain, but it is not disputed as to the payment of compensation, the amount may be less but the probability of getting an equal amount in near future none the less cannot be ruled out, and; if so, the financial condition of the company would be much improved. I am of opinion that it is a probable asset and should be taken in to consideration in determining the assets and liabilities of the Company. If the Company be wound up on hypothetical consideration that the compensation money will not be available and it turns out tomorrow that the compensation money is actually available an anomalous and preposterous position will be created. Further, as the amount of compensation is a matter of great importance it is desirable in the interest of both share-holders, as well as, the creditor that the Company's case as to the amount of compensation should be cogently and effectively put in order, that the compensation Received may be as large an possible and the proper persons for that purpose are the Directors of the Company, who can extract the maximum advantage out of it, which can only be done by keeping the Company going. See A.I.R. 1962 Bom. 133,In re Bilasraj Juharmal and (1947) 2 All. E.R. 104, In re Eastern Telegraph Co. Ltd. as quoted therein, Supra.

75. Let us now consider the petitioners case that it is impossible for the Company to carry on the business of the Company except at loss as there is no reasonable hope that the object of trading at a profit for which it was incorporated can be attained. The circumstances relied on are that the production of tea which was 8,657 maunds in 1966 has been falling down since 1967 and reached the rock bottom figure of 5,172 maunds in 1972. Cost of production per pound of tea stands Tk. 3.54 while selling price is Tk. 3.50. There is no likelihood of substantial increase within next 5 years as unlike other manufacturing industries, production cannot be increased overnight by additional investment. Even assuming that production will go up to 5,500 maunds per year in the near future, company cannot earn more than 15 lacs taking selling price at Taka 3.50 per pound. So taking annual expenditure at Tk. 15,03.314 as per Balance sheet for the year 1972, company will go on borrowing each year from the Bank for its working capital without being able to satisfy it and will perennially be unable to meet its present liabilities of Tk. 36,18,621.75, which amount would go on increasing for the accumulation of Bank's interest each year.

76. Respondent No.2, on the other hand has contended that production of tea was very much affected during 1971 as most of the laborers and Babus left the garden due to Pak Military operation in the garden. moreover the period 1972-73 was very bad time for tea growers in Bangladesh because of dislocation of export of tea, as more than 50 % of the tea used to be exported to former West Pakistan (now Pakistan), and the Government had to grant subsidy to the tea manufacturers at the rate 50 paisa per lb. in 1972 and at the rate 30% of the gross sale proceeds in 1973. These facts have not been denied by the petitioners in their affidavit in reply. Banks overdraft could not be liquidated due to this difficulty. Respondent No. 2 has submitted that position of tea industry is gradually improving with the gradual exploration of export market and the temporary setback in 1971, 1972 and 1973 will be fully recovered.

77. The petitioners, however. have challenged the above expectation of the Respondent in their affidavit in reply and have asserted that as per Bank's affidavit the company has an outstanding liability of Tk. 25,31,768.89 as on 22-8-74 to the Bank; it has borrowed 212 times more than its fixed assets and its paid up share capital. It has no money to run its affairs and it cannot meet its expenses far less the outstanding liabilities. It may be mentioned, that according to the Respondent No. 2, the fixed assets which has been valued at in the balance sheet is not the real value-book value is not the real value (and it is to be revalued) its present market value would be 50 lacs.

<u>78. That there were financial crises in the year 1971 to 1973 for the tea gardens of Bangladesh, there is no doubt about it and has not been challenged by the petitioners. What has been challenged by them is that the financial situation as it is prevailing the company will not be able to stand on its leg because there is no chance of trading at a profit. It is not for the Court to decide about the future prospects of the Company on its own views as to probable success or failure. But the problem involved is of the nature of a business problem. If there was at the relevant time a reasonable hope of tiding over the period of deep depression and emerging into a region in which the company might reasonably expect to carry-on at a profit, there would be no sufficient reason for the Court to wind up the company. See, A.I.R. 1936 P.c. 114, D. Davis Co. Ltd. Vs. Brunswick (Australia) Ltd. Supra, which also laid down that the onus is on the petitioner to prove that there was no reasonable hope that the object of trading at a profit was not attainable. See also A.I.R. 1941 Pat. 603, Sudhiya Nath Bhaduri Vs. Bihar National Insurance Co. Ltd., Patna; A.I.R. 1942 Bom. 231, Messrs. Vanaspati  Industries Ltd. Vs. Firm Prabhu Dayal Hariram; Supra. It may be mentioned that the learned Judge, Chagla, J. in the latter case, namely A.I.R. 1942 Born. 231, has expressed his doubt on the proposition of law bid down in Halsbury's Laws of England. Vol. V.  Halissham's edition  P.547 Art.885 to the effect that it may be just and equitable to wind up a Co. where it is carrying on business at a loss and its remaining assets are insufficient to pay its debts. In A.I.R. 1965 Ker 241, V.V. Krishna Ayer Sons V. New Era Manufacturing Co. Ltd. Palghat, Supra, it has been also observed:</u>

<u>"The principle laid down by Lord Cairns in In re Suburban Hotel Co. (1867) 2 Ch. Ap.737. that it is not permissible to argue from the mere fact that company has consistently made losses in the past that it has no reasonable prospects of earning profits in the future has been repeatedly affirmed and the decision itself has been taken to have established the fact that a company "has lost, is lose and will continue to lose" docs not of itself justify winding up order, at least when the capital has not been exhausted".(page 248).</u>

<u>79. In the instant case right from its start in 1954 up to 1970 the Company did not suffer any loss and during that period, it is not denied that it had paid a total dividend of about 300% to the share-holders, but from 1971 to 1973 due to financial crisis arising from abnormal circumstances causing dislocation in export market it has been suffering loss. Under these circumstances can it be said that the petitioners have been able to prove that there is no reasonable hope of tiding over the period of deep depression and the object of trading at a profit cannot be obtained keeping in mind that the Govt. itself have granted subsidy to keep the tea industry going? I am of opinion, in the facts and circumstances of the case that the petitioners have failed to prove that. The financial position of 1971 and 1972 should not be the criterion to adjudge the solvency of any Company in Bangladesh, particularly, if it is a tea Company, when the situation was very abnormal Mere loss in two or three years do not make the company commercially insolvent.</u>

80. In this connection a very relevant question has been raised by Mr. Rafiqul Hoque on behalf of Respondent No.2 regarding the locus stand of the petitioners, namely, they being fully paid up share-holders cannot maintain their petition alleging the company to the Insolvent and that it was just and equitable that the Company should be wound up. He has referred to (1879) 11 Ch. D. 36, in re Rica Gold Washing Co; (1966) 1 AII.L.R. 145, In re Other Construction Ltd (1966) 1 All E.R. 877, Re Expanded Plugs Ltd. and also to Buckley's Companies Act, 13th Edition.

81. In (1879) 11 Ch. D. 36. In re Rica Gold Washing Co., it was held that a fully paid lip share-holders who presents 2 petition for winding up the company must both allege in his petition and show by evidence that there are assets of the company of such an amount that ill the event of winding up he would have a tangible share or surplus as to receive.

82. In this case, Jessel, M.R. described the position of a petitioner holding fully paid shares as follows:

"He is not liable to contribute a anything towards the assets of the company, and If he has any interest at all, it must be that after full payment of all the debts liabilities of the Company there will remain a surplus divisible among the share-holders of sufficient. Value to authorise him to present a petition" (page 	42-43).

83. In (1966) 1 all E.R. 145, Re Othery Construction Ltd. a pennon was filed by a share-holder of 33. Fully paid up shares out of total shares of 1.00 10 the Company alleging that the Company was insolvent and that it was just and equitable that the Company should be wound up by the Court. It was held following the decision of (1879) 11, Ch. D. 36 (Supra):

''Where a fully paid up share-holder petitioned for a compulsory winding up a prima facie probability" that there would be a surplus of assets available for distribution among share-holders, or that the affairs of the company required investigation in respects which were likely to produce such surplus and as this petition alleged that there was a deficiency of assets, it would be dismissed" (Head note).

84. In (1966) 1 All. E.R. 877, Re Expanded Plugs Ltd., the petitioner, as a contributory, sought a compulsory winding up of the company on the just and equitable ground. The evidence showed that there would be no surplus available for distribution among share-holders. It was not disputed that the Company was in substance a partnership between the petitioner and another share holder. Applying the general principle as stated in (1879) 11 Ch. D. 36 and (1966) I All ER. 877, (Supra) it was held the petitioner had no locus standi to present a petition as a contributory since there was no surplus available for distribution and analogy with a partnership did not confer on the petitioner the locus standi that he lacked by company Law, accordingly winding up order would not be granted."

85. Backley, on the Companies Act, 13th Edition, 1967 at page 466 has said; "If the Company's assets are insufficient for payment of its debts a paid up share-holder has no interest. If he presents a petition he must allege and prove, at least to the extent of a prima facie case that there are assets of such amount as that in the winding up he will have a tangible interest. Semble, these principles are not affected by S. 225 (1)"

86. Mr. Mostafa Kamal, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, has contended, referring to S. 170(1) of the Companies Act, 1913 that such a rigid stand against a petition by fully paid up share-holder basing his case on the ground of insolvency cannot be justified. In this connection he has also referred to Palmer and Halsbury's on the point. S. 170 (1), Companies Act, 1913 which is almost similar to S. 225(1) of Companies Act, 1948 of England, runs as follows:

"On hearing the petition the Court may dismiss it with or without costs. Of adjourn the hearing conditionally or unconditionally, of make any interim order or any other order that it deems just, but the Court shall not refuse to make a wilding up order on the ground only that the assets of the Company have been mortgaged to an amount equal to or in excess of those assets, or that the Company has no assets."

87. Halsbury's Laws of England, 3.rd Edition, 1954, Vol. V. at page 541, describes the position of a fully paid up share-holder as follows:

"A fully paid up share-holder, may as a contributory, present a winding up petition and the Court cannot refuse to make a winding up order on the ground only that the assets have been mortgaged to an amount equal to or in excess of those assets or that there are no assets; but a contributory is not entitled to an order in such a case where there is no ground for a winding up order except insolvency and the pennon is opposed by other share-holders. In any case the Court has discretion and may refuse to make an order on a contributory's petition where the circumstances do not justify a winding up order. The Court will more readily make the order if the contributory alleges and proves that there is a reasonable probability of a surplus being left for distribution amongst share-holders."

88. In Palmer's Company Precedents, Part 2, 17th Edition (I 960) at page 43-44, the learned author has observed:

"A fully paid up share-holder is it contributory; and as such, entitled to present a winding up petition. It was held in several cases before 1907 that being under no further liability, he must satisfy the Court that the will be a substantial surplus of either actual or probable assets divisible among the share-holders; but S. 29 of the Act 1907 (now S. 225(1) provides that the Court shall not refuse to make a winding up order on the ground that the company has no assets. This section appears to apply to a contributory's petition. It is desirable, if possible however, to allege the existence of assets available for contributors. A contributory will not, however, be entitled to an order, if the sole ground for the petitions" Petition is insolvency, though it is otherwise where there is a case for investigation or other good grounds for a petition (underline is mine).

A contributory, unlike a creditor, is not entitled to a winding up ex debitojustiliae as between himself and an insolvent company."

89. In this connection reference may also be made to A.I.R. 1942 Bom. 231, In re line Industries and Recording Co. Ltd. (Supra), where Chagla, J, as his Lordship then was held that a share-holder is not under any obligation to satisfy the Court that on a winding up there would be surplus assets. But there is a special rule that the Courts have laid down in exercising their discretion in winding up on the petition of a share-holder, namely, that the internal management of the Company is own concern, and it is a much better judge of business prospects of a trading venture than the Court can ever hope to be. If, therefore the majority of share-holders show confidence in the management of the company and have faith in its future prospects, the Court has rarely interfered. The learned Judge has also referred to 39 Bom. 16 same case A.I.R. 1914 Bom. 190 In re Pioneer Bank Ltd. (1867) 2 Ch. A. 737; In re Suburban Hotel Co. (1871) Ch. A 641, In re London Subarban Bank; and (1880) 14 Ch, D. 104, In re Middles-borough Assembly Rooms Company

90. Similarly in A.I.R. 1965 Kerala 241, V.V. Krishna Ayer and Sons V. New Era Manufacturing Co. Ltd., Palghat, Supra, it has been. observed that a fully paid up share-holder even of an insolvent company is entitled to bring an application for winding up, but as he has no interest in winding up, because he has nothing to lose by the continuance of the Company and nothing to gain by its winding up, the Court is not readily moved to exercise it discretion by a person who is not really aggrieved unless he can make out a very special case indeed and the ground of company's inability to pay its debt is virtually unavailable to him.

<u>91. On a careful reading of the ruling and authorities discussed above together with S. 170(1) of our Companies Act, the position seems to be that a petition for winding up by a fully paid share-holder on the ground of in solvency of the company per se cannot be said to be not maintainable, but the Court looks askance at such petition as his interest is least affected in winding up being a fully paid share-holder there is nothing to lose by the continuance of the company and nothing to gain by its winding up The Court will therefore, seldom use its discretion in such a case unless the petitioner makes out a special case or there is a strong ground for interference justifying the use of its discretionary power on just and equitable ground. In this context I am tempted to quote the observations of Gower in his book on "The Principles of Modern Company Law", 2nd Edition (1908), page 596.</u>

<u>"Winding up is the ultimate remedy of the investor or creditor. If the winding up is by the Court all interests can be sure of even handed justice but at a price which may be heavy. Moreover, It IS justice according to law and shareholder should only invoke this remedy if satisfied that the legal rights attaching to their shares will give them a good slice off the goose which might have laid a golden egg had they not killed it."</u>

<u>92. The fact, that the majority of the shareholder, on the petitioners own admission, in the present case, support the Respondent No.2, shows their confidence in the present management of the Company and that they have faith In its future prospects, is also a very important consideration whether winding up should or should not be granted in such a case.</u>

<u>93. I do not find any special case or strong ground for interference justifying use of court's discretionary power to wind up on Just and equitable reasons, and in facts and circumstances of the case this petition by fully paid up share-holders on the ground of insolvency should also fail.</u>

<u>94. The petitioners nave alleged various acts of mismanagement on the part of respondent No. 2 which I have already detailed earlier In stating the petitioners case and the answers given by respondent No.2 have also been stated earlier in details. These allegations, if they are admitted to be correct, are at best irregularities in the management on the part of the Respondent No.2, which are subject matter of the domestic forum, namely the Board of Directors of the Company and not of the Court. The share-holders are the better Judge as to whom they would rely for management of the Company. These allegations may very well the learned Advocate for respondent has contended be made subject matter of investigation by the Registrar under section 137, sub 5(6) of the Act at the instance of the petitioner and also u/s. 138 of the Act by the Inspector appointed by the Government. However, I do not like to express any opinion on It.</u>

95. It appears from the allegations that. petitioners protest against the alleged mismanagement have antagonised the Respondent No. 2 and his group, the rest of the majority shareholder under his control against the petitioners, and they being majority they turn down all the suggestions and protest that are being made in either Board's meeting or in general meeting. The petitioners are thus reduced to a minority, and had to take recourse to suits against the company and management for non-submission of audited balance sheets which are still pending. One of the suits, namely, T.S. No. 378 of 1973, in which an injunction was issued restraining the holding of the annual general meeting on 31-12-73 of the company, has resulted in filing an application under section 76 and 79 (3) of the Companies Act before this Court for condo nation of delay by Respondent No.2 being Matter No.7 of 1974 in which the present petitioner No. 1 appeared and contested. It may be mentioned that matter has been heard by this Court along with this petition and this Court has allowed that application.

<u>96. These allegations cannot in my opinion also be treated as an oppression of minority by the majority. It is a question of internal management and it is the right of the majority to carry on the management. The petitioner No. 1 is one of the Directors out of six there is no allegation that the directors of the Company are misbehaving themselves. Respondent No. 2, the Managing Director, is but one of the Directors out of six and holds only 337 shares out of 10,000 shares in the Company he call at any time be removed if the other share-holders think that for the benefit of Company he should be removed. No collusion also has been suggested between the majority share-holders, other than the petitioners, and Respondent No.2, ousting, petitioner No.2 from the Management nor do I find in their conduct something to an injury of which the minority have a right to complain unreasonable, something like tyranny, something amounting (1880) 14 Ch. D.104 as quoted in A.I.R. 1942 Bom 231, Supra. Mere fact that differences have arisen between petitioner's group and the respondent No. 2's group over the management causing bitterness and that the petitioners are outvoted in the affairs of management by itself is not sufficient to lead to the conclusion that a deadlock has arisen in the affairs of the Company (See A.I.R. 1962) Born. 133, In re Bilasraj Juharmal)</u>

97. The petitioners have further tried, from the alleged strained relationship between them and the Respondent No. 2's group, to show that in the company which is a family business situation has arisen similar to that entitling the partners to dissolve their partnership In this context the learned Advocate for the petitioners have cited 17 D.L.R. (S.C.) 52, Shri Ladli Prashad Jaiswal Vs. The Karnall Distillery Co. Ltd. (1916) 2 Ch. D. 426, In re Yenidje Tobacco Co. Ltd. (1935) 1 Ch. D. 693. In re Davis and Collect, Ltd. which I have already discussed earlier As noticed there, the two latter decisions have also been referred in 17 D.L.R. (S.C.) 52, in which it has been held that in the case of a private limited company the tendency of the court has uniformly been to treat it more or less as a partnership and to apply the same principles in the winding up of a private limited Company as would entitle a partner to have a partnership firm dissolved. Commonly the exclusion of a partner from the management of the firm, the existence of a state of deadlock between the partners, or the justifiable lack .of confidence in the management have been regarded as just and proper grounds for dissolving a private limited company.

<u>98. In the present case, the petitioner No.1 have not been excluded or ousted from the management, he has not been excluded from any Board's meeting as a Director or from general meeting. If his suggestions are not accepted by others it is merely a case of his being outvoted, where others like him have every right to accept or not to accept his proposal. The petitioner does not reveal any circumstance which could be interpreted as resulting in a deadlock in the management of the affairs of the company. No justifiable lack of confidence, in my opinion, on the conduct of Directors in the management of the affairs of the Company can also be reasonably drawn from instances of alleged mismanagement on the part of Respondent No.2 cited in the petition.</u>

<u>Considering all the aspects of the case, I am of opinion that the petitioners have failed to make out a prima facie case justifying an order of winding up and therefore it is not a fit case for this court to admit it and to proceed further directing advertisement in the newspaper for further hearing which unnecessarily is bound to do enormous mischief and injury to the Company which is a running concern at a time when it is passing through a critical period of financial crisis  A.I.R.1914 Born.190, In re Pioneer Bank Ltd. A. I. R. 1959 Bom. 170 Western India Theatres Ltd. V. Associated Bombay Cinemas Ltd; A.I.R. 1965 Cal. 98, In re Sulekha Works Ltd; Supra.</u>

<u>In the result, this application is summarily rejected.</u>

End.

lawyer:
Fazlul Karim, Advocate, instructed by S.S. Huda, Advocate-on-Record ----- Far the Appellant. 
B.N. Chowdhury, Advocate, instructed by A. Rab-II, Advocate-on-Records ----- For the Respondent No.4. 
Ex-parte ----- For the Respondents No.1-3
Faqeer Shahabuddin Ahmed Attorney-General instructed by A.M. Khan Chowdhury, Advocate-on-Record-As Amicus Curiae.
parties:
Ayub Ali Howladar ----- Appellant.
Vs.
Election Tribunal Bagerhat, Khulna and others ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Kemaluddin Hossain, J.-This appeal is by special leave obtained by the appellant against the decision of the High Court Division dismissing his writ petition.

The writ petition was directed against an order of the election Tribunal 1, Bagerhat, in Election Tribunal case No. 22 of J 974 wherein the election of the appellant as the Chairman of Chingrakhali, Union Parishad, P.S. Morrelgonj, Khulna held under the Union Parishad and Paurashava election Rules, 1974, was declared void.

2. Parties called their evidence and also the. Tribunal requisitioned ballot papers from the authority but all papers were not sent, some were sent in very bad packing. The Tribunal felt sore about the callous manner of preservation of ballot papers and want of co-operation of the authority. The withholding of some ballot papers has resulted in appellant missing 97, and respondent, 826. And this has given rise to a knotty question in this appeal, the tribunal however on evidence found that there was no proper counting because of insufficiency of light. In support of his finding, he took into consideration that more than 5a deed and absentee votes were shown to have been cast in favour of the appellant. He held the Returning Officer wrongly counted 88 invalid votes as valid in favour of the appellant. After excluding invalid votes, he found the margin between the respondent Nani Chandra and the appellant at 38, which was less than the invalid votes cast for the appellant. He therefore concluded that the result of the election was materially affected for improper counting of votes and so declared the election void as a whole.

3. The appellant moved the High Court Division for the issue of a mandate in the nature of certiorari, but was unsuccessful. The High Court Division did not find any error apparent on the face of the record calling for interference. The appellant thereupon obtained special leave from this Division to consider three questions: Firstly, whether casting of some false voles without any clear finding that they were cast in favour of the appellant would be a ground to nullify the election Second. Whether the Tribunal in the absence of 97 ballot papers for the appellant and 826 for respondent Nani Chandra could act upon the ballot papers before it, and when the appellant was not responsible for the missing of those ballot papers Third Whether the Tribunal in compliance with Rule 61A followed the prescribed procedure of the Code of Civil Procedure in conducting the trial.

On a notice from this Division the learned Attorney-General has appeared and we had had the advantage of hearing learned arguments from the Bar.

Mr. Karim for the appellant at the time of hearing has abandoned the third question nor do we find any alleged procedural error committed by the Tribunal.

4. Two questions remain for consideration. We think that the second question should be discussed first. The question is, if at the trial before the Tribunal, all ballot papers cast in the election could not be produced by the election authority, and none of the parties to the proceeding is responsible for their non-production, and even though the missing of the ballot papers is post election affair, yet what is the duty of the election Tribunal to deal with the problem in such circumstances?

5. Record shows that the Tribunal called for all the ballot papers. Some ballot papers in very bad package arrived, but a large number was missing, 97 for the appellant and 826 for the respondent Nani Chandra. It also appears that the attempt to get missing ballot papers has failed.

6. Mr. Karim's contention is that, his client is not responsible for the missing of the ballot papers. In the absence of entire set of ballot papers, it is not possible or proper for the Tribunal to act on incomplete and insufficient ballots. According to him, this missing of ballot papers has taken place after the election. Post election fact cannot relate back to nullify the anterior fact of election. The tribunal ought not to have taken note of incomplete ballot papers, but proceeded on the presumption of regularity of official acts under S. 114(c) of the Evidence Act. Mr. Karim contends that there is every possibility that, had all the ballot papers been produced, the number of invalid votes in favour of respondent Nani Chandra might have been greater and the margin of difference in favour of the appellant increased instead of decreasing.

7. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury for the respondent Nani Chandra argues, that each ballot paper is an independent piece of evidence, and therefore rightly admitted into evidence and if from the ballot papers produced, a margin of difference decisive against the appellant could be spelt out it could be done in law. He further submits that presumption of regularity has been amply rebutted, when the tribunal found that quite a large number of invalid votes were cast in favour of the appellant.

8. The learned Attorney-General-referring to Rule Nos. 40, 42, 44 and 81 submits ballot papers are no doubt; good pieces of-evidence in an election dispute and the tribunal is to proceed on the presumption of regularity of official business under S. 114(c) of the Evidence Act. But this presumption is tribunal. It is for the tribunal to say, whether the evidence produced is sufficient to rebut the presumption under S. 144(e) of the Evidence Act. The qua-tum of evidence necessary to rebut the presumption is a question more of fact than law.

9. Some decisions have been cited from the Bar. They are: Niaz Ahmed Vs Azimuddin 19 D.L.R. (S.C.) 388; Abdus Sattar Rana Vs S.M. Zaidi, 20 D.L.R. (S.C.) 292; Rahis Mia Vs. K.A. Khan 22 D.L.R. Meat 909; Sam Sewak Jadav Vs. Hussain Kamil Kidwai 1964 S.C.A. (II) 553 A.I.R. 1964 S.C. 1249.

10. All the learned counsels have frankly conceded that cited authorities have little bearing on the question before us. We are to decide the question with the reference to the electino Rules and the rule of evidence on the subject. Some of the relevant election rules may be mentioned. Rule 34 provides for the manner of voting; Rule 35; the voting procedure; rule 36, how tendered votes are to be dealt with; rule 37, challenged ballot papers and rule 39, spoilt and cancelled ballot papers. Rule 42 says, inter alia, the Presiding Officer shall enclose and seal into separate packets ballot papers valid, spoilt, cancelled, used, and tendered, and the counterfoils of the used ballot papers Rule 44 provides among others that, the Returning Officer shall forward to the Sub-divisional Officer in a box or gunny bag; properly secured and sealed so as to ensure that. nothing is removable from the box or bag without breaking the seal, the documents received by him under rule 42 from the Presiding Officer with a statement containing the list of documents. Rule 81 says, on the expiry of sixth month from the date of the declaration of results of election, or, if an election petition has been filed under rule 56, as soon as possible after the disposal of the petition, the ballot papers and the sealed covers containing the books of unused ballot papers and the books of counterfoils shall be destroyed.

<u>11. A reference to the rules indicates that ballot papers are the principal pieces of evidence for adjudicating the validity of election, both for the purpose of declaration and trial. Rules also show that ballot papers in aggregate will decide the result of election, nonetheless each ballot paper is separate and distinct, and it stands or falls on its own merit. Aggregate valid ballot papers will no doubt decide the result of election, but then the aggregate cannot be treated a unity. This being the legal position of ballot papers, non-production of some will not render the ballot papers produced inadmissible. Mr. Karim's contention that non-production of all ballot papers has rendered the papers produced inadmissible cannot be sustained. That does not however support the submission of Mr. Chowdhury that the papers produced will rebut the presumption of regularity, and for the non-produced papers the said presumption will subsist. This is approbation and reprobation and cannot be accepted.</u>

12. We find that the question turns upon the sufficiency of evidence. It is a question of fact and will be determined on the facts of each case, and no hard and, fast rule can be prescribed. If the ballot papers produced are sufficient to adjudicate the disputed claims between the rival candidates, the Tribunal can proceed to decide the issue between the parties. But when the papers produced are small and the papers not produced large and adjudication is not possible, the Tribunal will not act upon ballot papers produced; but then the ground will not be one of admissibility but of adequacy of evidence. In the total absence of evidence of ballot papers, when none of the parties is responsible for their non-production the Tribunal may act on the resumption of regularity of official act under S. 114(c) of the Evidence Act. But this presumption of regularity is a rebuttable one. What should be the quantum of evidence to rebut this presumption will depend upon the facts of each case.

<u>The quantum of evidence is more a question of fact than law and therefore within the discretion of the tribunal to consider. The Tribunal in the present case committed no error in admitting the ballot papers that were produced before it. It has not founded its decision solely on this aspect of the case and so the consideration for sufficiency of evidence did not arise.</u>

<u>13. We may now turn to the first question involved in this appeal. Mr. Chowdhury for the respondent Nani Chandra has rightly pointed out that the conclusion of the Tribunal was based not solely on the question that 88 invalid votes were counted in favour of the appellant. He says this evidence was considered to reinforce his conclusion that there was no proper counting of votes in accordance with rules 40 and 41. He has also shown that of other reasons, one was insufficiency of light and the other was that many dead and absentee votes were shown to have been cast in favour of the appellant. It therefore appears that on the combination the evidence and circumstances the declaration of nullity was made. It is true that taken in isolation mere casting of dead or absentee votes without any evidence that they were cast in favour of the appellant will not invalidate the election but there can be no denying the fact that they are serious irregularities and violation of election rules and the Tribunal can and must take them into consideration to determine, whether the result of election has been materially affected by such irregularities. The Tribunal in the instant case, on evidence, has held so. Mr. Karim has very little to say in this regard. It cannot now be challenged in this Division.</u>

<u>We do not find any error in the conclusion of the Tribunal, or in the decision of the High Court Division. The appeal is therefore dismissed with costs.</u>

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Decree dated 9.4.90 passed by the High Court Division in Second Appeal No. 33 of 1973 with Civil Rule No. 77(S) 1983).
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal J : This appeal by leave by the defendant appellants is from the judgment and decree of a learned Single Bench of the High Court Division dated 9.4.90 in Second Appeal No. 33 of 1973 allowing the appeal, setting aside the judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka dated 10.8.72 in Title Appeal No. 94 of 1971, and restoring those of the learned Munsif, 3rd Court, Dhaka dated 31.5.71 in Title Suit No. 144 of 1964, decreeing the suit.

2. Three sets of plaintiff-respondents, plaintiff Nos. 1.-11, plaintiff No. 12 and plaintiff No.13 filed the suit for a declaration of title in respect of 48 acres, .09 acres and .1876 acres of land respectively of CS plot No.128, now SA plot No. 1357 at mouza Nutun Paltan Line, JL No. 250, PS. Lalbagh, District Dhaka contending, inter alia, that the suit land is their ancestral property consisting of homestead and kutcha houses where they reside with their family members on payment of rent to and upon obtaining rent receipts from the Dhaka Collectorate peacefully, quietly and without any interference or obstruction either from the Government or from any other person or persons. Besides the plaintiffs and their family members, many other destitute persons have been residing on the same plot for a long time in kutcha huts on payment of rent to the plaintiffs. Defendant No. 2, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Dhaka has been unlawfully issuing notices to the plaintiffs since 1962 under Government Lands and Buildings (Recovery of possession) Act, 1953 asking them to vacate the suit land on pain of forcible eviction. The plaintiffs' representations to the concerned authorities were of no avail and defendant No. 2 again issued scores of notices on the inhabitants of the suit land directing them to quit and vacate the same by the 16th June, 1964 in default of which they would be evicted by force. The plaintiffs filed the suit in 1964 asserting that they are the hereditary owners of the suit land and had obtained tenancy right therein under the Government. They paid rent to the Government upto 1962 where after the staffs of the Acquired Estate refused to accept the same.

3. The defendant-appellants contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the land of CS plot No. 128 was handed over by the Public Works Department to Khas Mahal Department on 31.12.1914 under order of the Government by Memo. No. 2881 dated 1.7.1914. Since then the Khas Mahal Department managed the same by giving temporary eksona lease for agricultural purposes vide Khas Mahal Settlement Case No. 38/40. During the wholesale acquisition in 1956 Khas Mahal Department was amalgamated with the State Acquisition Department and during the change of administration in 1956 some unauthorised persons took advantage of the transitional period and constructed some unauthorised sheds on the said plot and the plaintiffs are also some of them though they have no right, title and interest over the suit land. In accordance with the PRR received from the Settlement Department the tahsil office issued some provisional rent receipts. But since detection of wrong recording the realisation of rent has been stopped after 1962 and the PRR is to the process of correction. It is contended by the appellants that the plaintiffs trespassed into the Government Khas land in 1956 and they have not acquired occupancy right either.

4. At the trial the plaintiffs examined 3 witnesses, of whom PW 1 is plaintiff No. 2 and PW 3 is plaintiff No. 13. The defendants did not examine any witness nor adduced any documentary evidence.

5. The trial Court decreed the suit on the finding that Ext. 1 series, the rent receipts, some of which relate to the years 1936, 1938, 1940 1942, etc. establish a relationship of landlord and tenant between the plaintiffs and the Government from before the State Acquisition Act. Ext. 2 series, the SA Khatians, were prepared in the name of the plaintiffs as tenants which are the best evidence of possession and a conclusive evidence against the Government. The defendants have not produced any paper to substantiate their case that the plaintiffs were trespassers from 1956 or that the Government granted eksona settlement before State Acquisition Act. The trial Court also

accepted the oral evidence of PWs. 1, 2 and 3 and found the plaintiffs' long-standing possession in the suit land.

6. The lower appellate Court dismissed the suit on the finding that the plaintiffs failed to disclose either in the plaint or in their deposition as to how their predecessors got the suit land from the Government. Although PW 1 (plaintiff No. 2) stated in his cross-examination that the suit land is a wakf land of Masjid and Mazar the plaint is completely silent about the fact. PW 2, the only witness examined by the plaintiffs other than themselves, cannot be relied upon, he being ignorant about almost anything else that he was asked to answer. The rent receipts particularly Exts. 1-1(d) were not proved formally by anybody and the trial Court also failed to consider whether Exts. 1 and 2 series were collusive and fraudulent papers.

7. In Second Appeal a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division set aside the findings of the lower appellate Court by elaborately discussing Ext. 1 series, the rent-receipts, accepting them and holding that those were formally proved by PW 1 and were not challenged by the defendants and that the plea of collusion or fraud in obtaining them is not available to the defendants. Exts. 1 (e) to 1 (i) are proper rent receipts from 1936 to 1942 issued from the Khas Mahal Department in favour of some of the plaintiffs. SA khatians contain usually the names of those who have documents of title and possession in the lands and Ext. 2 series, the SA khatians, prepared in the names of some of the plaintiffs, are no exceptions. The plaintiffs also produced Ext. 3 series, tax receipts issued by the Dhaka Municipality and Ext. 4 series, Union Parishad tax receipts of 1961-62 showing the plaintiffs' possession of the suit land. Relying upon the case of Erfan Ali vs. Joynal Abedin Mia 35 DLR (AD) 216, the High Court Division found that notwithstanding the absence of any direct document of title the plaintiffs or their predecessors were accepted as tenants first by the Khas Mahal Department and subsequently by the Government and the plaintiffs have been in continuous possession of the suit land. It was not always necessary previously to settle land by executing a registered document but a settlement could be made by taking rent and issuing rent-receipts. The plaintiffs have been able to produce rent-receipts from 1936 up to 1961. The High Court Division reconsidered the evidence of PWs 1, 2 and 3 and found that the plaintiffs have been able to prove their continuous possession of not less than 85 years.

8. Leave was granted to consider the defendant-appellants submission that the High Court Division acted illegally in decreeing the suit for declaration of title merely on the basis of provisional rent-receipts, when the plaintiffs totally failed to prove any basic document of title in their favour and also erred in law in considering the rent-receipts as collateral evidence of title. Leave was also granted to consider whether the High Court Division rightly applied the ratio decidendi of the decision in 35 DLR (AD) 216 in the facts of the present case. Lastly, it was submitted that the High Court Division committed an error of law in reversing the final findings of fact of the lower appellate Court in second appeal when the judgment of the lower appellate Court suffers from no error or defect in the procedure.

9. Mr. AW Bhuiyan, learned Additional Attorney-General appearing for the Government, submits that the lower appellate Court's finding that Ext. 1 series, the rent-receipts, have not been formally proved by anybody has been wrongly reversed by the High Court Division.

10. As already stated there are three sets of plaintiffs. Plaintiff Nos. 1-11 lay claim on Schedule-A land comprising 0.48 acres of CS plot No. 128, plaintiff No. 12 lays claim on Schedule-B. 0.9 acres of land of the same plot and plaintiff No. 13 lays claim on Schedule-C 0.1876 acres of land of the same plot.

11. The plaint does not contain any genealogy of the plaintiffs. There is no description of the predecessors of the plaintiffs and it nowhere appears they belonged to the same family or families. Plaintiff No. 2 deposing as PW 1 nowhere says that he was deposing on behalf of all the plaintiffs. He proves the rent-receipts and the SA khatians by saying" I have filed rent receipts and the parcha marked Exts. 1 and 2 series". Plaintiff No. 13 deposing as PW 3 speaks about his interest in only 'C' Schedule land and without there being any references to any exhibits. PW 3 says that "we paid Union Municipal tax and I have filed the papers". Plaintiff No. 12 claiming only schedule-B land, did not appear as a witness at all, nor any witness was examined on his behalf.

12. The trial Court has not at all discussed how the rent-receipts are connected with all the plaintiffs or their predecessors. The High Court Division, in respect of Exts. 1 (a) to 1(d) says "these were issued in the names AD-2 of different persons who are very much parties here" and in respect of Exts. 1(e) to 1(i) it says that "those were issued from 1936 to 1942 from the Khas Mahal Department in favour of some of the plaintiffs here". Regarding Ext. 2 series the High Court Decision says "these SA khatians are in the names of some plaintiffs and their predecessors.

13. It is thus clear that the lower appellate Court took the correct view that the rent-receipts and the S A khatians were not formally proved by anybody. There is no clear finding from any Court which rent-receipts of what period stand in the name of which plaintiffs. There is no knowing what is the name of the predecessor of which plaintiff and which receipts stand in the name of whose predecessor. In such a vague state of affairs a declaration of title is the last thing that a Court of law will grant.

<u>14. The absence of a document of title in favour of the plaintiffs is an admitted fact, but both the trial Court and the High Court Division found from the rent-receipts, especially for the period from 1936 to 1942, the SA khatians and the tax receipts that the Government accepted the plaintiffs as its tenants.</u>

<u>15. There is absolutely no averment in the plaint as to the kind of land that the plaintiffs took possession of as far back as in 1936. Rule 209 of the Bengal Government Estates Manual, 1932 provided as follows,</u>

<u>"Town Khas Mahal lands consist of urban lands not used or likely to be used for agricultural purposes. They are governed by the Transfer of Property Act and not by the Bengal Tenancy Act except where lands though used for non-agricultural purposes now were originally leased to raiyat who had subsequently acquired occupancy rights. Agricultural lands within a municipal area, leased for cultivation, are not included within town khas mahals land."</u>

<u>16. Then there are "Government Estates" the settlement of which was governed by Rules 65 and 66 read with Rule 85 of the said Manual, 1932. Some formalities were required to be observed in granting settlement of either "Government estates" or "town Khas Mahal lands". Mere payment of rent to Khas Mahal Department may be a collateral evidence of title, but a collateral evidence does not assume the character of direct evidence of title. In the case of Elan Ali vs. Joynal Abedin 35 DLR (AD) 206, relied upon by the High Court Division, the plaintiffs had a sale deed Ext. 2 as a direct evidence of title. The provisional rents-receipts were only used as collateral evidence of title, not as direct evidence of title. In the present case, both the trial Court and the High Court Division made the mistake of treating the rent-receipts as a collateral evidence of title without asking themselves where, then, is the basic evidence. The suit land being Government khas mahal lands could not be leased out either permanently or on a yearly basis without there being some evidence of some formalities, either available with the plaintiffs or kept in the records of the Government. If the suit land was a "Government estates" then as per Rules 65 and 66 of the said Manual, 1932,"the initial settlement of all khas lands in Government estates is the duty of the Collector" and "all lands and holdings available for settlement are entered in Register VIII (rule 31)". As per rule 85 the tenants shall agree to a rent in writing or by thumb impression and shall also pay salami and execute kabuliyats when kabuliyats are necessary. If the suit land was a town khas mahal land certain formalities are required to be observed under the said Manual, 1932 both for short-term and long term leases.</u>

<u>17. Except for producing some rent-receipts Exts. 1(e) to 1(h) from 1936 to 1942 the plaintiffs have failed to produce any tangible evidence of settlement of suit land with them by the Government by following any of the procedure laid down in the said Manual 1932. It must be borne in mind that the plaintiffs were not claiming tenancy under a private landlord but under the Government, not under the Bengal Tenancy Act or the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act but by virtue of settlements from the khas Mahal Department. In the absence of any record of settlement by way of observing any formalities provided in the different Rules of the said Manual, 1932, the plaintiffs cannot be given a declaration of title over the suit land merely on production of collateral evidence. The High Court Division committed an error of law in this regard because even on the finding of formal proof of the rent-receipts and the S.A. khatians the legal conclusion from the so-called proved facts does not follow. The rent-receipts after 1942 are coming from 1958 (Ext. 1(c) and there is no explanation what happened to the intervening years from 1943 to 1957.</u>

18. With regard to the plaintiffs' possession of the suit land for 85 years, as found by the High Court Division, PWs. 1 and 3 being plaintiffs themselves are expected to beat their own drums, but PW 2 who is not related to the plaintiffs was not relied upon by the lower appellate Court on giving cogent grounds. The High Court Division did not touch upon those objections and accepted the evidence of PW 2 as that of independent witness. This was an unwarranted interference in a second appeal over the assessment of evidence by the lower appellate Court which is the final Court of fact. The lower appellate Court's finding on the plaintiffs possession has therefore been wrongly interfered with by the High Court Division.

19. For all the above reasons, the appeal is allowed. No costs.

End.

Md Shahidul Alam Chowdhury, Advocate  --- For the Respondent No. 1.
